We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness.

We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it with established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in accurately selecting variables and recovering relevant structures.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to strategically crafted malicious inputs, prompting the development of countermeasures against query-optimization attacks. Our research diverges from previous studies by exploring the vulnerability of DNN models to Man-in-the-Middle attacks. From an attacker's standpoint, conventional adversarial attacks prove ineffective as they necessitate multiple interactions with the model prior to execution, whereas MitM attacks can launch without this limitation. Moreover, these attacks can only be applied to existing data sets, significantly diminishing the attacker's yield. Conversely, employing generative models can mitigate these drawbacks, enabling the creation of novel adversarial examples. Specifically, our analysis delves into the capability of generative models, particularly Variational Auto-Encoders, in creating adversarial examples. Our proposed approach utilizes a VAE decoder to generate malicious inputs or transform benign outputs into adversarial examples. Our results show that our method enables successful MitM attacks on both MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets at an impressive rate, rivaling the effectiveness of existing query-optimization attacks. Moreover, our approach boasts considerable efficiency, executing 104 times faster than state-of-the-art query-optimization attacks.

Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories, particularly those found online. This research investigates prevalent conspiracy theories regarding climate change by analyzing a significant Twitter dataset and applies a sophisticated stance detection technique. Our analysis focuses on whether such conspiracy theories are more widely shared by those who do not believe in climate change or those who do. Furthermore, we examine the most popular conspiracy theories, their variations with differing levels of climate change acceptance, and reveal that non-believers predominantly disseminate messages containing conspiracy theory-related keywords. Notably, all conspiracy theories are not equally prevalent. Our findings also highlight their implications for effective climate change communication strategies.

A study focused on the production of dark matter in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV has been carried out using the CMS detector. This study analyzed a dataset of 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of collisions. It differs from earlier studies which focused solely on dark matter creation accompanied by a top quark pair by also investigating cases where a top quark was present individually. No notable anomalies were detected and as a result, upper limits on the mass of hypothetical mediator particles were established. Specifically, masses between 200 and 1600 GeV for a scalar mediator, and between 200 and 1000 GeV for a pseudoscalar mediator, were constrained. These limitations were derived by assuming the presence of a type-I seesaw mechanism and considering various valid coupling ranges. Apart from the mediation process, it is also demonstrated that the observed limits on dark matter production can be applied to models featuring vector mediators under certain conditions.

Given an n-exangulated category with specified properties, we establish that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality if and only if it possesses certain duality-based angles. We also determine a specific condition necessary for the presence of Serre duality. Assuming duality exists, we establish a one-to-one correspondence involving a bijection and specific category characteristics.

Building upon Kirkeboen et al.'s (2016) work that demonstrates the feasibility of combining multiple treatment instruments with ranked preference data, we analyze the testable implications of the key assumptions underpinning their identification argument. This analysis also offers a novel assessment of the biases resulting from these assumption violations. Ultimately, these findings empower researchers to evaluate the reliability of these assumptions and determine the practical impact of their breaches. Utilizing the identified method, we investigate the post-secondary field of study return on investment in Norway and Denmark, exploring differences between these two countries. Our results indicate that norwegian fields of study exhibit significant treatment effects, whereas danish fields of study show no effect or perhaps a slight opposite effect. These two countries' fields of study exhibit distinct behavior, with norwegian fields of study showing a moderate response and danish fields of study showing a strong but opposite response to an additional year of study.

To advance our understanding of matter's various forms, high-energy particle collisions with a wide variety of projectiles must be studied extensively.
Although scientists have utilized beams of numerous particles to make significant breakthroughs, creating and working with beams of antineutrons, specific hyperons and their counterparts has been notoriously challenging.
However, a recent high-tech research setup known as a super $J/\psi$ factory holds the potential to greatly improve access to these elusive particles. As a result, newly developed detection techniques and computational tools may soon enable scientists to measure elusive particle interactions more accurately. This, in turn, could lead to significant discoveries in high-energy physics.

Most of a multiple star system's final mass is accumulated during the first few million years of its existence, specifically during the protostellar and protoplanetary phases.  Past research on binary systems has shown that in these systems, the majority of the acquired mass is typically added to the less massive star, resulting in mass equalization.  Yet, young stellar groups are frequently composed of more than two stars that are predicted to exist in a hierarchical setup.  Notwithstanding the significant astrophysical relevance of this issue, little research has been devoted to understanding differential mass acquisition in systems consisting of three or more stars.  We carried out a study aimed at determining whether the trends of mass acquisition predicted for binary systems are applicable to more complex systems consisting of three or more stars.  Utilizing three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulations of the protostellar cluster formation process, we tracked the growth and mass acquisition of both individual stars and binary systems within a triad setup.  Our simulations reveal distinct differences in mass acquisition behavior depending on the relative masses of the less massive binary and the third system.  In systems where the less massive binary is significantly lighter than the third, the triad's final mass is evenly distributed, resulting in the addition of most acquired mass to the less massive binary, in accordance with previous findings related to binary systems. This manuscript examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes naturally incorporate geometric patterns suitable for describing irregular, periodically-distributed matter within the universe. We also establish mathematical proofs for their local representation, as well as the existence and uniqueness of the Einstein's equations under these specific spatial constraints. Notably, our research uncovers an interesting set of precise solutions, illustrating how these spacetimes can be used in cosmology to model a universe transitioning from homogenous, isotropic states in the early stages to more complex distributions with voids and matter peaks over time.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Mumford-Shah model, allowing for improved segmentation of gray-scale and vector-valued images affected by noise, blurriness, or missing data. Our model can be efficiently optimized using the alternating minimization algorithm, which converges under minimal conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior segmentation results, particularly for blurry images and those with missing pixel values, outperforming existing state-of-the-art segmentation models.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$).

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired systems poses a significant challenge due to its underlying hardware complexities. To overcome these challenges, a thorough comprehension of its fundamental building blocks is essential, coupled with the development of straightforward and user-friendly prototyping tools. To address this, an open-source emulator was designed, utilizing the Brian simulator and seamlessly integrating with existing workflows. This emulator successfully emulated error-free neural network behavior in software for individual neurons and networks of neurons connected in complex loops. Additionally, our research explored how neural networks with adaptive synapses can learn and adapt in response to external stimuli, including the formation of robust long-term memories through repeated training.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and on very short wavelengths. The dynamic evolution of these storm sources remains largely unstudied due to a lack of high-resolution imaging data in metrewave frequencies. By analyzing data from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA), this research identifies a new aspect of these storm sources associated with minor flares. It reveals the existence of two distinct modes of co-evolution: a "sausage-like" mode, in which storm intensity decreases while size increases, and a "torsional" mode, in which storm size changes correlate with sky-orientation changes. The researchers have also observed, for the first time in this context, the transition of these storm sources from the "torsional" mode to the "saussian-like" mode, facilitated by a flare. These findings support the theory of increased magnetic stress in complex active region structures that later collapse into instability, producing flares and particle acceleration until they stabilize into less complex states. The discovery may offer new possibilities for identifying such active region phenomena in the future.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that merges an optical grating chip and a magnetic coil chip. This novel setup minimizes the size and weight of the trap, requiring only a single laser beam to capture a population of approximately 10,000 cold rubidium atoms. The improved MOT architecture has potential applications in devices such as gravimeters, atomic clocks, and quantum memory systems, offering a reduction in volume, weight, and complexity.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established boundary conditions at a distant point, we examine this process with properties of the cloud specified within a finite sphere of radius. We use a series of models, ranging from simple to complex, to compute steady-state solutions, from Newtonian infall of radial particles to a general relativistic capture of angular momentum by particles in an elliptical orbit. We compare and analyze the mass accretion rates of these models, considering specific properties of the cloud such as its density and velocity dispersion. Our work also involves calculating the radial and radial-angular stress-energy flux components and the energy loss via gravitational waves, as well as the intensity of the black hole's electric and time components of the Weyl tensor, which represents the distortion of spacetime caused by the black hole and the cloud. We observe that models where angular momentum is involved show lower mass accretion rates than those without it, with the highest rate being roughly twice that of the standard Newtonian infall in our most complex model. Moreover, our findings suggest that a significant amount of energy is transferred from the cloud to the black hole via stress-energy flux and gravitational waves, as well as via the spin effects represented by the cloud's angular momentum and the conservation of angular momentum in the absence of a magnetic field. With our study, we provide a more realistic understanding of how a black hole grows by merging

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A longstanding issue regarding massive star origins involves whether these stars always form within dense clusters and, if found in less crowded environments, if they inevitably moved there.  Recent advances in wide-scale photometric surveys enable us to detect massive stars without bias in the less crowded regions of the galaxy.  This study examines forty candidate OB stars discovered by Mohr-Smith et al in the vicinity of Westerlund 2, with locations confined to a 1.5x1.5 degree square area, distinguished by their extinctions and K magnitudes.  Spectra from two extremely hot O stars show they are verified as O4V stars with masses exceeding 40 Msun.  Their velocity relative to Westerlund 2, measured against a binary-free reference point, is within specific km/s values.  Furthermore, with the aid of Gaia DR2 data on stellar motion, between eight and eleven O/WR stars might have been expelled from Westerlund 2 in the past million years, accounting for up to 25% of massive star expulsion efficiency, with their distribution showing near north-south alignment on the sky, implying a link between this outcome and sub-cluster unification coupled with the force of dynamical ejection.

This paper investigates the normalized ground state solution for a specific nonlinear equation. Specifically, we examine a problem involving a biharmonic operator and a Choquard type nonlinearity with a unique symmetry assumption. Leveraging a variational approach and a finite symmetry method, we have successfully identified the normalized ground state solution of the given equation.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper ageing and environmental factors, can cause severe readability issues for current text recognition algorithms. To overcome these challenges, we propose an innovative, end-to-end approach utilizing Generative Adversarial Networks that not only restores visual clarity but also improves the overall readability of the documents. This pioneering method differs from conventional binarization techniques, which primarily focus on enhancing visual quality, by integrating a text recognition module to optimize generated output. The effectiveness of this architecture was validated through comprehensive experiments conducted on Arabic and Latin handwritten texts, showcasing improved readability and visual quality. Additionally, our pre-trained model demonstrated exceptional performance on the H-DIBCO challenges, even after fine-tuning on synthetic, degraded text images.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation vital for optimal system performance, yet the IEEE 802.11p standard's limited pilots lead to inadequate channel tracking. As a result, conventional IEEE 802.11p estimators experience significant performance decline, particularly in high-speed scenarios. To overcome these challenges, researchers have explored deep learning (DL) techniques for channel estimation in IEEE 802.11p. Nonetheless, these approaches either underperform in extremely high-speed situations or exhibit substantial computational complexities. To resolve these issues, this paper introduces an innovative solution based on a long short-term memory (LSTM) model for channel estimation. The proposed method incorporates an LSTM unit for channel estimation, followed by a temporal averaging technique to mitigate noise, and analytically calculates the noise mitigation ratio to verify its effectiveness. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution surpasses the performance of recently proposed DL-based estimators, while also achieving substantial reductions in computational complexity.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging due to its inherently high degrees of freedom; when presented with an image, multiple plausible color combinations exist, and there may be no single definitive solution. Another related issue is Single Image Super Resolution, a task that involves converting low-resolution images into higher-resolution versions. This research targets a novel, automatic colorization approach, specializing in astronomical images and leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We experiment with employing various models in the RGB and L*a*b color spaces, relying on transfer learning and pre-trained ResNet-18 architecture, due to the small size of the dataset available. Our approach successfully produces aesthetically pleasing, high-resolution, and colorized results for images lacking these characteristics. The performance of the proposed model is quantitatively assessed by measuring distance metrics, including L1 distance and L2 distance, and by evaluating the generated images' realism and similarity to original images, utilizing the FID score and LPIPS metric, respectively.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently calculate Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) weights without relying on tedious iterative processes. Based on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our proposed algorithm rapidly achieves low error rates in the regression and classification of intricate datasets, such as the Griewank function and the MNIST database for image recognition. Its mathematical formulation allows it to accurately approximate highly complex nonlinear functions with a minimal margin of error, and it also facilitates the solution of Partial Differential Equations. The approach works by determining the weights for each neuron in localized data subsets where a corresponding approximation matrix remains invertible, thereby rendering hyperparameter optimization unnecessary. As a direct consequence, this minimizes the total computational time by an order of magnitude. With this efficient weight-computation scheme, ANN training can be expedited to the point where subsequent adjustments can be performed in real-time.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that the line waves produced can operate in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface integrated with an epsilon near zero substrate, which considers the effects of both dual and uniform reactive impedances.
However, this work specifically focuses on utilizing line waves in dual impedance structures.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged autonomy.  A new architecture for multi-agent LfD is introduced which enables the creation of reliable and efficient robotic systems in complex and large-scale environments by leveraging advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) through the implementation of a Federated Learning (FL)-based collaborative learning framework among humans and robots. This novel approach capitalizes on local edge computing and AI-driven data analysis amongst humans and robots to optimize robotic performance, while protecting user privacy by adhering to a decentralized strategy. A study was conducted at Amazon's Robotics Learning Lab to evaluate the new architecture's efficacy in real-world settings, specifically through a new application known as RoboDataplayer (RDP). Comparative analyses between the new architecture and conventional LfD methods demonstrated the former's superiority in solving complex tasks such as high-level navigation and motion planning within realistic environments. Thus, the new architecture offers a promising solution for building robust and autonomous robotic systems, particularly in multi-agent scenarios.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, offering a more efficient alternative to the standard estimate. The new estimator is both simpler and faster to compute than previous reductions of bias. The model can be applied to analyze a type of data that doesn't follow a normal distribution, and it has several applications in fields like medicine, social sciences, and economics. To evaluate the performance of the bias-reduced estimator, both theoretical analysis and simulation studies have been conducted. The bias-reduced estimator has been found to be efficient in practice, and these results have been compared to the standard estimate through both numerical computations and real-data applications.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been employed to solve the N-dimensional Radial Schrödinger equation for complex-valued potentials, and further generalized to consider finite values of anisotropy, temperature, and baryonic chemical potential. Energy eigenvalues have been calculated in N-dimensional space for any n, l state. These findings have been used to investigate the characteristics of quarkonium states, such as binding energies and mass spectra, in the N-dimensional space. Notably, anisotropy was found to decrease the dissociation temperature of quarkonia in the N=0 and mu = 300MeV ground state. In the oblate case, anisotropy resulted in a lower dissociation temperature than the isotropic scenario. Furthermore, introducing a baryonic chemical potential led to the conclusion that the leading-order Debye mass exceeds the quasi-particle Debye mass.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the difference in behavior between the two materials to the distinct magnetic characteristics of the two host elements, with one being a 4f and the other a 4f-5d hybrid material.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements in real-time geometry processing, these
representations are still unable to capture high-dimensional data, such
as real-world videos, due to increased computational complexity. In this
paper, we present an innovative solution by introducing an advanced MLP
architecture that efficiently processes high-dimensional data in real-time.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only labelled data. We're examining a special instance of covariate shift that also enables learning from unlabelled data, effectively merging adaptation with semi-supervised learning techniques. By drawing on causality concepts, we propose a novel method that requires learning from both the causes and effects of a target variable. This leads to the development of a semi-generative model, $P(Y,X_E|X_C,\theta)$, which is shown to be resilient against domain shifts in causal features. Moreover, this model leverages unlabelled data to directly map causes to their respective effects. Experiment results conducted on artificial data show considerable improvements in classification performance compared to solely-supervised and importance-weighting approaches.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric model for deep learning architectures by identifying connections to pre-existing geometric frameworks in quantum computation and diffeomorphic template matching. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm.

A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. To achieve this, the study uses a systematic approach to identify key factors influencing the network's predictions and incorporates 'expert' variables into a recurrent neural network to forecast future classification outcomes. Experimental results from testing on quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and additional jet data demonstrate that incorporating these expert variables enhances the network's performance, and that they possess a level of translency, simultaneously.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry groups were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical data on layer group symmetry was then tabulated and made accessible online.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir element are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate proportionally to 2ℏ/R, where R represents the sphere's curvature radius, yielding countable energy and momentum spectrums for freely moving particles. A theoretical maximum for possible momenta in S^3 corresponds to its diameter, the de Broglie wavelength λ_R = πR. Particles on S^3 possess wave-particle duality, with energy-momentum relations analogous to those on a flat plane, yet with additional physical characteristics resulting from the manifold's intrinsic curvature.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, the baryon composition involves two complex scalar fields, which form a chiral doublet. By incorporating these fields into the mass terms of the mesons, four of the Nambu-Goldstone Boson fields associated with the breaking of $Sp(6)$ can acquire a finite mass. Consequently, the remaining six degrees of freedom consist of three scalar bosons, three pseudoscalar bosons, and the Higgs boson, a W boson, and three fermion pairs. Notably, the interactions of the low-energy sector with the highest number of parts are consistent with the Standard Model, and the proposed model can be experimentally verified through the search for its signature in high-energy particle collisions.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current VPPM practices can inadvertently create vulnerabilities that may lead to physical harm. This study seeks to highlight the potential consequences of VPPM applications and dissemination as they stand today.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unknown details of proto-stars in binary systems. Specifically, mass measurements for binary components were taken at a distance of about 1,000 AU, demonstrating that the more massive star in each binary is generally observed at the center of the protostar. Furthermore, the total mass of the newly forming stars was found to directly correlate with the mass of the initial core from which they formed. Notably, it has been empirically determined that more massive cores produce more massive stars. Research on forming stars in binary systems, including those in the class 0 and 1 stages, has been conducted to explore how these objects form and to gain insight into the core formation process. 

In this study, spectral-line mapping was employed to identify the kinematic properties of a binary system named DH Tauri. Using data collected at 22 GHz for the $^{12}$CO, $^{13}$CO, and CSI 3 lines, it became clear that these lines follow the motion of the binary system's disk. Specifically, red-shifted lines indicate the direction of motion, while blue-shifted lines indicate counter-rotation. Since these lines are most prominent at the center of the protostar, it is proposed that they originate from near the center of the binary system's disk. 

Additionally, a CO isotopic ratio was calculated and found to be approximately 10 for DH Tauri. By comparing this value

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a localised, convexised representation of data distribution, resulting in sub-optimal performance. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach combines the robustness of arcsinh transformation with the generalisation capabilities of the Gaussian Kernel, yielding superior performance in comparison with existing methods, particularly for skewed data sets. Additionally, the technique's influence can be readily explored using partial dependence plots to monitor its impact on the separation of data components. The efficacy of the m-ar-K-FastICA method has been numerically validated through comprehensive numerical experiments, demonstrating its superiority to established methods like Kernel ICA and its variants. Furthermore, the technique has successfully addressed a practical challenge in the domain of spectroscopy, illustrating its potential for real-world applications through the analysis of a data set related to gas detection.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic system can identify unique, non-isomorphic graphs in a specific category, then a related proof system can do so as well, at roughly the same computational cost. This allows researchers to apply existing bounds from the latter system to the former, shedding new light on CPT's limitations. Establishing a polynomial CPT lower bound via a related PTIME-instance could resolve a long-standing question in finite model theory. Additionally, the findings provide a theoretical explanation for the separation between polynomial calculus and extended polynomial calculus within bounded-degree settings.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is defined as proper subrings set-theoretic union equating $R$. If such a collection exists, the ring covering number $\sigma(R)$ in $R$ is determined by the cardinality of a minimal collection, and a ring is $\sigma$ elementary when $\sigma(R) < \sigma(R/I)$ for any ideal of $R$, given it is non-zero, two sided and in $R$. The given text describes the discovery of first ring $\sigma$ elementary instances which possess non-trivial Jacobson radical $J$  and a ring that is non commutative in $R/J$, while determining ring covering numbers in $R$.

Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions linked to specific topics. By gaining insight into and visualizing these narratives, social media debates can become more informed and productive. To establish a systematic approach for identifying underlying narratives, we propose PAPYER, a comprehensive dataset comprising online comments about public restroom hygiene, marked by an abundance of unfalsifiable claims. A collaborative human-AI pipeline is presented that uses a combination of machine and human intelligence to pinpoint the prevailing narratives, thereby outperforming existing large transformer models and unsupervised topic models.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive event detection framework, capable of processing multiple social media platforms in real-time. It leverages a unified event model to consolidate diverse data from sources such as Twitter, YouTube, and Flickr. The approach incorporates a unified event representation learned through deep neural networks to resolve spatial and temporal ambiguity. Furthermore, it employs a distributed in-memory data store for efficient real-time processing. Evaluation on multiple datasets demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach. It is notable for its rarity of false positives and adaptability to diverse event configurations.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the usefulness of the weighted skew-spectrum as an optimal estimator of angular bispectrum amplitude in extracting non-Gaussian information on both galaxy bias and cosmological parameters, achieved by analyzing bispectra derived from galaxies and CMB lensing data simultaneously, resulting in significantly faster data processing times. We found that combining the Planck satellite and DESI will lead to a maximum $17\%$ variation in estimating galaxy bias and cosmological parameters when applying skew-spectra as opposed to bispectra. We confirm agreement between our theoretical models and those estimated using N-body simulations, where considering the gravitational non-linear effects from beyond perturbation theory and post-Born effect for CMB lensing data is essential. We also developed an algorithm to apply the skew-spectrum estimator and used it in preliminary analyses with simulated data through Markov chain Monte Carlo likelihood analysis to constrain bias parameters and the shot noise amplitude, suggesting that we might achieve percent-level estimates for the linear bias parameter $b_1$.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its subsequent dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Five methods (PCA, KPCA, ICA, AE, and DAE) are utilized to compress high-dimensional pixels down to 301 dimensions. The resulting pixels are used for classification, allowing a comprehensive assessment of each method's effectiveness based on classification accuracy, compression rates, and reconstruction errors. Our research employed three diverse hyperspectral image datasets (urban, suburban, and forest landscapes), gathered by the Remote Sensing and Spatial Ecosystem Modeling lab at the University of Toronto. Our analysis reveals that PCA, KPCA, and ICA methods preserve pixel signals well but show decreased classification performance beyond 90% compression rates. In contrast, AE and DAE achieve better results at 95% compression but see their performance deteriorate as the compression rate approaches 97%. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of considering both compression methods and rates when crafting an effective hyperspectral pixel classification workflow.

Neural networks are highly effective feature extractors but they pose significant challenges due to their large size. Understanding the parameters within various layers is complicated, resulting in the networks often being referred to as 'black boxes.' In contrast, simpler models are more interpretable but they are also much harder to find. Identifying and utilizing a sparse network that can be trained to replicate the same results is a viable option to improve network interpretability. According to the lottery ticket hypothesis, even large, dense neural networks harbor a smaller sparse sub-network that can be trained independently to achieve the same accuracy in the same amount of time. Our objective is to explore the existence of this trainable sub-network in the realm of natural language models, and we will accomplish this by examining and evaluating the most recent model compression techniques, such as quantization, knowledge distillation, and pruning.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the spatial arrangements of proteins. ProCS is calibrated with the help of high-resolution, experimentally determined protein structures. ProCS has demonstrated remarkable accuracy and speed in predicting amide proton chemical shifts across a wide range of proteins, achieved through the integration of a simplified, numerical description of amide proton NMR chemical shifts and efficient alignment techniques based on crystal structures. Comparison with other prediction methods available showed ProCS to be significantly more rapid, predicting about 200,000 residues in under 24 hours on a standard computer. ProCS's predictions have been found to be very reliable, with an average error of just 0.25 parts per million for nearly all amide proton chemical shifts. ProCS presents a valuable opportunity for precisely determining protein structures on a large scale, either by using experimentally determined structures as a starting point or by using the efficient molecular dynamics based alignment technique to arrange protein structures in a most conducive conformation.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

Describing the behaviors of complex systems comprised of strongly interacting elements requires concise expressions for their internal relationships. Ensuring the stability of these systems is the primary focus. Parquet theory is capable of achieving a level of self-consistency that encompasses all strictly pair-based interactions among elements. Grounded in a perturbative framework, the theory is comprised of a series of nonlinear integral equations that describe scattering events at all levels, constrained by principles of symmetry but also suffer from symmetry-related ambiguities. By imposing strict limitations on the scope of interactions, the vertex structure is heavily restricted, allowing for any scattering process to be fully understood with only a limited number of vertex configurations. The constraints of the theory can be expressed as a set of nonlinear equations in the language of Feynman diagrams, where certain types of diagrams are prohibited and others are heavily favored. The constraints of the theory can be expressed as a set of nonlinear equations in the language of Feynman diagrams, allowing for a wide range of physical scenarios to be accurately modeled.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction tool remains to be developed. To address this challenge, a new method was created that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory and many-body perturbation theory to study the critical behavior of exciton condensation. Applying this method to two models, the one-dimensional TiTe2 and the two-dimensional C2H3Cl, the calculated phase diagrams and critical temperatures match experimental results and outperform previous predictive models. This innovative approach enables the development of a critical endpoint in the phase diagram, which is a key milestone in the pursuit of achieving exciton condensates through natural material variations.

In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of one such organization, with a combined dataset totaling 107,486 messages, to explore content and timing of dispatchers' responses. Their findings reveal a disparity in response times, with higher-rated community members receiving faster responses from dispatchers. Furthermore, emotional support played a significant role, with responses to sensitive incidents timely but to other reports taking longer, indicating dispatchers prioritized incident severity and emotional consideration. Moreover, constructive responses from dispatchers increased the likelihood that community members would submit more reports in the future. These results identify valuable characteristics for developing effective, scalable community-driven safety systems and highlight the importance of emotional support in such systems.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised active learning approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a minimax framework. Our method incorporates a network that minimizes entropy and an entropy-maximizing classifier, while a discriminator is trained to distinguish labeled and unlabeled data. We then select the samples with the highest entropy that the discriminator identifies as unlabeled for human annotation. Experimental evaluation on image classification and semantic segmentation datasets demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in the Million Song Dataset using several elements, including
melodic quality, texture, volume, and rhythmic patterns. By analyzing the popular
hits listed on the Billboard Hot 100 and randomly selected songs, we found that
most hit songs tend to be musically straightforward with characteristics close to
the average. This discovery aligns with the theory that songs with moderate levels of
variety tend to be most appealing. Furthermore, we investigated the changes in
these song characteristics over time. Our analysis shows significant patterns of
change, including an overall decrease in song intensity since the 1960s, an
increase in song complexity in terms of musical textures overall, but a decline
in that complexity in hit songs. In contrast to the notion that popular songs sound
more uniform over time, we found that hit songs in 1969 sound just as diverse as
they do today in terms of melody and rhythm. However, using different analysis
methods and data sources yields some differing conclusions.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement involves sequences of random groupings denoted as $\{\mathcal{P}_t\}_{t \ge 1}$. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a continuously increasing set of items $\{1,2,\dots, Rt\}$. When time progresses to $t$, a fixed number of items $R$ are appended to this set; a fraction of these added items joins existing groups based on probabilities defined across different time intervals, initiating new subgroups separately from the ones that merged with existing groups. The items integrating existing groups make selections according to the group's current size proportionality, acting independently from each other. Theorems concerning the asymptotic quantities within specific groups are proved along with central limit theorems explaining deviations from the identified trends in relation to: individual subgroups' growth, and the subgroups' collective fluctuations in growth. The same set of theorems applies for the subgroups' collective fluctuations in growth when the greatest subgroup's growth in comparison to other subgroups is assessed. Our analysis shows that a single group, given an infinitely extending timeline, holds and maintains dominance over others through the course of its size progression, and this prediction has been translated into several other prominent stochastic processes - specifically: 'Balls and Bins', 'Generalized Chinese Restaurant Process', 'Generalized Urn Model', and the 'Preferential attachment random graphs'.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Our approach involves using these labeled segments to train a Gaussian Mixture model, which is then employed to impute a reward function from the human-labeled regions. Our method was validated through experiments in two practical scenarios: 1) identifying areas of interest in unexplored environments and 2) locating optimal pathways in unknown environment configurations.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids, specifically pointed vortex loops and their variations, within finite domains. These singularities, inherent in solutions at concentration points, pose both theoretical and practical challenges. Theoretical models often resort to limit processes to make sense of such singularities. In our work, focused on a closed domain with a rectangle as a surface and a specific prescription for the velocity field, we demonstrate that an approximation of the velocity field through singular value decomposition efficiently handles these singular points, even when distributed in a complex, high-order geometry.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal parameter that can be estimated in two steps, initially modeling treatment and outcome to incorporate potential confounders, then applying predictions to ATE estimators, such as AIPW, with potential alternatives being Machine Learning algorithms due to their non-parametric nature and capability to handle complex relationships. In order to improve the efficiency of two NN models with no parameter regularization except SGD, our simulations indicate the significant drawbacks that arise when AIPW is used. In an effort to improve this, the proposed nAIPW offers the same double robustness and first-order asymptotic efficiency as AIPW, while also possessing the same properties as AIPW. Additionally, when imposing l1 regularization on the first step NN models, nAIPW with l1-nAIPW yields consistent estimations and offers a more efficient alternative to l1-AIPW.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current research into lepton flavor universality violations in B-physics, warranting greater theoretical attention in the coming years. Enhanced data samples from Belle-II, as well as LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS, will be crucial in further investigating the topic. Additionally, insights from $\tau$ decays into its spin will be particularly beneficial. If experimental findings of new physics prevail, it is anticipated that new CP-odd phases will be required by naturalness arguments. Considering the relatively small $\tau$ mass compared to B-meson masses, it may offer a more tractable environment to probe the underlying theory producing these flavour violations.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and surface heat transfer, in a simple yet comprehensive arrangement. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the formation of baroclinic waves through adjustments in rotation rate and temperature differences between the wave pattern's center and periphery. Our analysis of these experiments sheds light on the sensitivity of wave development to specific parameters and offers a valuable comparison with numerical simulations of the quasigeostrophic equations, helping to validate and verify atmospheric circulation models.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalises the parameters, by minimising the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that deals with the challenge of learning a nearly optimal policy when a fraction of data in the training set has been compromised by an adversary. Our study begins by examining a worst-case scenario involving the linear Markov decision process and finding that even with the adversary only modifying the reward in each data tuple, a certain threshold of optimality gap cannot be avoided. Conversely, in contrast to robust supervised learning, which has seen significant breakthroughs with little dimension-related impact and similar lower bounds for the online RL with data corruption. Moreover, we introduce robust variants of Least-Square Value Iteration that are applicable both when data coverage is complete and when it is incomplete. These robust LSVO variants show promising performance, but in instances of data incompleteness, they require prior knowledge of epsilon - the fraction of data that has been compromised. Our work on robust RL with data corruption raises important questions and opens up new areas of research, while also highlighting the complexity of robust offline RL, necessitating more efficient and robust learning algorithms free from adversarial influence to achieve significant advancements.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm in real-world applications.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts, with both approaches underperforming when confronted with challenge data, underscoring a need for clearer definitions in method comparison.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors utilizing electric currents have been explored, and like Brownian machines, they generate directional rotation from random tunneling events. Despite their potential to drive molecular machines of the future, their theoretical modeling is understudied. Here, we create a mathematical model for simulating these systems and verify its validity by applying it to a renowned molecular motor, where the model accurately reproduces existing experimental findings. Furthermore, we utilize our model to extract hard-to-determine microscopic properties and examine the influence of non-unique direction of rotation.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we demonstrate the possibility of determining whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an equivalent one-way model, with a limit to how complex this transformation can be. Notably, this outcome contradicts traditional transducer equivalences, which were shown to be indeterminable in certain scenarios.

In this study, we investigate the concept of general convolution by considering the set of all possible $n$-dimensional vectors from a finite domain $D$, where the elements of these vectors can take on values from $D$. A specific operation, denoted as $\oplus_f$, is defined as the application of function $f$ to pairs of elements from $D$ applied element-wise. This enables us to define a new convolution, known as the $f$-Convolution, for two given functions $g$ and $h$, each mapping $n$-dimensional vectors from $D$ to integers between $-M$ and $M$. By applying $\oplus_f$ to pairs of $n$-dimensional vectors, $g \otimes_f h$ is calculated as the sum of the products of the function values of $g$ and $h$ for each possible pair. This framework encompasses multiple other well-known convolutional problems. A naive approach for computing $f$-Convolution would involve exhaustive enumeration, with an estimated time complexity of $\widetilde{O}(|D|^{2n}\mathrm{polylog}(M))$. In our main contribution, we propose an algorithmic improvement, demonstrating that $f$-Convolution can be computed in $\widetilde{O}((5/6 \cdot |D|^2)^{n}\mathrm{polylog}(M))$ time, for domains $D$

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a new analysis using multiple atmospheric models and a controversy surrounding its mass and orbital parameters, a best-fit atmosphere that matches spectra in the K-band was found, resulting in a estimated mass of $\sim$ 44.1 $\pm$ 2.2 M_J and an effective temperature of $\sim$ 650 K, with a reduced uncertainty of 25.4 $\pm$ 3.2 M_J and 40 K, offering improved constraints; however, a fit in the N-band yielded a higher mass of $\sim$ 52.8 $\pm$ 3.3 M_J and a temperature of $\sim$ 600 K, with a lower uncertainty of 28.4 $\pm$ 11 M_J. Although this analysis did not conclusively resolve the controversy surrounding GJ 229B's mass, a subsequent study suggested that the object's mass was likely within the range of 40-78 M_J, with a 68% confidence level, based on cross-correlation analysis, providing a potential solution to the mass uncertainty problem.

To search for the potential existence of the unique $0^{--}$ state, we created a systematic approach to designing tetraquark operators. In the process, we found that $0^{+-}$ tetraquark operators without derivatives are not possible. Due to the distinct Lorentz structure of the $0^{--}$ currents, it is prevented from incorporating corrections from four-quark terms into its spectral density, leading the gluon condensate to become the primary factor influencing the spectral density as power correction within the context of the finite energy sum rule. Our results from the sum rule analysis with the use of seven designed interpolating currents, however, indicate the lack of evidence to support a resonant signal related to the exotic $0^{--}$ state, leading us to conclude its absence below 2 GeV, in accordance with current experimental data.

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ caused by $\bar{b}\to\bar{c}c\bar{s}$ decays. The precise prediction of $\phi_{s}$ within the Standard Model makes it a favorable means for detecting signs of new physics. The experiment's $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_{s}$ measurements are discussed in detail, encompassing the 2011-2012 data set of 3.0~fb$^{-1}$. Future analyses are expected to contribute significantly through the incorporation of additional results derived from decay modes with reduced branching fractions.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we utilized numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties related to the transition of $^{137}$Te ($7/2^-$) to $^{137}$I with various final $J$-values. We conducted a comprehensive shell-model analysis based on a effective nuclear interaction and examined the influence of a particle-hole configuration. We compared our results to experimental findings showing good agreement. Specifically, we looked at matrix elements of the weak interaction, nuclear transition strengths, and energy differences between experimental and calculated $\beta$-decay energies. Our study highlights the reliability of shell-model simulations in understanding the intricate nuclear interactions governing $\beta$-decay attributes.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed methods to support multiple quantity trade requests and established fully formalized matching algorithms for double-sided auctions. These algorithms come with rigorous correctness proofs. Additionally, we formulated new theorems for verifying the uniqueness of a matching in the context of double-sided auctions, encompassing requests for both buy and sell orders. To achieve this, we created an original certificate that proves a particular matching is the unique best match under specific, pre-defined price rules. Our generated certificates enable the automatic verification of uniqueness through reasoning tools, allowing for a straightforward uniqueness test. Our work also introduces a novel notion of price consistency, which ensures that a double-sided auction has at least one matching quantity. We established a price consistency test using a fully formalized proof and showed that this test can efficiently verify the correctness of existing financial markets. Moreover, we explored how our results can be applied to more complex market scenarios, such as allowing for market participants to cancel their requests.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic structure, defined over a specific and limited character set. It is further established that Szabados's conjecture is true for a considerable class of non-regular patterns. This includes all low-convex patterns of relatively simple complexity.

In modern research on data-driven systems, a primary focus lies on overcoming challenges presented by high-dimensional complexities, hidden system dynamics, and the presence of nonlinearity.  The dynamic mode decomposition technique has proven valuable in creating models from large data sets, yet the effectiveness of this method diminishes in cases of highly nonlinear systems. Conversely, sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics is able to learn comprehensive models, but its capacity is limited by the size of the feature vector used. A new approach aims to combine the strengths of these existing methods. By employing a low-rank dynamic mode and developing a sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics framework, a high-dimensional nonlinear dynamic system can be efficiently modeled. The resulting system, which integrates sparse polynomial chaos expansion for handling nonlinearities and a low-rank structure for dimension reduction, can be employed for systematic uncertainty analysis and validation. The proposed method was evaluated through simulations of two complex systems, namely a laminar flow and a laminar flow with a cylindrical obstacle, resulting in highly accurate reconstructions and excellent performance in both high-dimensional and nonlinear dynamic contexts. Furthermore, the method demonstrated the effectiveness of utilizing sparse polynomial chaos expansion and confirmed the benefits of incorporating low-rank dynamic mode decomposition structure.

The timeless appeal of chess persists, with its strategic intricacies still captivating players across the globe, particularly when it comes to mastering the intricacies of Opening Theory which requires extensive knowledge and years of dedicated study. Our innovative approach harnesses the collective wisdom of online chess enthusiasts to provide insights previously reserved for expert chess players. Firstly, we establish a chess opening network that evaluates the similarities between different opening strategies. This helps us identify clusters of commonly used openings and their connections, insights not easily extracted from existing classification systems. Additionally, our model successfully forecasts future opening preferences and verifies these predictions against actual results, demonstrating superior accuracy over random forecasting. Lastly, by utilizing an advanced algorithm, we assess the level of difficulty for different openings and the skills required to execute them proficiently.
