We provide criteria to select these pivotal units under the given interference framework and conduct numerical experiments to assess the effectiveness of our method in detecting interference compared to existing methods that do not utilize predictions.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-destructing dark matter particles within a star are being conducted. In the core of a star that has not yet undergone nuclear reactions, it's observed that the interactions between these particles and the star's constituent atoms via a particular particle can produce an unusually high number of neutrinos, which may equal and potentially surpass those produced by the star's nuclear reactions early on. This process primarily involves two reactions: a collision of two dark matter particles resulting in neutrinos or intermediate particles that then decay into neutrinos, which may be confined to less than 1-2 percent of the star's volume and persist throughout the star's lifetime. This information is then used to assess potential impacts of this process on the cooling of a star in the context of existing constraints on dark matter particles.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data collection, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 40 million galaxies, translating to a density of 6.8 per square arcminute. A low-level systematic bias was found in this research, providing a groundwork for extensive cosmological studies when the full 4800 square degree survey is completed. Introducing ShapePipe, a cutting-edge pipeline leveraging Ngmix for precise galaxy shape detection and metacalibration for accurate shear calibration, the study extensively validates the pipeline through Point Spread Function, galaxy shape tests, and realistic simulations, confirming minimal systematics. Analyzing the shear two-point correlation function reveals a low-level systematics influence compared to cosmological contribution. Shear bias was found to be under 5 times 10^-4 and up to 10^-3 in residual multiplicative bias, confirming the efficacy of the pipeline. Using COSEBIs, no significant B-modes are detected in second-order shear statistics, displaying pronounced correlations between E-modes and known clusters, including the stacked tangential shear profile at higher than 4σ significance around Planck clusters.

A notable consequence of a finding made by Veech more than 50 years ago, relating to the mod $2$ form of the Kronecker-Weyl theorem, has to do with sequences of irrational rotations of the form $\{q\alpha\}$. In the event that a certain number $\alpha$ resists being closely approximated by rational numbers and another number $b$ in the interval $(0,1)$ differs from the rotation sequence for no integer $m$, then, as $N$ approaches infinity, the parity of the sizes of sets consisting of numbers of the form $\{q\alpha\}$ within the interval $[0,b)$ that correspond to $q$ values up to $N$ displays evenly distributed occurrences.

The text also discusses how it answers a query put forth by Veech, thereby providing a revised mod $n$ form of a prior result (as stated in Theorem 3.1). A characterization, based on specific values, of circumstances under which evenly distributed occurrences result (as stated in Theorem 3.2) is also proposed. Lastly, two separate conditions that ensure evenly distributed occurrences are presented (as stated in Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 3.4).

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and quantum Monte Carlo simulations using the experimentally determined parameters are employed to determine the critical temperatures associated with BKT transitions as well as long-range order. Finite-size scaling of the spin stiffness based on our in-plane theory shows a perfect match between theoretical and experimental critical temperatures, clearly indicating that the complex magnetic phase diagram of [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2 is determined by field-induced XY anisotropy and concomitant BKT physics.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model presents two possible dark matter creation mechanisms - the axion-like particles and the inert doublet bosons - either of which can account for dark matter density alone.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum circuits comprising Clifford and T gates. The efficiency improvement stems from deriving a novel upper limit for the number of stabilizer states required to express $m$ copies of the magic state, $|T\rangle$. The findings reveal that a superposition of no more than $O(2^{\alpha m})$ stabilizer states can accurately represent $|T\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\alpha\leq 0.3963$, surpassing the previous best-known estimate of $\alpha\leq 0.463$. This advancement allows for the development of a classical algorithm capable of approximating the output probabilities of $n$-qubit Clifford + T circuits $U$ within a specified inverse polynomial error margin, using a time complexity of $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)2^{\alpha m}$. The authors also establish a stronger bound on the stabilizer rank of symmetric product states $|\psi\rangle^{\otimes m}$, where $\psi$ is a stabilizer state, yielding $\Theta(m)$ in the worst case. This discovery leads to the creation of a sampling algorithm for approximating the global wave function $|\psi_0\rangle$ of near-classical hardware, resulting in an improved bound of $\epsilon^{-\frac{2\alpha m}{n}}$ for the relative fidelity between the sampled state and $|\psi_0\r

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting, to calculate essential parameters for the energy 
density equation of state within the FRW universe, analogous to a quintessence model.
We will reassess complex quintessence by modifying its potential and analyzing 
scalar field dynamics, followed by evaluating the differences in and stability 
of two scenarios, non-interacting and interacting.
We will examine the plausibility of these scenarios as real universe descriptions 
by calculating the fractional energy density, $\Omega_{D}$, and analyzing two parts 
of the universe, time-dependent and present.
We emphasize that $\Omega_{D}$ should be within the 0.5-0.75 range, as a value 
outside this range may indicate an anomaly in the data. 
We also emphasize that a real universe description should not exhibit growth and

We claim that the stability of two scenarios, non-interacting and interacting, can

Matter-momentum coupling behavior.
We claim that a real universe description should not exhibit debt and momentum

We claim that the differences in and stability of two scenarios, non-interacting and

debt and momentum anomaly.
We verify that the interacting scenario exhibits debt and momentum anomaly in the

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team constructed a binary catalog of around 2,700 candidates through the analysis of their light curves, radial velocity fitting, the extraction of

Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in specialized or general-purpose chips for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs provide an economical alternative to dedicated hardware TRNGs. Nevertheless, existing SRAM-based TRNGs suffer from reduced throughput, elevated energy expenditure, prolonged latency, and a limitation to generating random numbers in parallel. In order to overcome these shortcomings, this paper presents SRAM-TRNGarvd, an innovative SRAM-based TRNG designed to address all these problems. By utilizing a customized SRAM access sequence, SRAM-TRNGarvd enables the simultaneous generation of numerous random numbers through multiple memory banks, thereby enhancing its throughput, reducing latency, and increasing energy efficiency. A detailed explanation of the proposed architecture, along with experimental results from a produced prototype chip, is presented in this paper to validate its efficacy. A comprehensive analysis of the proposed chip's performance reveals that it surpasses state-of-the-art SRAM-based TRNGs in almost all aspects.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, a theoretical analysis was performed, integrating ab-initio electronic structure calculations with a general single-electron tunneling theory. The outcomes demonstrate that these tiny molecular constructs can process electrical signals at extremely high speeds while also storing information over extended periods and exhibiting a substantial ratio between active and inactive current levels. Additionally, simulations have shown that self-organized monolayers built from these molecules could also function as efficient resistive switches with comparable properties and the capacity to withstand flaws and irregularities in electrical charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. Recent research has focused on evaluating causal representations using functional techniques. This document, however, takes a different perspective by translating the causal representation into a form that can be directly computed using functional techniques. The report also addresses potential issues related to numerical stability and outlines a strategy for addressing these problems.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states, similar to analogous work done on Sturm-Liouville operators by renowned mathematicians. A related theory involving the CMV matrix already addressed this topic, yet our approach is unique as it focuses specifically on the mentioned quantum walks and also yields valuable properties of Green functions. These properties enable us to derive a precise formula for a positive-matrix-valued measure, ultimately allowing for a direct computation of the spectral measure in a particular model known as the two-phase model.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the coexistence of these phases. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical behavior within a linearly coupled $q$-deformed optomechanical system. Composed of two deformed cavities interacting with mechanical mirrors and coupled through tunable channels, this study reveals that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and scale of optical transformations. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that $q$-deformation can modify the boundary between strong and weak optical interactions, potentially enriching the study of optical phenomena near these boundaries. Additionally, the analysis of thermodynamic phase transitions in this system reveals that $q$-deformation can accelerate these transitions, but may also eliminate them, depending on the value of $q$. Finally, exploring possible applications of $q$-deformation in optomechanical systems, this study proposes that $q$-deformation could serve as a controlling parameter in optomechanical systems, potentially for using sound waves to encode quantum information.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

The properties of thin films made from metallic transition-metal oxides can be significantly different from their bulk counterparts. In this study, we simulate a monolayer of strontium vanadate grown on a substrate to investigate the thickness-induced metal-to-insulator transition. We found that two different terminations lead to the same insulating behavior at equilibrium but exhibit distinct behavior when doped or subjected to a gate voltage. Through many-body calculations, we revealed various nonlocal fluctuations resulting from antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, stripe, and checkerboard orbital ordering instabilities. By considering the role of orbital degrees of freedom, we explain how these instabilities emerge and demonstrate how ultra-thin film reconstruction and changes to coordination polyhedra result in unique material properties.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In the past, scientists discovered an extension of typical dynamics, resulting in "anomalous" diffusion that accounts for distributions characterized by long, power-law tails. One such physical system - laser-cooled atomic ensembles - offers an optimal platform to study such phenomena, primarily due to its distinctive friction force. This interplay between laser cooling and anomalous dynamics is likely to reveal profound and predictive insights into both equilibrium and non-equilibrium statistical physics. In experiments involving cold-atom systems, scientists can manipulate and adjust various system parameters to observe changes in the system's behavior, and this has been achieved by analyzing non-normalized states associated with rare events, utilizing tools derived from infinite ergodic theory, resulting in new findings.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on years 2020 and 2021. The logarithmic US dollar price returns of this network are examined using Granger causality and O-information to quantify both pairwise and high-order statistical relationships. The Granger causality results indicate peaks in significant events, while the corresponding network structure exhibits stability, with most influential nodes being cryptocurrencies. Contrasting with pairwise analysis, stable coins appear in few synergistic connections, but when considering high-order relationships, they dominate synergistic circuits, highlighting their role in higher-order effects. Furthermore, a high volume of total transactions in US dollars in the first semester of 2021 triggered a shift in the cryptocurrency network towards increased complexity. The study demonstrates that both pairwise and high-order approaches to financial systems offer valuable insights into cryptocurrency analysis.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturated conditions needed for homogeneous water droplet formation. The application of quantum chemistry in modeling this process has improved significantly due to its enhanced precision and efficiency in calculating the configuration of particles. Nonetheless, even advanced approaches continue to rely on the classical nature of nuclei, which is uncertain for many particles. The current study evaluates the influence of zero-point motion in the simulation of small clusters of sulphuric acid and water using path integral molecular dynamics at the density functional theory level. Generally, the incorporation of zero-point motion results in the distortion of the mean particle structure, promoting greater proton transfer than in their classical counterparts. The incorporation of zero-point motion in the simulation has implications for the understanding of particle dynamics, particularly in reactions, but its effect on the precipitation process is less certain due to the potential stabilizing effect it has on the particle's structure.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a cover over their codomain, resulting in new compact perception pairs that compactify their original counterparts, which possess totally bounded datasets. Moreover, we present compatibility conditions for these embeddings and demonstrate that they're satisfied by our constructions.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers investigate whether this analogy accurately describes the collective behavior of quantum Hall states and other chiral topological systems. By analyzing the Haldane model, which simulates different environmental conditions, they examine the consequences of two scenarios: one with variable gravity and electrostatic forces, and another with variable temperature and chemical potential resulting from interactions with surrounding electrons and phonons. The study reveals that this thermal analogy does not hold; while an uneven gravitational force induces specific energy flows, a comparable uneven temperature has little to no effect in systems that exchange energy with their surroundings weakly. Additionally, the similarity between an external electric charge and the system's internal energy potential is also invalid under these circumstances.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, such as regularization, hyperparameter optimization, and architecture planning. For deep learning models, understanding how complexity is controlled has been a challenging task, given that many conventional methods are unsuitable for their inherent complexity. Our research introduces a concept called geometric complexity, quantifying the variability of model functions using a discrete Dirichlet energy metric. By combining theoretical analysis with empirical evidence, we demonstrate that several widespread training heuristics, such as parameter and spectral regularization, as well as parameter initialization techniques, serve to control geometric complexity.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  Techniques such as transfer learning and data augmentation have significantly improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art models in this domain.  Past research has explored the potential of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and variants like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), among others, in solving automated essay grading.  Our study focuses on the effectiveness of transformer-based architectures, specifically BERT and RoBERTa, in conjunction with data augmentation methods for developing a versatile and efficient automated essay grading model across diverse topics.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to future generations. The model considers the benefits as a multiple objective problem, analyzing the opportunities available to current individuals with varying economic statuses and how those opportunities impact their children's chances for a similar social upgrade. By combining multi-agent decision-making with intergenerational modeling, this research explores how societies with varying levels of social mobility structure their educational systems. The resulting strategies for limiting social mobility reveal how societies balance present and future needs through the distribution of opportunities.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, alongside non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs.
A comprehensive description of Delegated RingCT, along with security evidence and an implemented prototype, are presented, which we subsequently test through benchmarking analysis.
While Delegated RingCT may not possess the same level of anonymity compared to other RingCT implementations, we propose that its ability to be compatible with DPoS consensus mechanisms provides a reasonable trade-off for enabling a more efficient and scalable decentralised cryptocurrency with preserved anonymity capabilities.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring 5.7 (expected to be 5.9) standard deviations above background noise.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a significance of around 3.3 to 3.4 standard deviations and the measured rates of boson creation are also recorded.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated single-source corpus lacks the diversity of modern Hebrew, found primarily on the web. This research addresses this issue by presenting a new, open-access UD Hebrew treebank. This corpus, created by sampling various topics from Hebrew Wikipedia, provides a much-needed upgrade to NLP's understanding of contemporary Hebrew. The project evaluates its own annotations, validates results using automated tools, and achieves new state-of-the-art results on UD NLP tasks by combining advanced language models with innovative approaches. Additionally, the project updates and releases the existing UD HTB annotation scheme, incorporating the improvements from the new Hebrew corpus.

We maintain fixed $p \in [1,\infty)$ and $K \in (0,\infty)$ and a probability measure $\mu$. It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the dimension $d$ is less than or equal to $\frac{32e^2 (2K)^{2p}\log n}{\varepsilon^2}$, and for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, the inequality $ \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} - \varepsilon \leq \|y_i - y_j\|_{\ell_p^d}^p \leq \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} + \varepsilon$ holds. Additionally, the paper discusses induced metrics $\gamma_p^{\text{iso}}$ and $\gamma_p^{\text{conv}}$ for isotropic and convex spaces, and it is shown that for any $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse teams can create new models and data, leading to collaboration opportunities. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative learning, since adjusting an existing model to address a new problem can negatively affect performance on earlier tasks handled by other teams. To address this issue, the authors developed the 'Catastrophic Forgetting Countermeasure,' or Coffeecam, which utilizes a dual approach to prevent forgetting and enable cooperative learning. Coffeecam combines task-specific weight regularization with a meta-algorithm for parameter tuning, ensuring high performance on both original and adapted datasets. The approach can be applied to various existing Continual Learning methods, and we demonstrate its efficacy by adapting it to the more demanding goal of adapting mechanical models to variations in material properties, where previous methods have consistently struggled.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined model predictive safety filter (MPSF) design that utilizes system level synthesis techniques to create an expanded safety area for linear systems impacted by bounded disturbances. The resulting SL-MPSF method ensures system safety with fewer and less extreme adjustments to control inputs. Furthermore, we propose a specific variant of SL-MPSF that retains scalability and significantly decreases online processing requirements, which is the major drawback of traditional MPSF designs. The benefits of our safety filter design over state-of-the-art MPSF designs are then demonstrated through numerical examples.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero- and few-shot learning abilities with promising results, yet their underlying dynamics are not yet fully understood. For instance, there is limited knowledge about how learning in-context changes when using varying training corpora. Our research aims to explore the influence of a pretraining corpus's origin and size on the performance of a Korean-centric model. Notably, we discovered four crucial findings: Firstly, a pretraining corpus's domain significantly affects the model's ability to learn in-context. Conversely, a pretraining corpus's language does not substantially impact its in-context learning capabilities. Furthermore, a pretraining corpus's size shows no correlation with the model's performance in certain zero-shot tasks. Lastly, a pretraining corpus composed of relevant yet formally distinct languages can still facilitate in-context learning in some cases, even though it may not be directly related to the target task.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, intricate structure of these formations disintegrates. To investigate the long-term effects of this process, we conducted 30 magnetohydrodynamic simulations of kiloparsec-scale, kiloparsec cold clouds under conditions typically seen in galaxy clusters. Our results indicate that filamentary segments of these clouds quickly cool and separate from the surrounding hot intracluster medium before ultimately fragmenting and creating numerous smaller clumps. These fragments act as nuclei, fostering further condensation through processes including Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, thereby nearly doubling the cold gas within a 75 million-year period. Cloud expansion appears to be determined by factors such as density and localized heat-producing mechanisms that either cause the clouds to shrink and crumble or to grow through shattering. Magnetic fields are found to have a moderating effect on the cloud's growth while its topology plays a role in its crust's development. Through spectral analysis, we identified a range of sound patterns that can inform us about the physical characteristics of galaxy cluster cold gas structures across 20 million years. Our research implies that galaxy cluster hot gas contains embedded, intricate structures that are no longer in equilibrium with their surroundings and are therefore destined to survive and potentially influence the surrounding environment in irreversible ways.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The
presentation includes precise measurements of observables connected to the
unitary triangles stemming from unitarity constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-
Maskawa matrix describing quark mixing, alongside recent $C\!P$ violation
measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons. Specific emphasis is given to an
analysis that initially identified $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and made
the most accurate measurement of this effect within the charm system to date. 
These analyses rely on data gathered from proton-proton collisions in 2011 and
2012, collected by the ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb experiments.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique polarization properties and their counterparts in bosonic string theory are significantly weaker. A remarkable relationship exists among these amplitudes, where one is proportional to the others. Calculations of their ratios confirm a long-standing theory prediction made by Gross in 1988. Additionally, the total count of newly calculated high-energy amplitudes in superstring theory is consistent with those from recently discovered fermion interactions in string theory.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first divided into CVC-like units based on a demixing algorithm, which are then grouped into transient and steady-state units using clustering algorithms. The latter are further stabilized into F0-phoneme units. The paper investigates the effectiveness of CVC-like units, particularly those with a C onset and vowel tail structure, in representing the complex transient patterns of speech. The results indicate that these units can accurately capture the unique characteristics of speech, enabling high-quality synthesis without transcription data in a vocabulary-independent manner.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable outcomes. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of walking and climbing experiments on a 10 kg hexapod robot.

We have developed two overarching methods to quantify the manipulation of quantum states using probabilistic protocols constrained by specific quantum resource limitations.
Initially, we formulated a fundamental criterion for achieving a physical transformation between quantum states using a previously introduced resource metric.
This approach led to the discovery that the metric is not only necessary, but also sufficient, for one-shot resource conversion in various resource theories, effectively rendering more restrictive protocols unnecessary.
By employing this metric, we were able to refine the performance limits of one-shot and multi-copy probabilistic resource distillation protocols.
Concurrently, we introduced a comprehensive technique for calculating achievable probabilities in resource transformations through a series of convex optimisation problems.
This approach enabled us to precisely assess the trade-offs between probabilities and the amount of a particular resource, ultimately yielding optimised protocols.
Furthermore, we successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our methods by applying them to the study of quantum entanglement and coherence.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing vertical excitation that caused resonant behavior and eventual instability. Meanwhile, horizontal excitation led to a pattern of stable and unstable cycles, all of which collapsed into a stable equilibrium eventually. The research revealed a complex and intricate mapping of reservoir angles and their corresponding rates of change, as well as a phenomenon where small changes in one parameter drastically altered the system's dynamics, resulting in a diverse array of dynamic states.

In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust and efficient communication protocol. Notably, our proposed method, DR-DSGD, outperforms DSGD and RPROD in various settings, particularly in terms of communication efficiency. Furthermore, we analytically prove the almost sure convergence of our algorithm under specific conditions. Finally, extensive numerical experiments confirm that our solution achieves superior results compared to the existing solutions.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues to utilize our research to determine non-equilibrium characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process by which powerful jets form is studied under different magnetic field strengths and mass accumulation rates. The data show that strongly magnetized clouds produce fast-moving jets only when the protostar gains a relatively small amount of mass per year, typically no more than 10 to the minus 3 solar masses. However, this low-mass rate also means that less-strong magnetic fields are required to produce the high-velocity jets. For very high mass accumulation rates, the high-velocity jets appear initially, but quickly weaken and then disappear completely, which makes it impossible for these low-velocity outflows to form early in the protostar formation process, especially in magnetic clouds that are very weak, leading to different star formation processes than what is typically observed.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance and safety for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment function that represents the interaction between performance and saturation. Through analytical analysis, it is demonstrated that this function possesses critical properties, facilitating the design of an efficient algorithm. In addition, it is proven that this algorithm is stable, efficient, and compliant with constrained system limitations, as verified using Lyapunov stability theory. Ultimately, numerical simulations are used to illustrate the effectiveness of this proposed method.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how various gravitational interactions affect an object orbiting the Earth, specifically considering its shape and the impact of sunlight pressure. To achieve this, it provides mathematical predictions for the object's equilibrium positions, taking into account its area-to-mass ratio, initial conditions, and the object's variations in eccentricity. Estimates are also developed for the time intervals in which these orbital changes occur, which is crucial in categorizing the object's orbit under different influences. Validation of these estimates was conducted through numerical modeling and the application of specialized tools, such as the Fast Lyapunov Indicator, which helps identify and visualize patterns related to resonance phenomena. Ultimately, this work aims to lay the groundwork for modeling the impact of sunlight pressure in the framework of established celestial mechanics models, specifically the Extended Fundamental Model and the Second Fundamental Model.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model, especially for high-intensity excitations and in scenarios where spatial confinement occurs.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to determine the 3D pose and shape of these objects. Our first achievement is developing PACE3D* and PACE2D*, which are novel optimisation algorithms allowing for precise calculation of both shape and pose using single or combined data from 2D and 3D keypoints. These algorithms can effectively handle complex non-rigidity issues by incorporating an attribute learning component from a small set of annotated samples. Our experimental tests reveal that PACE3D* and PACE2D* exhibit superior performance and efficiency when compared to existing techniques, particularly on real-world datasets.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method for estimating the efficacy of a new treatment in basket trials has been developed to assess multiple diseases from a single trial using a single control group. Our approach uses Bayesian statistics to maximize the probability that the new treatment performs better than the standard treatment across all the diseases studied. A numerical example demonstrates how to apply this method to specific clinical trials.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a fully observable shape, PRNet is suited for partial-to-partial registration tasks, surpassing traditional and deep learning-based approaches on synthetic datasets. Our approach features self-supervised learning of a suitable geometric representation and a keypoint detector for common point identification, alongside learned keypoint-to-keypoint correspondences. Experimental results demonstrate PRNet's ability to consistently predict keypoints and correspondence across varying views and objects, while its geometric representation is also transferable to classification tasks.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree by finding the least integer c such that the quotient $G/\gamma_{c+1}(G)$ possesses the $R_\infty$ property. In this research, we derive the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of Generalized Solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups $\Gamma_n$ and explicitly calculate the lower central series for $\Gamma_n$. Additionally, we decompose nilpotent quotients of $\Gamma_n$ by the lower central series, and we identify the nilpotent subgroups of orders 2, 3, and 4 in $\Gamma_n$.

Instead of presuming hypothetical new physics will be found at future colliders, 
we consider a different possibility where there isn't any. In this case, 
our main goal would be to find out if the unusual Standard Model fits within a vast landscape of possibilities. A crucial step to reach this goal would be to determine the instability scale of the Higgs potential. Achieving this requires reducing uncertainty about two key elements: the strong coupling and the mass of the top quark. Specifically, the mass of the top quark can be accurately measured by analyzing pairs of particles near their threshold at lower luminosity rates, around 10 to the 33, cm to the minus 2, second to the minus 1, conditions. As a result, the measurement of the mass of the top quark would no longer be dominated by the Large Hadron Collider, but rather by the Large Electron Positron collider, re-examining data collected between 1990 and 2000.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of a systematic investigation into the distribution amplitudes of several mesons using lattice QCD, focusing on bi-scalar correlators and distribution amplitudes specific to mesons. This study employs a propagator-based approach to obtain the distribution amplitudes directly from the lattice. We examine three distribution amplitudes for the pion and rho vector meson: vertical stroke T
\phi_\perp(\x, \x')\vert^2, vertical stroke T
\phi_\parallel(\x, \x')\vert^2, and $\phi_\xi(\x, \x')$. Our results are first calculated at a specific separation of space-time distance for each meson and then extrapolated to any distance using a parametric representation technique, yielding distribution amplitudes in the light-cone framework. Our lattice results are compared with available theoretical predictions and experimental data. Notably, we obtained the longitudinal distribution amplitude of the rho meson for the first time.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities without manual labels presents significant difficulties due to the considerable time and resources needed for annotation. Current techniques typically address a novel modality either by fine-tuning a pre-trained model or by dividing the tasks into independent image translation and segmentation steps. In contrast, we present an innovative approach that combines segmenting multiple modalities with translating images into a target domain, all while minimizing target domain images without labels through self-supervised segmentations. This framework serves as a pre-training strategy, followed by fine-tuning in a domain-adaptation framework using limited target domain images for segmentation supervision. We evaluate our approach on PASCAL-S Segmentation and PongTFP boundary detection benchmarks, achieving notable results with high scores on unseen modalities with little to no target domain images available.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including parameter sharing, Radial Basis Function kernels, and
adversarial training, to develop a novel RNN architecture for generating future
video features and anticipating actions. By using only the initial video frames and
a reduced number of parameters, Feature Mapping RNN efficiently generates future
features, which are then used in a multi-layer perceptron equipped with an RBF
kernel layer to accurately forecast actions. In our experiments, Feature Mapping RNN
achieved superior performance on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and UT-Interaction datasets
compared to existing state-of-the-art models.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two-component electron beam model can be interpreted as the superposition

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of four dimensions.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if there exists a conjugation operation $C$ on $H$ such that $TC^\ast CT = C^\ast T^\ast T$. In the context of function mappings, a self-map $\varphi$ of the open unit disc can be described using a linear fractional expression. This work investigates the conditions under which the composition operator $C_\varphi$ and weighted composition operator $W_{\psi, \varphi}$, where $\psi$ is another function, are both C-normal operators for specific conjugation operations $C$ and $\psi$.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study focuses on p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk within a p-vertex graph, illustrating a connection between combinatorial objects. Additionally, the article explores a d-dimensional space where the integers' gcd function determines a convex polyhedron with significant symmetry, related to the previously mentioned graph. Lastly, the report investigates a random walk starting from a random vertex in this polyhedron, with the distance from the origin measured in terms of the lattice's euclidean structure. As a result, the researchers establish the presence of both a median, which converges to a sphere's center, as well as a set of outliers whose size diminishes as the walk progresses.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on the ModelNet dataset confirm the superiority of our proposed point cloud cleaning method over existing approaches, making TPC an essential tool for assessing the robustness of point cloud-based neural networks against deceptive transformation-based attacks.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating ALOHA and CSMA protocols to minimize the impact of narrowband interference, introducing a new metric to gauge performance based on network throughput. In the case of ALOHA, we analyze the probabilities of interference and system efficiency under different system parameters. We observe that FMCW network behavior diverges from typical wireless communication patterns. In some scenarios, increased packet transmission can decrease interference probabilities. We introduce a clear channel assessment process, known as medium sensing, for CSMA, also defining metrics to gauge its effectiveness. In our analysis of CSMA, radar units transmit data after confirming an empty transmission path. We examine CSMA's medium sensing success rate, interference probabilities, and system efficiency under different system parameters. Unlike standard communication networks, the optimal strategy in some scenarios may involve the highest feasible attempt rates for maximizing throughput. Extensive simulations are conducted to validate our analytical findings and compare the efficiency of slotted ALOHA and CSMA. In our analysis, CSMA consistently outperforms ALOHA across all practical use cases.

Recent experiments employing various methods have sought to detect the entangled two-photon absorption phenomenon across a range of materials. Our work investigates the possibility of observing this phenomenon in a realistic experimental setting, taking into account factors like real-world limitations on photon polarization and optical anisotropy within the material. A distinct signature of entangled two-photon absorption is observed, and our findings show that it is feasible to detect entangled photons interacting with a specific material resonance, provided that the entanglement's coherence length significantly exceeds the material's anisotropy's coherence length. Notably, our results demonstrate that entities other than photons can exhibit entangled absorption, including entangled dual-ray-particle states and entangled neutral-meson states.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time feature incorporation. Our model
time-sharing factorization technique allows for resolving the challenge of
distinguishing between similar entities over time. Our model's hyperparameters were
tuned via grid search, resulting in remarkable performance on three public
datasets across multiple time-aware entity prediction tasks. Notably, we achieved
new state-of-the-art results on certain PKDD 2020 challenge task variants.

In the field of rigid-body impact sound synthesis, the sound produced by the ground is often overlooked. However, in this study, an idealized ground sound model, rooted in elastodynamic theory, is used to determine under which conditions ground sound is perceivable, rather than being masked by the sound produced by the impacting object or its transient vibrations. An analytical model derived from this theory allows for the calculation of the acceleration of the ground surface in a precise and mathematically closed form, which can then be applied in various simulation methods to generate the sound waves. It is found that ground sound can be audible under certain circumstances when the sound produced by the impacting object is inaudible, specifically when a heavy object strikes a soft surface and when the point of impact is positioned at a shallow angle relative to the listener's location.

A prevalent form of demonstrating Bell nonlocality known as the all-versus-nothing proof is presented without the use of inequalities. This concept consists of two main species, referred to as "always-type" and "sometimes-type", which have received significant research attention. Past studies on "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs have primarily involved perfect correlations from stabilizer states. This has led many researchers to conclude that perfect correlations are the sole means of yielding "always-type" all-versus-nothing proofs. Contrary to this prevailing notion, our study offers a "always-type" all-versus-nothing proof rooted in non-stabilizer state, specifically the five-qubit IBM basis state |00000>. This state is generated by applying the gate sequence $X_{2,3}S_{1,4}X_{0,5}$, where the subscripts denote specific qubit positions, on the classical key state |00000>$.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating minimal movement. Molecular orbital representations of these systems introduce random MO models, retaining the degeneracy of the flat bands even in the presence of disorder. The zero modes in chiral systems with an imbalance in sublattices fall into this category. Following a general description of constructing flat bands through MOs, various examples are examined with numerical proof, including the sawtooth lattice in one dimension and the hyper-Pyrochlore lattice across any number of dimensions, extending the principles seen in two-dimensional Kagome and three-dimensional Pyrochlore lattices to higher dimensions.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, we've used first-principles calculations to investigate its electronic, vibrational, and superconducting properties. Contrary to expectations, however, the hydrogen boride system fails to possess a notable superconducting critical temperature. Hydrogen in this compound impairs the bonding between boron atoms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of electron-phonon interaction. Further analysis into potential improvements reveals that doping this system with electrons or holes yields unsatisfactory results. Ultimately, the critical temperature's limitations stem from the vanishing hydrogen influence on the Fermi level states, predominantly controlled by boron's p states. Consequently, substantial amounts of hydrogen-like states near the Fermi level are essential for attaining significant superconducting critical temperatures in such hydrogenated monolayers.

Research on the division of quantities into equal parts continues to evolve within the field of combinatorics. This study specifically delves into the concept of 'flattened' partitions, where items are divided into a minimum number of equal parts with some items repeated (occurring multiple times within the same group), with particular focus on the maximum size of each group when divided by a certain number. We examine a related combinatorial idiom, represented by the entry for OEIS number A124324, where each term's numerical value corresponds to the count of these 'flattened' partitions, with additional constraints being the total quantity (n) and a variable (d) indicating how items are to be evenly distributed. Several distinct approaches have been developed to address this issue, with one being a recursive relationship and the other being a formula based on the combination of two mathematical expressions, with both having been derived empirically and later confirmed through proof. Additionally, our research extends the existing knowledge on this topic by a small but significant amount (by a factor of d+1) and also explores a related, previously unstudied combinatorial idiom, where results were previously unknown (up to a certain limit of n) for the existing part of the Flattened Parts sequence (A124324).

We categorize and understand a certain aspect of attractiveness in groups that use arithmetic, and derive statements indicating a dual nature related to their stable components, characteristics, patterns, and associated algebraic structures. To accomplish this, we study the movement patterns over the characteristics of the part of these groups that are stable and have manageable properties, particularly demonstrating the rigidity where any stable movement remains unchanged, which gives us new information about the rigidity of these groups, along with the rigidity of their subgroups, patterns, and associations. Furthermore, we understand the stiffness of their characteristics, which gives us new information about the rigidity of these groups, along with the rigidity of their subgroups, patterns, and associations. Additionally, we study the cohomology of these groups and make connections between it and the movement patterns over the characteristics of these groups, which gives us new information about the rigidity of these groups, along with the rigidity of their subgroups, patterns, and associations.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against electric and electronic failures, a backup system is triggered by an arbitration logic that prioritizes functional safety above all else. To uphold these safety standards, stringent quality controls are applied to system components yet crashes remain a possibility due to the interdependence of software and complex system dynamics. Through the use of interactive manual control and understanding how human and robotic collaboration adapts to crises, this research explores the potential for training drivers to effectively handle system failures. It investigates how drivers can learn to reliably activate emergency procedures by leveraging the specific characteristics of designated control interfaces as critical factors in rescue strategies. Within this context, the study delves into the practical implications of transferring driving skills from conventional to highly automated driving scenarios, with a focus on failure handling.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical processes.  Many scholars, such as Ishiguro and Levey, rely on a Weierstrassian perspective; in contrast, Arthur draws comparisons to the Lawvere-Kock-Bell framework, a non-Archimedean approach known as Smooth Infinitesimal Analysis (SIA). A critical examination of Arthur's comparison reveals significant misunderstandings regarding the nature of the continuous, polygons with an infinite number of sides, and infinitesimal quantities. Additionally, claims by Rabouin and Arthur, suggesting that Leibniz considered infinite quantities to be inherently contradictory, rely on an incorrect blending of Leibnizian concepts of bounded and unbounded infinites - a distinction previously noted by early Knobloch. Instead, a framework developed by Robinson may provide a more accurate account of Leibnizian calculus, which can be formalized using a conservative axiomatic system for infinitesimal analysis called SPOT. This formalisation covers concepts such as the bounded/unbounded distinction, a distinction between quantities that are or are not assigned to points, a generalised equality relation applicable to quantities differing by negligible terms, and a continuity principle.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using mildly non-linear scales from data that will be obtained from interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments. Assuming that the experiments will be like CHORD and PUMA, we run a series of analyses on mock data that accurately represents how these surveys are conducted at redshift z=0.5, comparing these to the performance that can be expected from stage 4 optical galaxy surveys. The impact of removing foregrounds using methods that rely on simulations is accounted for in the analysis, which shows how it affects the accuracy of the parameter estimation. The 10 parameters that are varied in the analysis include the 6 standard cosmological parameters, 3 parameters that account for the way that the sky is mapped, and 1 parameter that measures foreground power, as well as 3 parameters that are used to model systematic effects. The accuracy of the parameter estimation is assessed by comparing a best fit model to a clay pot model where the power spectrum is measured in a range that goes from 10 to 180 Mpc-1. The 1-sigma accuracy for the 6 standard cosmological parameters is as follows: for CHORD like data it's 1.6%, 2.2%, 2.2%, 2.2%, 2.2%, and 2.2%; for P

Christensen and Hasannasab established that if a hypothetical operator T transforms sequence vectors $e_n$ into $e_{n+1}$ for all natural numbers, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the operator T is one-to-one and onto. In this article, we explore additional results concerning the operator T and the associated sequence $e_n$. Initially, we prove that if a hypothetical operator S, which is similar to T but with a different effect, exists and there is a natural number c such that $S^n(e_1)$ results in cv for n greater than or equal to c, then the sequence is linearly independent only when the operator S is one-to-one and onto. In addition, we deduce a corollary related to the standard basis, establish a result concerning the dimension of the sequence's span under the operator T, and address the uniqueness of the operator when it acts on specific vectors.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating data like reviews, summaries, and narratives when user-item rating matrices are sparse. Nonetheless, these models are inadequate to learn optimal user and item representations. Collaborative filtering methods, including user-based and item-based, due to their efficiency and clarity, have long been utilized in building recommender systems by generating profiles for each user and item based on their historically interacted items and users. Our research integrates these methods with context-aware document models by taking into account users' perspectives on these items. Additionally, our model offers the advantage of online personalization where the system can adjust the user and item representation profiles upon detecting new user interactions without requiring updates to the model's parameters. Our proposed algorithm was tested and demonstrated superior performance on three real-world datasets when compared to baseline methods.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness leads to infinitesimal freeness in expectation. This consequence is demonstrated with a universal, unitarily invariant matrix model based on a specific sum of independent complex Hermitian Wigner matrices.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on isospin breaking and
the mixing between $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$, which is primarily caused by meson-meson
interactions. Our analysis shows that even though the $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$
resonances play a crucial role in these reactions, the branching ratios do not
directly depend on their widths. Instead, the branching ratios are heavily influenced
by the $s\bar s$ content of the resonances and the transition amplitudes $a_0^0\to
J/\psi \pi^0$ and $f_0(980)\to J/\psi \pi^0$, which can be calculated using the
Lattice QCD, string theory or other approaches to study hadron physics. Our study
suggests that the decay reactions can serve as a means to better understand the
$s\bar s$ content of the $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$ resonances.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical capabilities to track multiple beams from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI): a) a pupil tracker captures images of reference lasers using a $2 \times 2$ lenslet array, while b) a field tracker captures images of the science target; c) a pupil imager re-images the telescope's pupil, and d) an aberration tracker captures images of a Shack-Hartmann sensor.
