The camera's detector images are analyzed using dedicated software to determine beam stabilization parameters, every 0.7 seconds. The obtained parameters are then applied to a) adjust the GRAVITY instrument to align with VLTI; b) actively stabilize the telescope's pupil and field of view; c) perform defocus correction, as well as various engineering tasks. The camera has successfully transitioned into operational use, with data reduction and on-sky characterization results having been documented.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension complexity. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers (CkSwO) issue and shows how it yields an efficient scheme with specific parameters when dealing with a limited set of supplier doubling dimension values and a specified number of anomalies. Conversely, for the more constrained Capacitated $k$-Center problem - a subset of CkSwO, - we demonstrate that achieving an analogous parameterized solution when dealing with highway dimension is computationally challenging, falling under the W[1] hardness class, whereas we find it relatively simpler with doubling dimension values. This distinction is the first documented case where a problem exhibits W[1] hardness with highway dimension, despite being manageable with doubling dimension values.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

We examine solving polynomial linear systems with errors using a result from Buesing, Jaulimes, Kozlov, and Moussong, and our findings demonstrate that using degree switching techniques, a number of evaluations equivalent to $2 \deg f + 2 \deg g + 2$ is both necessary and sufficient, assuming a baseline cost for constant evaluation. This result applies to systems of polynomial equations with errors where both the matrix of coefficients and the vector of inclusions are affected by noise.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that symmetry protects a type of photon bundle emission. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, the system only emits photons in 2$n$ correlations, and this emission's purity is improved by the parity symmetry, mainly due to reduced odd-correlated photon emissions. The parity symmetry of the system can be controlled and adjusted with a magnetic field to switch between even and odd correlated photons. This research advances the study of photon bundle emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime and enables the exploration of protected multi-quanta phenomena.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED for vector ρ and ω mesons, a mass spectrum as a function of momentum and chiral chemical potential is determined. Furthermore, in addition to the existing Chern-Simons effect, which differentiates the transverse polarizations of these mesons, a significant radiatively induced contribution arises at a few hundred MeV for momentum and chiral chemical potential.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a certain extent (+-n^(1-delta) with high probability) thereby achieving the goals outlined above.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This method is most useful for scenarios with intricate matter distributions and conduction source terms.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves identifying the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20-kt liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. For optimal results, the experiment's instruments require precise energy resolution and quality, which was accomplished through a rigorous selection process of the detector's components. This study focuses on the evaluation of the 20-inch PMT's performance within the JUNO experiment, specifically examining the optimal choice of final components through a comprehensive analysis of the 20-inch PMT's characteristics, its application within the JUNO context, and the resulting optical components shortlisted for the experiment's use.

In practical scenarios like power consumption forecasting and air quality analysis, long sequence time-series forecasting (LSTF) is indispensable, encompassing sequences of any length that are considered comprehensive. Employing sophisticated models like Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformers in a multi-step forecasting context leads to conflicting optimization objectives, resulting in compromised accuracy. Our primary concern revolves around devising a technique to generate comprehensive, high-quality future sequences of any desired length. Our proposed neSTF framework leverages the strengths of both the above-mentioned models and combines them using a multi-stage technique. Initially, a deep learning model temporarily stores sequence data in hidden states and subsequently uses a separate transformer module to refine and optimize the generated future sequence data. Our neSTF framework serves as a versatile base model that can be further enhanced by incorporating optimization techniques, adapting adapter strategies, and adapting the scoring system. Our empirical investigations demonstrate that our proposed base model outperforms existing approaches in diverse real-world and benchmark scenarios.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on traditional optical systems, with the standard unit in use at the LBT incorporating a wavefront corrector, a wavelength-dependent rotator, and a map of desired dispersion. However, we've found that including a full description of the desired wavefront pattern, along with the rotator's wavelength-dependent schedule, is unnecessary. By replacing the rotator with a fixed, wavelength-independent tracker, and incorporating a variable linear translator to promptly adjust the position of the ADC for observations off-axis, we've developed a simplified optical system. The variable linear translator allows the ADC to be rapidly moved into place, and it can also be used to finely focus the system, if needed.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform.

Bosonic dark matter, modeled as an ultralight wave-like field near its Compton frequency, can be detectable even when its direct measurement is not sensitive enough to detect the signal directly due to its high frequency, because the signal will also be present at very low frequencies and can be effectively extracted with appropriate detection methods. A notable aspect of this approach is that the low frequency signal can be successfully analyzed using only time domain data without the need for frequency domain analysis, which is particularly beneficial for evaluating signals from deep space observations, especially when dealing with data from radio telescopes like the Arecibo Observatory. A novel method has been developed that incorporates a Bayesian approach to detect the signal by comparing the likelihood of the observed data against a null hypothesis, utilizing the time domain data directly to extract the low frequency component. This approach uses a time domain metric that effectively captures the variation of the signal across time, as well as its significance, by assessing the signal's power spectrum density and its time localization using the Chan statistic. When applied to simulated data, this approach effectively detects the low frequency component, confirming its sensitivity to the ultralight bosonic dark matter model. Additionally, this method has been used to re-analyze recent data from the Arecibo Observatory, yielding positive results that suggest the possibility of detecting the low frequency component, which could be related to the NANOGrav and LIGOScientist collaborations' recent findings on the nature of dark matter and gravitational waves.

This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). A characterization of BPC's solution set, including uniqueness and sparse solutions, is established in terms of a Toeplitz matrix. The uniqueness and characteristics of BPC's solution rely on the eigenvalue properties of this matrix. The solutions range from a single, weighted Dirac mass for certain conditions to infinitely many Dirac masses in other cases. The number of Dirac masses in each case is influenced by the rank of a positive or negative semi-definite matrix. The positive or negative definiteness of the matrix also determines the weights of the Dirac masses as either nonnegative or nonpositive, respectively.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method enhances the transported field by projecting it onto a higher-order function space before solving the transport equation. In contrast, the other method utilizes a mixed finite element approach to concurrently solve for both the transported field and its vorticity, introducing a stabilisation strategy to mitigate spurious wave modes. Both methods are validated against the standard finite element scheme and exhibit a higher-order approximation of the transported field, especially when high-order interpolants are used.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked various concerns regarding ethics, encompassing skewed predictions and data security risks. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-Wada basins transition into partially Wada basins under such weak dissipation. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the emergence of Wada points on the boundaries of these basins in three-dimensional systems. Ultimately, this research indicates that Wada basins in three-dimensional systems exhibit distinct dynamics compared to their two-dimensional counterparts.

A theoretical model involving an intricate scalar field that connects to (electron, muon) or (muon, tau) pairs is considered within a certain "duration" window when the mass difference between two lepton types is relatively large. In this model, upon certain conditions being met, the observed muon anomalies could be fully resolved, while a long-lived, massive particle from one of the lepton pairs would travel a considerable distance between its birth and death. This particle, which would interact via a force unrelated to the Standard Model's electroweak or gravitational forces, might be produced in areas with high energy, such as particle colliders or high-energy cosmic rays impacts, and then propagate through the detector or even outside it. If it were a muon, it could potentially escape detection by looking at displacement in time, and if it were a hadron, it could be found by examining products of its decay. Thus, this theoretical model offers an innovative strategy for detecting long-lived, massive particles of unusual nature.

Human action understanding in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
which this study addresses by proposing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN).
Compared to current deep learning-based methods, HAN stands out due to its
capacity for (1) extended temporal structure capture; (2) explicit modeling of 
temporal transitions between frames and segments, and (3) the ability to learn key 
regions in frames and temporal segments through its multi-step attention mechanism.
Evaluations of the model on established action recognition benchmarks indicate
remarkable performance superiority.

Investigating the thermodynamics and cosmic censorship conjecture in Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through scalar field scattering yields results that support the first law of thermodynamics for non-extremal black holes, confirming that the singularity in such black holes is hidden by an event horizon. The validity of this theory for near-extremal and extremal black holes is confirmed by analyzing their minimum function values after the scattering process. The findings show that neither near-extremal nor extremal black holes can become overcharged due to such processes. The outcome of scattering when a certain relationship between the electric potential and scalar field is met is that the extremal black hole retains its extreme properties. In contrast, when this relationship is not met, the scattering causes the extremal black hole to transform into a near-extremal black hole with a different mass and charge configuration.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

We re-examine a widely accepted model for complex semiconductor production lines and analyze it in the context of states, inflows, and outflows being represented by measures on Borel spaces. This investigation arises from the lack of optimal solutions for transitioning from a smaller to a larger equilibrium state with zero inventory levels in the standard L1 framework. Novel contributions involve addressing the issue of non-differentiable velocities with discrete objects and a bounded domain subject to inflows and outflows. A locally optimal strategy is developed, and its near-optimality and convergence over time are established under mild conditions. Furthermore, a numerical application is demonstrated to validate our theoretical findings.

Cybersecurity has gained significant importance over recent years, with the detection of cyber threats emerging as a critical task due to the immense damage a single breach can inflict on companies. The incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into this task has improved it, allowing high-quality classifiers to detect attacks efficiently; however, these classifiers demand substantial computing power or memory. The scenario presents a problem, particularly when these classifiers need to operate on low-resource devices or prevent performance overload on devices at the network perimeter. A novel solution to overcome this challenge is proposed by NBcoded, a light attack classification tool that effectively combines noisy data removal and efficient data encoding, leveraging the benefits of Naive Bayes classifier while reducing resource requirements. In this study, three NBcoded implementations are developed using three Naive Bayes likelihood distribution assumptions (Gaussian, Complement, and Bernoulli). By comparing the results, NBcoded shows promising performance, achieving a 99.6% or higher Delivered Correctness Rate in classification, with its computational cost and memory requirements significantly lowered, at just $0.02/MAC and $0.5/MEM respectively.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We introduce a concept of Schreier growth gap, a function that measures group growth, by examining its implications on G's set actions. We then explore Schreier growth gaps for solvable groups. If G is metabelian and finitely presented or torsion-free, but not virtually abelian, it possesses a Schreier growth gap of n^2. If metabelian G has a Krull dimension of k, it will have a Schreier growth gap of n^k, such as the Schreier growth gap n^d for the wreath product C_p ∋¬ ℤ^d and n^(d+1) for ℤ ∋¬ ℤ^d. For solvable groups of finite Prüfer rank, a Schreier growth gap of exp(n) applies unless they are virtually nilpotent, a criterion which also applies to solvable groups linear over ℚ. Lastly, a wide range of torsion-free solvable groups have a Schreier growth gap of n^2, a group type that also includes those linear over ℚ.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations in the form of a rich semantic mask, are presented to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The D-Wave hybrid solver and classical solvers on Azure Quantum were utilized to solve the problem, yielding hybrid approaches that outperformed classical methods in solution quality due to lower objective function values, regardless of problem size variations.

Modern artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods are now employed to automatically identify physics principles and governing equations directly from measurement data. Nevertheless, formulating a universal physical law using data exclusively proves to be difficult without proposing a corresponding discrepancy model to account for the theoretical-measurement discrepancies that inevitably arise. By reexamining the long-standing problem of simulating the falling motions of objects, this work highlights several critical issues that need to be resolved to reliably derive objective physical laws from noisy experimental data. It's particularly demonstrated that initially converged models of object fall sometimes generate realistic trajectories but can't be generalized to objects with different mass ratios, thus we're still lacking a universal "law of physics" that can accurately predict the behavior of all objects under any given set of initial conditions.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly lower speeds than light and distinctive characteristics: substantial transverse momentum and unusually large energy loss per unit length. The study focuses on particles detectable by their tracks in the inner detector and energy loss measurements in the pixel layers of the detector, thus able to capture particles with lifetimes as short as one nanosecond and masses ranging from 100 GeV to 3 TeV. The study explores the possibilities of long-lived particles in supersymmetric models, considering the production of $R$-hadrons, charginos and staus, with mass limits that extend well beyond previous search findings in various scenarios.

We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized losses. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and devised an optimization technique to achieve high efficiency in single-photon sources. This method incorporates a taper section to smoothly bridge the mode mismatch between the cavity and the nanobeam, ultimately enhancing the Purcell factor and source efficiency. Furthermore, we observed the resilience of our design in the face of real-world fabrication imperfections affecting hole variation in the taper-nanobeam system.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak, a technique which has been applied to various substances like silicon dioxide, boron oxide, polybutadiene and amorphous germanium. Studies on temperature-dependent boson peaks in silicon dioxide and glycerol have also been conducted. Furthermore, x-ray Brillouin scattering measurements have demonstrated that longitudinal sound wave damping in silicon dioxide and glycerol follows a soft potential model prediction, $\omega^4$, particularly in the low-frequency regime.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations to understand single-particle behavior and 
production processes. These calculations involve extremely complex equations, 
beyond current analytical methods' capabilities. This study proposes a 
semi-numerical technique using differential equations with specific boundaries 
at unique points to solve these complex equations with high accuracy. These 
calculations can be done using numerical methods like sector decomposition and 
are then translated into physical scenarios with a series solution, providing 
precision of at least eight digits. This method has an integrated accuracy 
checker and is shown to work with challenging examples like self-energy and 
vertex integrals and two-loop box integrals.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume. However, exact construction of the scattering matrix for complex media is challenging. We introduce a generalized scattering matrix for three-dimensional complex media and derive a weighted distribution function through rigorous calculation. The extracted probability distribution correctly accounts for internal correlations within scanned samples, even considering multiple scattering events. The obtained scattering matrix enables precise computation of weight factors, thereby facilitating extraction of the induced current distribution from measured far-field data. The approach is validated by comparing theoretical and experimental weight factors for different wave patterns and frequencies.

Researchers have identified the far-side counterpart to a well-studied spiral arm in the center of the Milky Way, which is observed expanding. This far-side arm, detected through carbon monoxide emissions, can be followed in a map of Galactic longitude and velocity as a faint feature extending at least 20 degrees. Both the far-side and near-side arms exhibit comparable features including velocities, widths, heights, and mass distribution. Based on further investigation using 21-cm data, it's found that these spiral arms are primarily composed of molecular gas. This new evidence lends support to the presence of a bar structure at the center of the Galaxy and should aid in understanding its properties.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being employed to uncover a broad range of solutions, rather than just the optimal option. This phenomenon is evident across different domains, from multi-objective optimization to indirect discovery in chemistry and design by optimization in architecture. Recently, multi-objective coevolutionary algorithms have shown promise in directly generating diverse solution sets, which often outperform other approaches. However, these algorithms struggle with two major issues: a slow convergence rate and poor scalability. This study introduces a novel multi-objective coevolutionary algorithm designed to mitigate these challenges. The proposed framework incorporates two distinct populations, one focused on diversity and another on convergence, which are paired and subjected to fitness sharing to enhance diversity. Additionally, a dimensionality reduction technique is applied to pre-process a dataset, reducing the complexity and allowing the algorithm to operate more efficiently. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is validated through a comprehensive evaluation of 12 benchmark functions and 4 real-world industrial cases, which reveal it to be a scaleable, efficient, and diverse solution generator.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring how agent preferences are assigned. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing that any stable matches in this scenario can be represented as a single layer of connections within a specific graph structure, known as a hypergraph. This means that any stable matches in this setup can be translated into a complete set of matches given the use of specific metrics and specific mathematical functions. For groups of 11 or fewer agents, using specific valuation methods, stable matches can always be found and, using a specific polynomial-time algorithm, can be determined with certainty. However, when using more general groups of agents and a different type of valuation, the process of determining whether a stable match exists can be computationally complex, particularly in situations where valuation methods are uniformly random. A specific type of valuation, symmetric and general, offers an alternative solution - in this scenario, stable matches can always be determined and, using a particular polynomial-time algorithm, can be determined with certainty. Additionally, in a specific situation with a high number of groups of agents

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon
interaction affect valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. When we restrict
our study to constant strain conditions, we observe that two mechanisms, cone tilt
and deformation potential, yield analogous effects on valley Hall responses.
However, this equivalence does not apply when the coupling involves position-dependent
velocity of electrons. The presence of a significant valley Hall effect near a
neutral charge condition in the isotropic scenario mirrors that seen with changes
in bond lengths, while in the anisotropic scenario, geometric valley Hall
transport is most pronounced near the charge neutral point, even when the
anisotropy is caused by strain rather than bond lengths. The substantial valley
Hall effect observed in the anisotropic scenario remains intact even when the
transport is controlled by a minimal energy band gap. Furthermore, the valley
Hall effect in the anisotropic scenario shows minimal decline with increasing
temperature within the range of 0 to 100 K, thanks to the limitations imposed
by the thermal energy by the valley intermixing energy. The substantial valley
Hall effect observed in the anisotropic scenario is also insensitive to the
transport length over which the electron-phonon interaction is evaluated. The
significant valley Hall effect in the anisotropic scenario is predicted to have
two key implications: it enables valley manipulation through roads with
anisotropic Hall resistance, and it results in valleys that are nearly fully
populated despite being far

We examine the class of all metric spaces with their distances measured by Gromov--Hausdorff distance. The subsets of spaces with bounded distances are called clouds, representing maximal subclasses within this group. Scaling the distances of a space by a positive factor yields a transformed metric space, belonging to the same Gromov--Hausdorff class. This type of transformation can cause some clouds to jump into others, as noted in our previous study. To explain this phenomenon, we investigated the stability of these space transformations. This paper demonstrates that any cloud having a stabilizer with nontrivial action will contain a unique central metric space, such that transformations from the stabilizer all converge to this space, thereby indicating that it is zero distance away from all others within that group. The key proof for this lies within our previously established cloud completeness theorem.

A microstrip-fed patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with broad bandwidth and a wide angle of coverage has been successfully developed and tested for integration in planar arrays. The designed antenna has a significant bandwidth of 13.1%, operating between 34.1 GHz and 38.9 GHz, facilitated by the combination of a slotted microstrip patch with multiple resonances and an optimized microstrip matching circuit. Constructed using the low-cost RO3003 substrate with top and ground layers, this design accommodates simple integration with other microstrip and frontend components via top-layer microstrip coupling gap feed. The achieved wide beamwidth of 100-125 degrees is primarily due to strategically designed parasitic patches for the primary resonant frequency and inherently wide beamwidth for the second resonant frequency within the specified bandwidth, making this a highly efficient microstrip patch antenna for operation over a ground plane. The input impedance and radiation pattern observed through measured data closely agree with the simulated results.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the surrounding environment. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by a single laser. It is demonstrated that, under specific conditions, the precision achieved using this method surpasses that attainable through traditional quantum metrology, employing only local manipulation and measurement.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions by up to 50\%. These observations support the idea that gluon production is increased in high-energy collisions.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without traditional two-qubit gates by utilizing an inherent, always-active connection between qubits. Building on this principle, our research explores how digital-analog simulation can be used to study fermionic systems, specifically the Fermi-Hubbard model, using a fermionic SWAP network and a method to correct for the negative influences of adjacent qubit connectivity on results. Focusing on the effects of noise in the simulation of fermionic systems, we examined various connective structures and discovered that a specific arrangement of qubits, in which only every other qubit is connected, is ideal for simulating fermionic systems while minimizing noise, although this may not always be feasible in practice. When noise is taken into account take into account the probability of error, it becomes evident that a minimum distance of energy between adjacent qubit states, which is directly related to the difference in energy levels in the Fermi-Hubbard model, is necessary to prevent errors in the simulation of fermionic systems.

A common issue in machine learning lies in striking a balance between optimizing performance and robustly handling out-of-distribution (OoD) scenarios. Certain methods rely on complex penalty terms that can be difficult to optimize, as they either over- or under-penalize the model's predictions. 

We introduce an approach that begins with an initialization enhancement, where a pre-trained network with extensive knowledge is modified to produce a base that serves as a solid foundation for further training. This internal OoD detection mechanism proves effective in multiple scenarios and can be implemented using pre-trained representations without requiring pre-labeled OoD datasets, which can be time-consuming to prepare. 

Our method exhibits excellent results in two real-world cases: (1) evaluating a natural language generation model's reliability and (2) detecting concept drift in real-time on YouTube videos. In both instances, our proposed solution outperforms a network that relies solely on its own optimizations.

Achieving the formation of intricate structures and rapid concentration of light within or through disordered mediums is an arduous endeavor due to variations in refractive index, unpredictable light scattering, and speckle noise generation. To address these challenges, we've developed a novel weighted-mutation-assisted genetic algorithm (WMA-GA) with an R-squared-based fitness function that enhances image clarity, precision, and rapid convergence in forming complex structures within scattering media. As a companion technology to our previous iterative engineering of structured scattering systems, WMA-GA seamlessly integrates with numerical models of the scanning system, data acquisition, and data processing, thereby enabling the rapid construction of intricate patterns and high-throughput bioprinting of the scattering medium itself. We present exemplary results of focusing to 10 micrometer accuracy on a 500 micrometer-scale area alongside the theoretical background and practical implementation of WMA-GA and its companion technology of iterative engineering of structured scattering systems.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via retargeting. Building upon Dukes and Vansteelandt (2020), we distinguish our research from Kallus (2020) in Section 1 by highlighting their distinct assumptions, variations, and research objectives. In Section 2, guided by Li et al. (2020) and Liang and Zhao (2020), we analyze the efficient policy evaluation problem using data from both the training and testing distributions. Our results demonstrate that under specific growth conditions, efficient value function estimates can yield strong performance, although connections with the existing literature reveal limitations under slower testing sample size growth. In contrast, the testing sample size requirement for DRITR is more relaxed than that of efficient policy evaluation using combined data. In Section 3, we emphasize the broad applicability and utility of DRITR.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality, low power consumption, and simplified readout architecture. However, these sensors have limited functionality and high noise due to the use of thin epitaxial materials and ancient technology used in their fabrication. Since these sensors are already in production, modifying the existing process to utilize a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate can effectively increase their detection capacity and reduce noise. This study investigates the effectiveness of a high-resistivity substrate on small collection electrode size and noise levels through detailed device characterization and simulation. The results demonstrate that such a substrate enables efficient detection of large hits and reduces noise of small signals, ultimately allowing for improved detection capacity and efficient use of small collection electrodes. This achievement leads to reduced power consumption and higher event rates in experiments, as confirmed by the production of detectors utilizing this process change.

Advanced telescopes strive to spot planets at closer distances, lower masses, or older ages than ever before, with the ultimate goal of directly identifying habitable-zone planets with masses similar to those of Earth. Despite recent technological improvements, a significant barrier remains, with the ability of current high-tech ground-based telescopes limited by image speckles that obstruct our view. This challenge has made it difficult to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere and the telescope's instruments themselves. To overcome this issue, researchers have proposed a new system known as the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST), a wavefront sensing and control algorithm that enables the system to operate at the speed of milliseconds even when it detects extremely faint signals. We have successfully tested FAST in the laboratory, showcasing its capability to effectively eliminate the distortions introduced by the atmosphere at the speed of milliseconds.

This study presents a novel exogenous model to tackle the challenge of negative interest rates, maintaining the mathematical ease of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model, and accurately replicating the observed yield curve. It combines the difference between two separate Cox-Ingersoll-Ross processes, incorporating the deterministic-shift adjustment. For quick alignment with the current swaption prices, the Gram-Charlier expansion is employed to calculate swaption prices within the proposed framework. Multiple numerical evaluations validate the accuracy of this new model.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the design of DUNE's Near Detector, so we calculated the anticipated sterile neutrino decays within the detector's volume. According to our projections, DUNE may establish a limit comparable to past predictions made for LBNE. We visualize these results for each neutrino type – electron, muon, and tau – indicating that DUNE has a promising capacity to explore previously unexplored areas of sterile neutrino parameter space before the SHiP experiment joins similar research initiatives.

Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report effect sizes that are correlated due to this shared structure. Typically, meta-analyses assume independent trials; however, this assumption is usually not applicable according to the Hierarchical Generalizability Theory. Previous research developed a method to incorporate these correlations into the meta-analyses, but it relied on specific assumptions about the effect size distributions in each trial. A new method has been created to estimate the variances and covariances robustly, even when trial effects do not meet these specified conditions. The new method uses a consistent estimation approach that is similar to the standard unbiased method, with the only exception being the use of a cluster-robust estimator. However, with a small number of studies, the variance estimates are biased and vary widely; thus, a bias-corrected method has also been developed. The bias-corrected method calculates a bias-corrected estimate by combining the existing study results with a set of hypothetical new study effects that would be required to meet the assumed consistency, with the variances and covariances estimated using the robust estimator in this hypothetical scenario. The estimated risks and risks differences are then obtained by applying the standard arithmetic mean weighted by precision. The proposed methods have been created in a software tool called Hierarchical Mixed Meta-Analysis (HMMANalysis), with numerical examples and a step-by-step case study demonstrating its effectiveness.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process has shed new light on the particle number definition, particularly as it relates to conservation laws. Research has found that particle radiation is not a product of gravitational force-driven pair creation, but rather an outcome stemming from disparities in the laws governing particle number definition. In the far distant future, the source of emitted energy corresponds to zero-point fluctuations characterized by exponentially large wave numbers, prompting a reassessment of the black hole evaporation paradigm.

The effect of transverse momentum broadening on parton propagation through a large nucleus is investigated using various models in the color dipole framework. These models generate different values of a key coefficient that influence broadening calculations. Results obtained via numerical analysis are then compared with LHCb and ALICE experimental findings for nuclear broadening in the context of J/Psi particles. Notably, models that align with small-x data are shown to yield transverse momentum variations consistent with measured values, especially in cases where rapidity is in the forward direction. Additionally, model consistency with ALICE measurements is found across various centrality levels.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The video explores the dynamics of a liquid jet that enters a channel filled with the same fluid. As the jet interacts with the surrounding stream, it becomes encircled by a sheath of entrained air. This sheath plays a significant role in the dynamic behavior of the jet and its penetration into the stream. Additionally, we examine the instability effects that develop on the liquid jet and the consequences of these effects on its behavior in the context of fluid dynamics.

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory is preserved even during crashes. Nevertheless, the volatility of system caches still poses a challenge, leading to data inconsistencies across system crashes. This paper introduces a novel algorithm named RERT to address this issue, utilizing redundant error-tracking tables in combination with rolling back and advancing through snapshot chains to guarantee data reliability. Developed from the base RMT algorithm and inspired by software log management, this method ensures the integrity of key-value stores against crash failures. We experimentally demonstrated that RERT's overhead is acceptable, yielding only a minimal performance impact, with the effect on performance dependent on data KVT redundancy, specifically in reads being the primary performance influencer.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize the distribution of ergodic disintegrations: the probability of escape for individual bodies, the exponent representing narrow escapes, the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum, and the distribution of lifetimes. Our results showed that escape probabilities matched theoretical predictions with high precision, marking a significant improvement over previous statistical theories. Furthermore, the measured values of the exponent near marginally unbound escape thresholds agreed well with an independent, flux-based prediction. However, calculating the predicted absorption as a function of binary energy and angular momentum proved challenging due to the low frequency of collected data points. Additionally, our results showed that the distribution of lifetimes was closely associated with the predicted broad spectrum resulting from hierarchical disintegrations. By combining these findings, we developed a new statistical framework encompassing both hierarchical and non-hierarchical three-body disintegrations. This general model may be utilized to inform the understanding of asteroid and Kuiper belt shear dynamics.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider in 2015. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions, involving a total of 5.02 TeV per nucleon pair. The findings show that suppression of both prompt and non-prompt mesons increases with the level of collision centrality, at an extent comparable to that found in previous 2.76 TeV collisions. The study also found that suppression of J/$\psi$ mesons does not vary by rapidity but decreases slightly at high transverse momentum levels above 25 GeV/$c$ when compared to lower momentum levels. The study found that suppression of $\psi$(2S) mesons is greater than that of J/$\psi$ mesons over the entire examined momentum range.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, a modification in one component may
unintentionally impact other parts, hindering overall system performance. This is
addressed by conducting regression testing, which re-evaluates system sections
aimed at preventing adverse effects. However, pinpointing these affected areas
proves challenging, making it essential to identify system changes through a
different approach. We apply singular value decomposition to group software
modifications by their functional roles, allowing for more efficient detection
of areas requiring retesting during subsequent updates. By leveraging parallel
calculations on shared memory systems, we enhance testing speed, ensuring optimal
results can be obtained even as software systems scale up.

A new technique is proposed to forecast suicidal ideation based on the integration of clinical data and real-time feelings records, employing advanced deep learning and machine learning methods. A cutting-edge approach called Deep Survival Analysis is used to accurately predict suicidal ideation from Electronic Health Records and feelings records collected in real-time. A key contribution of this study lies in the collaborative model it presents, where feelings records are collected in real-time through Ecological Momentary Assessment and are combined with clinical data to forecast suicidal ideation, providing healthcare providers with vital warnings much earlier. Experimental results confirm that the combined model outperforms individual predictors, and further, that incorporating feelings records enhances the precision of forecasting suicidal ideation from clinical data alone. Moreover, the study reveals that the feelings data bring unique insights into the timing of suicidal ideation, preventing false negatives. Finally, sensitivity analyses using hypothetical scenarios for feelings data retrieval and clinical data availability are also presented.

Our research reports a significant $\sim 5\sigma$ discovery of polarized X-ray emission within a range of 3-6 keV originating from Cassiopeia A with the IXPE. Our findings reveal a combined polarization level of $1.45 \pm 0.30$%, obtained after summing the polarization vectors from a large region, under the assumption of circular symmetry. Analysis of the synchrotron radiation suggests an average polarization level of $\sim 1.8$%, while the forward shock region indicates a nearly 5% polarization. Our model considers both thermal and non-thermal radiation contributions using detailed Chandra data for a spatial-spectral analysis. Our individual pixel search revealed several tentative polarization detections at $\sim 3\sigma$ confidence, indicating considerable turbulence in smaller regions than our current angular resolution allows. Our findings confirm that Cassiopeia A's X-ray emission is predominantly composed of a non-thermal synchrotron component, as inferred from previous Fermi-LAT observations.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within pure neutron matter and quark matter, each representing distinct phase regions.  By comparing different equation of state models, we identify distinct sound velocity patterns at lower and higher densities. At lower densities, sound velocity is largely determined by the incompressibility modulus, while at higher densities it's primarily determined by the constant slope of the thermodynamic potential. Our analysis also demonstrates that the adiabatic index is directly tied to the sound velocity, resulting in an overall prediction that the dense matter sound velocity will follow a similar pattern across different equation of state models, potentially leading to a standard model in the field.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, highly distorted fluid surfaces with complex topology are generated. In order to analyze these distortions, we have developed a novel technique for extracting the critical information needed to study these interfaces in detail. Our technique involves a dynamic characterization of the interface through a process of skeletonization, where a graph representing the interface's surface topology is created and used to generate the interface's shape. The resulting framework has been successfully applied to visualize and quantify the dynamics of high-velocity gas-liquid interfaces, and has also been utilized to validate existing numerical models of these systems. Additionally, the approach has shown promise in providing a framework for designing and operating efficient protocols for optimizing interface interactions in various applications such as fluid control systems.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers by utilizing their spike proteins as "swimmers". This novel finding broadens our understanding of viral behavior in an environment that is protective against many other types of viruses. To make this observation, the researchers developed a cutting-edge technique to observe the viruses at the edge of visibility and found evidence of their movement using advanced imaging methods. This data was further supported by theoretical models suggesting that the viruses' movement is driven by their spike proteins. This phenomenon could potentially be harnessed to target specific cells within the body that are protective against viral infection.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within these crystals permits the existence of chirally behaving phonons, which correspond to atoms circling their equilibrium positions. Given that inversion symmetry and time reversal symmetry govern the total pseudo-angular momentum of the system, this momentum is zero. By introducing dopants, it is theoretically possible to modify the crystal structure, potentially transforming it from a state with inversion symmetry to one with a lower symmetry. Our experimental findings focus on the crystal structure of the potassium compound, showing that it loses inversion symmetry at a particular temperature and transitions into a state with a lower symmetry at a different temperature, where the total pseudo-angular momentum becomes Hall. This transformation is attributed to the emergence of chiral phonons at a specific frequency, whose circulation of atoms just compensates the overall pseudo-angular momentum of the system. The discovery of chiral phonons could lead to significant advancements in the field of spintronics and the production of spin-polarized electrical current.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals and doped semiconductors. However, our findings reveal that, when the conventional approximation is surpassed, nonadiabatic Born effective charges become well defined in metals within a specific frequency range. We also observe that, unlike in insulators, the summation of nonadiabatic Born effective charges from sublattices in metals does not equal zero but rather correlates directly with the Drude weight. These conclusions were verified through calculations using density functional perturbation theory, as applied to aluminum, and to two doped compounds, electron-doped tin disulfide and strontium titanate.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their relevance on a particular scale. As earlier research by Betchov predicted decades ago, this scale is equivalent to the Kolmogorov length, although it's still many orders of magnitude greater than the average free path. This finding suggests that the non-random, or deterministic, form of the Navier-Stokes equation is insufficient for modeling the turbulence dissipation range within molecular fluids. Instead, the fluctuating hydrodynamics equation by Landau and Lifschitz provides a more accurate description within this range. Specifically, our analysis implies that the exponentially decaying energy spectrum and the extreme intermittency in the far-dissipation range of turbulence predicted by deterministic Navier-Stokes equations will generally be replaced by Gaussian thermal equipartition at scales below the Kolmogorov length. High-Reynolds-number simulations based on the stochastic shell model corroborate our theoretical predictions, and demonstrate that the extreme intermittency in the inertial range can extend deeply into the dissipation range, leading to large variations in the thermal equipartition length scale. Our study rectifies previous arguments for the validity of the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation at any Reynolds number and provides a theoretical and physical interpretation of the fluctuating Navier-Stokes equation as a "theory-of-the-effective-field" below a certain cutoff wavenumber $\Lambda$. Furthermore, our high-Reynolds-number simulations show that the most turbulent fluctuations can

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it lacks observable manifestations when time-reversal symmetry prevails due to opposing influences of internal and external states cancelling out. The distinctive response characteristic of a topological insulator manifests as a nonlinear magnetoelectric effect, whose field-theoretical properties and computational models are explored. This contrasts with another phenomenon where a magnetoelectric interaction traps a charge equal to $\pm e/2$ upon exposure to a magnetic monopole, commonly referred to as the Witten effect. The time-reversal symmetry being explicitly violated, as in the case of a topological insulator doped with a small amount of atomic impurities, allows the manifestation of the magnetoelectric current known as the Nikolaev effect.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass various forms of interaction, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process known as design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions and highlights the need for more controlled assessments to inform future research directions.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid/supersolid state.
Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflation virtual "condensate" component.
Consequently, it is anticipated that exotic particles that could explain dark matter will not be detected at the LHC.
Moreover, it is suggested that the de Sitter horizon associated with holographic dark energy acts as a complete absorber for static detectors, given its infinite redshift effect.
As a result, thermal radiation emitted from this future de Sitter horizon may be the source of dark vacuum energy.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By assuming a proximal gradient method is able to recognize the differentiability manifolds in a nonsmooth objective, we show that incorporating Riemannian Newton-like techniques alongside the proximal gradient steps results in a significantly improved convergence rate for specific nondegenerated nonsmooth nonconvex optimization problems. Moreover, our algorithm is accompanied by a numerical study that includes optimizations regulated by $\ell_1$-norm and trace-norm.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our research presents numerous results regarding the characteristics and examples of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. It has been proven that if $I$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ where the product of three non-zero ideals is completely contained in $I$, it then holds that either the product of the first two ideals is completely contained in $I$, or the third ideal is completely contained in $I$. Additionally, it is demonstrated that if $I$ is not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ but a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal, then $I^3 = 0$. Furthermore, the characteristics of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within principal ideal domains and Dedekind domains have been determined

We present new findings for two semileptonic decay processes, $B^0$ decaying into $\rho^-$ and a lepton-neutrino pair, and $B^+$ decaying into $\rho^0$ with the same pair, utilizing data from Belle II's sample equivalent to 189.9/fb, collected using the SuperKEKB $e^-e^+$ collider. To identify these decays, the research involved reconstructing the full recoil B-meson within hadronic end products, after which the researchers computed total branching ratios by performing statistical fits on missing mass square and dipion mass in the candidate signal, determining the former to be $4.12 \pm 0.64 (stat.) \pm 1.16 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$ and the latter as $1.77 \pm 0.23 (stat.) \pm 0.36 (syst.) \times 10^{-4}$. These findings are primarily subject to systematic error due to nonresonant influences on B-meson decay patterns.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of necessary technology, expertise, and
financial resources for sophisticated equipment. While countries like Japan have
introduced more cost-effective and accessible smartphone-based solutions for
automated road condition monitoring, many other countries continue to search for
efficient alternatives. To address these issues, this study contributes in
several key ways. Firstly, it examines the suitability of Japan's approach for
global implementation. Secondly, a substantial, multi-national smartphone-based
dataset consisting of 26,620 images is developed. Thirdly, a set of adaptable
models capable of detecting and classifying road damage in multiple countries is
proposed. Lastly, recommendations are provided for other countries seeking to
adopt successful strategies from their peers. The created dataset is available at
https://github.com/sekilab/RoadDamageDetector/.
