Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions by utilizing expert behavior to directly train agent policies.  The question is, can we confidently know that the policy being trained is, in fact, the expert's policy, or might it possibly be a suboptimal trajectory?  We've found that current ways of testing imitation learning frequently fail to guarantee that the policy being imitated has been truly learned.  We've developed two new approaches based on different f-formulas that can more accurately capture an agent's diversity of behavior, leading to better performance in both online and offline settings when searching for trajectories within an agent's knowledge bounds.  Our results show that these new approaches significantly outperform current methods in identifying the optimal policy when no explicit expert feedback is available.

A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function of the first (Population III) stars hinges on the ultimate fate of secondary protostars that form in areas where outflows from initial (primordial) protostars have ejected material. This material has become enveloped in a surrounding shell, whose thickness and properties vary based on the initial mass of the ejected material. We carried out a set of numerical simulations aimed at determining how the magnetic field affects the ultimate destiny of secondary stars within these shells, using the PM1D code to model the dynamics of collapsing clouds, with results showing that if the magnetic field in the cloud is extremely strong (exceeding 10^-10 G), it causes the cloud collapse to halt and gives rise to a stable filament, whereas weaker magnetic fields lead to altered and faster cloud collapse patterns with reduced fragmentation of the protostar formation region. When comparing simulations of secondary star formation within a 10 times more massive shell versus a more rarefied shell, with either strong or weak magnetic fields, the outcome showed that strong magnetic fields in thick shells prevent protostar formation, whereas in thin shells, the resulting protostar either undergoes further collapse to become a more massive core or, with a strong magnetic field, it either gets spun up into a disk or, with a strong magnetic field and efficient angular momentum transfer, it gets spun down into a solution. In scenarios with weak magnetic fields, thin-shell protostars either get spun down or they collapse,

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate existing notions of redundancy among association rules. We explore alternative definitions of redundancy and introduce new characterizations, highlighting relationships between these concepts. We demonstrate that two distinct notions of redundancy exist, differing in how full-confidence implications are treated. We establish a deduction calculus for each of these concepts, show how to create the smallest possible bases, and also examine redundancy with multiple association rules. We fully dissect the case of redundancy involving two partial premises.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps are being explored as a promising approach to equip advanced wireless networks with situational awareness. They will likely serve a pivotal function in enabling UAV communications by allowing the assessment of signal strength and interference levels at unknown locations. Different from conventional radio map estimation techniques, which depend on uncontrolled sensor measurements, a new method proposes that a UAV collect data at designated locations along a carefully planned route to quickly obtain a reliable map. This route is optimized using a measure that identifies the most informative locations to collect data from. A novel real-time Bayesian algorithm has been created to constantly update the map estimate and the associated uncertainty metric with every new data point, allowing the process to take place in real-time.

This paper outlines a novel approach, GLA, for identifying unusual patterns in discrete time series by leveraging observations over time. At their core, Hidden Markov Models (HMM) capitalize on the idea that these time-series often exhibit underlying structures, which can be used as a baseline to pinpoint deviations. In order to apply this concept, the training process involves optimizing HMM parameters to maximize the probability of observing the given data, given the constraints of the model. However, this method's main drawback lies in its susceptibility to overfitting, which can be mitigated by introducing a measure of regularization. The proposed GLA algorithm represents this trade-off as an optimization problem, resolving it using gradient descent, an online algorithm designed to analyze time series one step at a time, which enables its real-time application. The efficacy of this approach was demonstrated through experiments involving artificial and real-world data, which showed it outperformed existing methods in identifying anomalies.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modality combination, this investigation extends to exploring the effect of incorporating thermal images on verification robustness. Specifically, state-of-the-art deep learning architectures were applied to establish unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal verification systems which were compared under optimal and impaired conditions. Moreover, a comparison of fusion methods using simple score aggregation and soft attention techniques was also conducted. Experimental results obtained on the SpeakingFaces dataset showed that a multi-aspect verification system outperforms unimodal and bimodal approaches by significant margins, both in noise-free and noise-present scenarios. To promote research in the area and guarantee replicability of this research, our source code, pre-trained models, and dataset preprocessed for analysis were made freely accessible on our GitHub repository.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by appending existing examples to create new instances. We've found this approach to be both simple and cost-effective in boosting the performance of pre-optimized Transformer and Conformer models. Specifically, enhancements of up to 2.83 WER and 6.87 WER are seen in the LibriSpeech-960h test sets, and even higher when models were combined with fusion. Moreover, augmenting data in this manner prior to fine-tuning resulted in notable improvements of as much as 5.38 WER and 8.32 WER on the LibriSpeech-960h test sets. We've also observed that the effectiveness of this method is susceptible to factors such as the type of training data and the specific model architecture utilized. As such, we recommend exploring various data distribution methods to maximize the potential benefits.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLEs were explored and we established the consistency and asymptotic normality of these estimators through both theoretical analysis and a simple correlation argument. We also discussed how to calculate the variances associated with these estimators. Our theory is comprehensive and can be applied to various well-known situations such as estimating a parameter that is a mixture of two known parameters $\eta(\theta_1)$ and $\eta(\theta_2)$. Moreover, our theory can handle estimation of the distribution function $F$ where $\eta(\theta)$ is a function of the distribution function $F$. One such example includes estimating the distribution function in a sample selection problem. Ultimately, our results showcase the versatility of our theoretical framework and the effectiveness of our correlation argument in establishing asymptotic results.

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy data analysis in building management systems, the current research builds upon the one-sided differential privacy framework to account for inter-record dependencies. Furthermore, the paper quantifies total privacy breaches when the adversary possesses record interdependence information, as well as demonstrates the creation of an optimization problem for an efficient trade-off between utility and privacy.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not unusual to come across gas and dust emission substructures.
These substructures may have connections to the formation of planets themselves.
Our investigation into the AS 209 gas substructures employed thermochemical modeling using RAC2D and precise observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales project.
Our observations of C$^{18}$O J=2-1 revealed a distinct trough in the center of the disk that couldn't be fully explained by temperature or density considerations.
We discovered that incorporating C and S into the model led to a gas substructures pattern very similar to that observed.
Our results indicate that gas substructures in AS 209 are driven by the disk's surface chemistry rather than the effects of grain growth or evaporation.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial clustering, in fact, the predicted correlation dimension in certain areas is found to be comparable to that of random point patterns. Moreover, we calculated the expected travel time between the start and end of these structures over various timescales and discovered that these times often surpass the age of the Milky Way, implying that these structures are not compact, bound groups but rather dispersing groups. Additionally, we analyzed the chemical composition and radial velocity patterns of these structures, but they did not display distinct patterns. Ultimately, our comprehensive examination of these structures within the context of their spatial, dynamic, and compositional characteristics has led us to conclude that they are not uniquely correlated entities and, as such, do not represent distinct, remote blue horizontal branch associations.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps that enable users to create entire outfits piece by piece while knowing whether each added item will enhance or detract from the outfit's aesthetic appeal. To address this limitation, we've developed a novel Visual Incompatibility Prediction task, where each garment item is predicted with a visual incompatibility score indicating how likely it is to cause visual discordance when worn with other items in an outfit. To achieve this, we've designed a new dataset, CompVis Fashion Incompatibility (CFI), featuring fine-grained semantic labels for outfit pieces, enabling us to tackle the prediction task with a more refined label structure. We've then implemented a dual-stream attention network, combining fashion style and type cues with color-based attention, yielding state-of-the-art performance on the CFI dataset and demonstrating robustness on multiple benchmark datasets, outperforming previous approaches with similar semantic label structures. With this predictive framework, the potential for reducing the trial-and-error nature of outfit creation has never been higher. The code and dataset will be publicly available at: https://github.com/dvdsmples/vision_for_fashion_incompatibility

The framework of quantum resource theory has significantly advanced quantum physics, enabling the unification of diverse research areas through the concept of 'esoteric' quantum states. To develop this unified approach, it is necessary to categorize quantum states into privileged classes. Typically, these classes are defined by means of-preserving transformations or geometric methods. This work introduces a novel purification method that generalizes previously established methods while offering an innovative purification formula for any means-preserving map. This formula provides a unique purification for free states, revealing their maximal component. Additionally, it facilitates the separation of quantum states into two primary categories: those with 'excess' and those with 'deficiency.'

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move up to the surface and how they break apart can be precisely measured. When we expand a liquid substrate surrounding the particle raft, observed material failures occur either by the particles breaking off from the surface they're on, or by the raft itself breaking apart before that. Our research reveals that both of these breakdown methods have unique characteristics. If the particles detach from the surface, they do so uniformly and shrink gradually, influenced by a critical time that depends on the forces holding the particles together, while the breakdown of the raft itself behaves differently, shaped by a combination of its mechanical strength and the expanding pressure from the surrounding liquid. A timescale that considers how long it takes for the particles to detach from the surface and is affected by the mechanics of that interaction can also help us understand and compare material breakdown at various pressures.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. In our investigation, we consider whether the mobility can be enhanced through epitaxial matching of GaN to certain II-IV nitride materials. Our analysis shows that matching GaN to uniaxially compressed strained InSiN or ZnGeN2 results in significant improvements, as the negative mass terms associated with the holes in these materials cancel out the positive mass terms, thereby reducing hole effective mass and increasing carrier mobility along the compression axis. Nevertheless, our findings also indicate that thermal stress poses a significant threat to the mobility gain, especially at high temperatures. Consequently, we suggest growing thin, strain-suspension layers to minimize thermal stress and enhance hole mobility in GaN-based transistors.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments.

We examine isothermic surfaces with a Hopf differential that decomposes into a real function and a specific quadratic differential with a singular point. However, this differential is nonzero and holomorphic throughout the rest of the surface except at this singular point. By focusing on a patch excluding the singular point, we find new isothermic surfaces applying the Darboux and Calapso transformations. Furthermore, we investigate how the transformed patches behave as they approach the singular point and check for continuity in that region.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in terms of convergence. Moreover, this research offers a new perspective on the limiting object of nonparametric estimates of $P$. Furthermore, it is shown that these findings are significant for various spectral analysis techniques for Markov transition operators. Our study also provides a novel asymptotic perspective on the kernel conditional mean embedding, which underpins numerous techniques in kernel-based nonparametric inference.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We explore and define the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated properties. We derive recurrence relations, identities and present comparable results for $\lambda$-analogues of Whitney-type $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and provide a formula reminiscent of the Dobinski-like formula.

The consideration of temporal contexts within knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance for enhanced performance in resultant models, and consequently, in applications that rely on these embeddings. Despite this opportunity, previous research has given it little attention, and models developed to account for time frames often show only slight improvements over their static counterparts. Rather than adapting static models, many current studies have created new models designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs. We propose an alternative approach, SpliMe, that takes advantage of the effectiveness of existing static models by modifying the input data. Our method is informed by the techniques of signal processing and past work in graph embeddings. Our findings show that SpliMe outperforms existing temporal KGE methods, and in certain circumstances, can produce results comparable to the best models, including those designed specifically for temporal knowledge graphs.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for ongoing research regarding infinite graphs and their associated C*-algebras. Moreover, this note specifically explores insplits and outsplits as key examples of strong shift equivalences, demonstrating that these equivalences lead to Morita equivalences that maintain consistency across various weighted gauge actions. Consequently, a question is raised about whether strong shift equivalence can be expressed as a product of insplits and outsplits.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions.

To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and maps it to a covering simplicial complex Y, also with a high dimensional expander structure, by employing a covering space via a probabilistic technique using lifting maps. This algorithm creates a sub-complex Z, a subset of Y with a significant probability, which maintains its high dimensional expander properties and further allows for the creation of a sub-complex with arbitrary degrees of local spectral expansion.

This innovative method offers the first known construction of high dimensional expanders with local spectral expansion arbitrarily close to 1, and it also provides the first known construction of a complex with arbitrarily small local spectral expansion that is also a covering space for a graph with a large gromov gap.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested their performance on multiple task configurations. We subsequently developed and tested a prompt that was optimized for its task representation, and discovered that including answer options in the prompt can significantly lower performance. We believe our findings will stimulate further investigation into the role of task representations in prompts, and could lead to the creation of a comprehensive prompt dataset similar to those existing for task inputs.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's framework. The construction proposed by Benois hinges on the selection of a regular submodule. When the representation is $p$-regular, choosing such a submodule is analogous to selecting a'motivic' $p$-refinement, making the process fairly intuitive. However, when the representation is $p$-irregular, things become more intricate as regular submodules are categorized by a flag variety, resulting in an abundance of choices that involve continuous parameters. Despite these complications, our analysis in select examples highlights how Hida theory and eigencurve geometry can facilitate the identification of a limited set of choices that possess notable arithmetic and'mixed-motivic' significance.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
model to leverage the atoms' sensitivity while minimizing the impact of noise 
without requiring the resolution of complex mathematical equations. In a key 
test, our Rydberg-deep learning system has enabled the direct extraction of 
encoded information from frequency-division multiplexed (FDM) signals, marking 
an important breakthrough in this field, and holding the potential to 
revolutionize the sensing and communication of complex MW fields.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the oscillating CO$_{2}$ density in the upper Martian atmosphere, spanning between 120 and 190~km in altitude, is monitored. This observation sheds light on the effects of gravity waves (GWs), allowing scientists to analyze the behavior of GWs in the upper atmosphere under isothermal conditions and understand the role that the atmospheric background temperature plays in the propagation of GWs. Data obtained from past missions including the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, in combination with the new MAVEN findings, reveal an association between GW-induced density disturbances and the atmospheric background temperature, primarily found in the ODY mission's data collected over polar regions. Conversely, the MGS and MRO datasets show no such correlation. It appears that the presence of temperature and density fluctuations, as well as the characteristics of GWs, rely on the location of the observing spacecraft with respect to the Martian temperature cycle caused by the frozen carbon dioxide, which significantly affects the behavior of GWs in the upper Martian atmosphere.

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons, which can then interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions occur when high-energy ions surpass the range of the strong force, enabled by virtual photons exchanged between the nuclei, whose numbers directly correlate with nuclear electric charge. Given its exceptional energy levels, the LHC serves as the most powerful photon source ever constructed, particularly in favouring photoproduction of heavy vector mesons due to their inherent affinity to photons. Recent experiments examining the forward J/psi production in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV using the ALICE detector are featured.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample one second of audio. Our approach presents a unified model able to produce visually relevant high-fidelity sounds and generate these in under the time it takes for audio playback on a high-end graphics processing unit. We train a transformer that draws upon a codebook obtained from a variant of VQGAN optimized to produce compact spectral samples and utilize these to generate spectral samples, which are then transformed into waveforms through a parametric decoder. Our model maintains the capacity to manipulate input by introducing a style loss and a loss estimating the spectral content within a style-disentangled dataset. It produces sounds resembling those in a dataset after removal of processing steps and can synthesize novel, visually relevant sounds.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and expert tips for efficiently training fully recurrent neural networks, drawing from the Multiple Object Tracking module within our IPO studio software.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates how implementing timely moderate measures can resolve the trade-off between medical efficacy and economic impact, and attributes this finding to the broader concept of 'economic irreversibility,' illustrating its analogy to the principles of thermodynamics. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with linear or sublinear complexity, making it the first system to do so, and has outperformed existing special-purpose and general-purpose systems in benchmark tests.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the AHE is absent. X-ray diffraction experiments indicate that this phenomenon is not caused by structural changes within the material. The investigation further reveals that even in the helical state, Mn$_3$Sn exhibits a significant AHE, which can be attributed to finite spin wave contributions. This discovery paves the way for using pressure-tunable AHE as a tool to modulate spin wave dynamics and explore topological AHE phenomena in helical antiferromagnets.

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. Notably, recent studies have established Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) as the
prevalent approach for RE. In particular, the reliability of DNNs in the forms of supervised
and distant supervision methods makes them highly sought-after solutions. However,
the reliance on substantial labeled data and the supersession of DNNs by newer Relation
Extraction techniques raise concerns over the long-term viability of DNNs in this domain.
Therefore, this article serves as a comprehensive overview, focusing on recent advances
in RE, particularly those of distant supervision relations, where data augmentation via
synthetic data is transforming the landscape of RE. In addition to addressing key challenges
and open issues, we outline promising avenues for future research in this area.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is used to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports is time-consuming and
overwhelming for radiologists, particularly if they have to generate multiple reports
from the same imaging data. Investigating this issue has become more accessible due
to the public release of large annotated datasets, such as the MSKC-10 dataset. It
contains 1,093 diverse medical images along with their accompanying annotations.
 Our solution to this issue involves developing a system that generates coherent
adaptation data by fusing anatomical information with the existing unmarked imaging
data within the same category as the provided annotated data. The generated data
are then utilized to train a diffusion model. The resulting AnatomOR radiologist
assistant significantly outperforms its unsupervised and semi-supervised
counterparts in generating medical reports. It also surpasses several established
radiologist-generated reference data in terms of report quality, demonstrated by
a recent medical image generation challenge called the MIRC-10. Our results show that
integrating anatomical information and generating adaptive data enhances the overall
performance of medical image learning and reporting. It is available at
https://anatomor.github.io/. You can access its code at https://github.com/AnatomOR/AnatomOR.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to technical reasons, the proof requires an extension of the concept of Euler classes to reduced Euler classes, initially developed by another researcher, which creates an interesting correlation between these two areas of study, often having analogous terms but with distinct definitions. The new findings highlight the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, as previously studied areas, and now also their relation to reduced Euler classes.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping cross-checked with a non-parametric test revealed a rising trend in the number of cryptocurrencies with synchronized daily returns in US dollars throughout our study. Finally, our analysis of normalized filtered daily returns using the Del Bue et al. method revealed that from 2016 to 2020, the prices of cryptocurrencies in US dollars converged with those of the analyzed safe-haven currencies and stock indexes, experiencing a year-over-year increase of 35.9%.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation at early time periods. Expanding the existing weak noise theory, which reformulates large deviations into a nonlinear hydrodynamics problem, we reveal its complete solvability through a link with the integrability of the Zakharov-Shabat system. Employing the inverse scattering technique and a newly developed Fredholm determinant framework, we arrive at exact solutions that depend on the specific initial conditions of the KPZ equation, allowing for further generalization to other initial conditions.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed with data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These measurements are then applied to various solar wind plasma intervals. One such interval is scrutinized, yielding valuable insights into its power spectral density fluctuations spanning from the inertial to sub-ion range. Two possible explanations for these density patterns exist, suggesting that they are a result either of specific wave types and interactions at varying scales or a broader physical phenomenon, the two-scale coupling model, influencing the observed turbulence at all scales.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the background from defect information within the fabric's image blocks. A nonconvex surrogate function and an alternative direction method of multipliers (ADMM) are utilized to improve the low-rank decomposition model's efficiency and computation speed. Ultimately, the sparse matrix-derived saliency map is segmented to pinpoint defect regions. Experimental findings demonstrate that this method outperforms existing techniques and successfully detects fabric defects.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems, we introduce a new DRL-based approach that reduces overfitting by limiting the memory consumption of the navigation agent. Conventional DRL methods overfit due to the intrinsic bias of the local critic architecture, which we address by designing a new critic that retains the global view, thus reducing the need for vast observational data to correct policy guidance. We also introduce an Max-Min regularization technique to prevent excessive target overconfidence, which maintains a healthy balance between risk and reward. Our model's observational time is merely 1/10 that of the state-of-the-art, and it exhibits reduced overconfidence and increased navigation success rates.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

The formation of heavy black holes within nuclear star clusters is a well-established theory, but their evolutionary history remains unclear. Certain nuclear star clusters reside at the center of galaxies that date back to the universe's early days, coinciding with the time when stars first formed. To understand how heavy black holes developed, we studied the merger of light black holes, formed during the early universe's initial star formations, and predicted that a significant proportion, around 30-70%, of these light black holes would move into and reside within nuclear star clusters. To verify this, we utilized a reliable model to track the merger of light black holes, starting at 15 billion years ago, and moving through their incorporation into and eventual residence within nuclear star clusters, where they would go on to form heavier black holes, for a specific case study of a galaxy's central nuclear star cluster located 11.5 billion light-years from Earth. For the time period when the universe's initial star formations occurred, our model indicates that a substantial number, around 40-90%, of these light blackholes would move into and reside within nuclear star clusters. For the case study of a galaxy's central nuclear star cluster located 11. 5 billion light-years from Earth, our findings show the incorporation of heavy black holes, with the merger of light black holes, starting at 15 billion years ago, and moving through their incorporation into and eventual residence within nuclear star clusters, where they would go on to form heavier blackholes,

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on active and reactive power control strategies for ESS.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other diagrams, specifically those that go through the $\psi(2S)$ or a three-body decay of $\rho$. The measured branching ratios for $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ are potentially within reach for the BESIII and LHCb Collaborations. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi\pi^+\pi^- \gamma$ decays may be used to determine the couplings $g_{X\psi\omega}$ and $g_{X\psi\rho}$, respectively, which would offer insight into the isoscalar and isovector components of the X(3872) wave function.

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift within the Brillouin zone. In cases of defects, this shift occurs along closed paths in real space, with both instances characterized by non-trivial spin connections. This approach is utilized to determine the spin connections of three-dimensional Topological Insulators containing topological defects. The edge dislocation on the surface of a Topological Insulator generates a spin connection controlled by torsion, allowing electrons to move in confined circular areas and two-dimensional regions. The edge dislocations break parity symmetry, producing a current measured by the in-plane spin component on the surface, with this current accompanied by a tunneling density of states calculation for edge dislocations.

Consider the scenario where $p$ lies between 1 and infinity, $
u$ ranges between 0.5 and infinity, and $\mathcal{S}_
u$ denotes the set of all non-flat half-planes that include the origin and have an angle $\pi/
u$ with the positive x-axis. We generate a corresponding $p$-harmonic measure, $N_{
u, p}$, by solving for a continuous function $u$ on $\mathcal{S}_
u$ that satisfies specific partial differential equations and normalize it so that the functions have mass 1 on $\partial \mathcal{S}_
u$. Our solution allows us to calculate exact values for $N_{
u, p}$'s behavior as $x 	o \infty$, leading to multiple notable conclusions. For instance, at $p = \infty$, we recover a known set of measures. Our results are also compatible with existing work by Barlow-Beltrram-Paulsen and work in progress by Kapula-Kroeger-Rose, thus showing multiple notables conclusions. For instance, at $p = \infty$, we recover a known set of measures. Our results are also compatible with existing work by Barlow-Beltrram-Paulsen and work in progress by Kapula-Kroeger-Rose.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wave height observations, and extreme weather patterns is examined in the North East Atlantic between 2007-2018. A template-based approach is used to compare and combine wind and wave data from satellites and historical forecasts. Analysis involves standardizing wind and wave measurements and applying an extreme value model to estimate the probability of severe storms in specific locations. Results from this investigation reveal a significant decline in extreme weather correlations among Metop satellite wind speeds, wave forecasts, and wave measurements over a 18-year period.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept called manipulability ellipsoids effectively encodes human pose data and task-dependent information, significantly contributing to teaching robots human-like motion through emulation. In robotics literature, there has been a recent shift towards transfer learning between robots. However, no method has been developed yet to transfer learning from one robot to another using task-dependent information encoded in manipulability ellipsoids. This paper bridges this gap by presenting a novel approach to achieve knowledge transfer between two robots using manipulability ellipsoids. The proposed method allows a teacher robot to compress its pose data into these ellipsoids, which are then used by the student robot to recover its parameters. This allows the student robot to replicate the teacher's pose without needing the original data. We validate the effectiveness of the proposed method through simulation studies using pose data collected in a factory environment.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible Z boson pair production background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two b jets and two leptons, examining the prospects for observing Higgs boson pair production in 13 TeV proton-proton collisions with the ATLAS and CMS detectors, particularly when the Z boson decays leptonically. To identify the Higgs boson pair event, our method evaluates the contribution of finite width effects and final state invariants such as the diHiggs jet momentum and the dijet mass, in addition to the matrix element-based analysis variables. By combining these variables, we achieve a significant improvement in signal extraction, attaining a purity of 80\% with the correct identification of the Higgs boson pair in 87\% of events, surpassing the previously proposed analysis which had a purity of 64\% and correct identification in 67\% of events.

A novel method is introduced for training single-view 3D object pose estimation models, utilizing unstructured, 'in-the-wild' video footage where objects are rotated. These scenes are commonly encountered and can be easily gathered (e.g. cars navigating roundabouts, planes near airfields). The combination of traditional structure-from-motion techniques and cutting-edge object detection methods yields a surprisingly accurate 3D pose estimate when compared to established datasets. Building on this foundation, a novel self-supervised regression technique is developed to refine the estimates and minimize initial errors. The proposed method proves competitive in rigorous evaluations against established self-supervised and fully-supervised approaches for single-view 3D object pose estimation in diverse real-world settings.

Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to the adoption of false information; in fact, a proposed novel framework can discern one's attitude toward this misinformation. This new framework leverages neural networks and attitude consistency to classify stances toward COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation. A novel neural framework, utilizing knowledge graphs to organize stances, successfully identifies attitudes toward this misinformation with outstanding results, outperforming other current approaches. Experiments were conducted on the recently created CoVaxMIS dataset, a comprehensive collection of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation gathered from Twitter discussions.

Advancements in attosecond science hold great potential to unveil the core electronic behavior of matter, contingent on achieving two interconnected technological milestones linked to high-order harmonic generation sources. Firstly, achieving a higher photon flux would allow researchers to measure even the faintest electronic processes, while also attaining better spectral tunability would grant selectivity in targeting specific electronic transitions. Breakthroughs are made feasible by parametric waveform synthesis, giving scientists the capability to craft controllable, highly-tunable high-energy electric transients. Our findings demonstrate that by manipulating the waveform of the driving laser pulse via its relative phase and carrier-envelope phase, it's possible to exert fine-grained control over attosecond pulse characteristics. This innovation not only amplifies experimental possibilities in the realm of attosecond science, but also paves the way for a highly sophisticated, coherent manipulation of free-electron paths.

Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data that is no longer accurate. This involves accounting for potential companions that can create recurring periods in time shifts. A study discovered a low probability (0.00005%) of detecting new companions using eclipse time shifts. Researchers analyzed data on Algol ($\beta$ Persei) and found tentative signs of up to five additional companion candidates, which are believed to have orbital periods ranging from 1.863 to 219 years. These signals are consistent across 236 years of data and also matched the first 226.2 years of the data, accurately predicting eclipses for the following 9.2 years. The companion candidates' orbital planes are thought to be aligned due to the stable and unchanging eclipses of Algol since the early observations of Goodricke (1783).

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario.

Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient incorporation of observed data. Despite achieving significant success across a wide array of differential equations, further improvements to computational efficiency are required for this approach. To address this need, enhancing training point generation is an important direction of investigation. Both adaptive and quasi-uniform sampling techniques have previously been explored, each showing benefits. To leverage these insights, we introduce Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, which combines an adjustable nodal distribution method and a memory mechanism. We then conduct experiments on both linear and nonlinear PDEs, evaluating its accuracy and efficiency relative to traditional sampling methods.

This study examines the behavior and simulation of multi-domain ferroelectric FETs by analyzing the oscillations in their electrostatic conduction band profile, which are characteristic of these devices. We model these dynamics by solving coupled two-dimensional Poisson's equations and energy equations, and find that the system converges to a stable thermodynamic state through energy minimization. Our analysis also shows that the movement of domain walls within the ferroelectric material leads to the negative capacitance effect, which in turn affects the device's drain current and variability due to the domain period. We also investigated how the domain wall's soft or hard state transition influences the device's electrical properties and transport. Our simulations are verified through both experimental observation and phase-field modeling.

A significant knowledge gap exists in understanding the Cargo ecosystem's architecture and how vulnerability dissemination occurs within it. Existing studies that generalize security management approaches across multiple ecosystems often overlook the unique technical characteristics of individual ecosystems, hindering direct applicability of security governance strategies to Cargo. To address this disparity, this research employs knowledge graph techniques to construct a dependency vulnerability graph for Cargo and presents an innovative algorithm to identify vulnerability dissemination paths and scope. By conducting a comprehensive empirical study on Cargo's ecosystem, this research investigates vulnerability traits, propagation extent, and factors influencing vulnerability dissemination, revealing that Cargo's security vulnerabilities primarily stem from memory-related issues. Notably, 18% of libraries still harbor vulnerabilities even after updating to the latest version, while 19.78% of Cargo's ecosystem versions are affected by propagated vulnerabilities. This study's findings offer actionable insights for Cargo administrators, developers, and library owners to enhance ecosystem security and presents new concepts for bolstering Cargo's overall security posture.

For analyzing ergodic properties in stochastic dynamical systems, it's essential to demonstrate irreducibility. This paper confirms the irreducibility of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations subjected to discrete jump noises and shows these results apply universally, imposing minimal restrictions on noise conditions. A critical factor in this study is the authors' and T. Zhang's previously established criteria for irreducibility in stochastic equations with jump noises. This proof is then utilized to demonstrate ergodic behavior in stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations and includes scenarios of weak dissipation with jump degenerate noise.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 TeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to identify and count charged hadrons over wide pseudorapidity ranges at the Large Hadron Collider's maximum energy level of 13 TeV, supplementing current detector capabilities with a secondary tracker located between the existing ones, and propose an experimental design for a new detector layer. Three simulated experiments have been conducted to assess the effectiveness of the new design in various physics conditions, demonstrating the capability to record at least 10^7 charged hadrons for pseudorapidity extensions up to 5 units or more over pseudorapidity ranges exceeding 4.5 units. As an alternative, I also examine the feasibility of exploiting the existing detector architecture to measure the hadron production over a reduced pseudorapidity range from -1 to 2, primarily leveraging the silicon tracker within the Inner Detector for the simulated 'TIS experiment conditions.

Deep learning models, specifically Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (DCNNs), are capable of generating robust image representations, but are limited when dealing with orientation transformations. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel model, Orientation Convolution Networks (OCNs), based on Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs), which can learn representations that are less sensitive to orientation changes. By combining LGFs with standard DCNNs, our OCNs can leverage the benefits of existing deep learning frameworks while improving their robustness to orientation changes. Our proposed LGFs are optimized through an evolutionary algorithm and outperform state-of-the-art baselines in various recognition tasks, achieving up to a 40% decrease in false acceptance rates with moderate computational overhead. Additionally, our simulations demonstrate the potential of our LGFs to drive the development of more robust, semi-human image recognition systems.

This study seeks to enhance the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud learning. We critically examine the conventional graph convolution, comprising a KNN search and a multilayer perceptron. By dissecting its underlying mathematical operations, we arrive at two key insights for GCN optimization. Firstly, the 3D point cloud representation's geometric structure is efficiently propagated across the GCN through a simplified associativity criterion. This allows us to rewrite the graph convolution as a series of matrix multiplications based on this criterion, replacing the costly KNN search. Secondly, we identify that the multilayer perceptron can be approximated by a matrix factorization under the criterion. This enables us to simplify the GCN by factorizing the convolutional matrix, thereby reducing the number of parameters. We further observe that successive graph convolutions can be combined into a single layer. Ultimately, our efficient GCN approach allows for substantial inference speedup and up to a 50% reduction in training time while maintaining comparable learning results.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in conceptual meaning but can take various forms visually. Unlike existing Trojan attacks, which embed inconsequential triggers into clean images, our method incorporates significant image details that are difficult to distinguish from the rest of the image. To accommodate this, we propose a novel generation approach, which produces unique and complex trigger images using significant image components from the target model's training dataset. Our approach can create robust and resilient Trojan triggers that are nearly undetectable, using a minimal amount of attack images, and has been validated on several benchmark datasets.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope at the Las Campanas Observatory. By splitting the 50.4 x 53.5 field of view into four subfields, and further segmenting these into 21 individual 0.6 x 53.5 slices, we'll achieve four pseudo-slits, spaced six arcminutes apart. This will allow for a spectral range of 1800 Angstroms with a resolution of 2000. Our current progress includes preparing the optics, coating the first slicer, crafting the mounts, and writing the software, all aiming to enhance IMACS's functionality by facilitating the efficient examination of expansive astronomical objects like nebulae and galaxies.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, key experimental and theoretical findings from a recent analysis by Beck {\it et al.} (Eur. Phys. J. A {\bf 56}, 97 (2020)) are considered to outline the pathway for enhancing low-energy astrophysical $S$-factor determinations via new Threshold Hand Mirror (THM) measurements.

A crucial aspect of discovering and studying exoplanets is identifying terrestrial planets resembling Earth. New studies emphasize the significance of considering volatile depletion in star composition to predict the bulk composition and internal structures of these planets. In this research, we create theoretical models of 1.13 to 1.25 solar mass K-type main sequence stars to investigate how stellar composition affects planetary devolatilization. Our work involves coupling a core-collapse supernova model, 1D stellar evolution, and planetary thermal evolution. Our findings indicate that Planck's radiation field has a limited impact on devolatilization compared to initial thermal fluctuations in young stars, and that planetary devolatilization increases with decreasing stellar mass and metallicity. Our results show that K-type stars' convective zones are generally deeper than in G-type stars, leading to more intense devolatilization. However, our study finds that stellar composition has a relatively small impact on total gas loss through mass outflows and stellar winds, ranging from 10^-4 to 10^-2 Earth masses over a planet's lifetime.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two railway environments under varying conditions, resulting in a superior performance compared to a conventional DNN.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. Now, another example is given which also contests the conjecture originally presented by those authors.

We investigate functions defined on the vertices of the Hamming graphs H(n,q), focusing specifically on those with support contained in the direct sum of the eigenspaces U_i(n,q), U_{i+1}(n,q),..., U_j(n,q) where 0 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ n. Under certain conditions, specifically when n is greater than or equal to the sum of i and j, and when the size of the alphabet is 3 or greater, we identify the functions with minimum possible support and establish a characterization for those with such a minimum. In scenarios where n is less than the sum of i and j, but with a sufficiently large alphabet size of at least 4, we identify similar properties of functions. In particular, we establish a characterization for the functions within the eigenspace U_i(n,q) with minimum possible support in several specific scenarios.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks and their dynamics, but users had to run it locally as a standalone application. To address this limitation, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based platform allowing users to interact with COPASI models through their web browser.
