Built with R using CoRC and Shiny, ShinyCOPASI mirrors COPASI's interface for seamless exploration and enables running tasks available in the original software within a browser. It supports comprehensive models and provides access to advanced features like optimization and sensitivity analysis, along with data export options. Users can utilize a dedicated server to perform background computations, returning results to the web browser. ShinyCOPASI models can be shared and accessed through a dedicated database, available at http://shiny.copasi.org/.

Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and complex differential equations involving both deterministic and stochastic factors.

We are investigating quantum group analogues of the free group factors' radial subalgebras, specifically those of class functions, within the context of compact quantum groups. We found that the algebras of class functions for the free orthogonal quantum groups cannot be maximally abundant *-subalgebras (MASAs) under certain conditions. Central to our research is the concept of a quasi-split inclusion. We demonstrated that the inclusion of the class functions' algebra is quasi-split in certain unitary quantum group scenarios. Additionally, we showed that the resulting subalgebra is non-abelian. We obtained another key finding related to its relative commutant in such instances. In contrast, we constructed specific bicrossed products based on $SU_q(2)$ for which the class functions' algebra constitutes a MASA.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to a local quadratic contraction rate and the costliness of its iterations for many states. Informed by its relation to the semismooth Newton method and the efficiency of its inexact variations, inexact policy iteration, a class of algorithms for large-scale finite MDPs with local contraction guarantees, was introduced. This method is further exemplified through inexact GMRES policy iteration, which applies GMRES for the policy evaluation process. Notably, inexact GMRES policy iteration outperforms policy iteration and optimistic policy iteration by 5.8 and 2.2 times, respectively, in a 10000-state MDP.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and ordinary power series of $I(\mathcal{D})$ share the same equivalence for a specific subclass of weighted directed trees. Moreover, the paper also identifies both the required and sufficient conditions under which the symbolic and ordinary power series of oriented line segments exhibit equalities.

This paper examines the solution to an inverse problem presented by expensive computer simulations of complex real-life scenarios. Specifically, researchers focused on an expensive hydrological model designed to generate realistic data for Athens, Georgia, USA. The objective was to create a practical and efficient approach to reduce the cost of these simulations without compromising the accuracy of the solutions. A combination of global optimization techniques, efficient search algorithms, and effective programming strategies was employed to effectively tackle this challenge. The developed approach was thoroughly tested and validated on a range of scenarios, and its results were compared with alternative methods, ultimately demonstrating its superiority in accuracy and reliability.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required to guarantee the reliable learnability of complex concepts when evaluating a robust model's accuracy and considering the influence of random example exposure, according to Gourdeau et al. (2019). Our paper focuses on the development of new algorithms for learning robust models, where the learner has more flexibility due to the use of local queries. We create the first robust learning model, along with its corresponding algorithms, under the well-mixing assumption (WMA). Our models take into account both random example exposure and local membership queries (LMQs). We develop two new algorithms, the first one adjusts the robust model's accuracy according to the current local bias and uses LMQs, while the second one uses dualistic averaging to optimize robust model performance, all while having access to LMQs. We show that both algorithms meet the required conditions for robust learning as proven in Agarwal et al. (2020), under the given data distribution and WMA. Our work further modifies and expands the findings of Gourdeau et al. (2019), showing the relationship between robust model accuracy and local bias, as well as the dependence of robust learning's success on the current local bias, all under the given data distribution and WMA.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a lone photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead-lead nucleus. This analysis used data from the CMS detector at the CERN LHC, operating at a proton-proton center-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV. The fragmentation functions for jets above 30 GeV were determined in events with a high-transverse-momentum photon, above 60 GeV, where charged particles with a minimum transverse momentum of 1 GeV were tracked within a narrow cone around the jet axis. By pairing with a high-transverse-momentum photon, the trajectory of the parent parton can be well constrained. In central lead-lead collisions, variations in fragmentation functions compared to those measured in proton-proton collisions were detected, however, little deviation was seen in collisions occurring outside the 50% most central range. Jets within the central lead-lead events exhibited a higher yield of low-energy particles, paired with a decrease in high-transverse-momentum particles, roughly transitioning at a point around 3 GeV. This study is the first to demonstrate alterations in parton (dominated by quarks) showers traversing the QGP with a known initial trajectory, also offering a controlled comparison to test theoretical models.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings that non-alternating central binomial series could be solved using level four multiple zeta values, we now show that alternating versions require level eight and can be solved using an alternative approach. This involves the substitution of hyperbolic trigonometric 1-forms for their standard trigonometric counterparts.

Follow-up research on WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, previously reported by Meisner et al in 2020, has yielded an assortment of peculiar attributes for the object. New images taken by Keck/MOSFIRE and HST/WFC3 cameras have established that the object is among a select few with extremely faint proper motion, indicating it has a very low temperature. Specifically, WISEA J153429.75-104303.3 displays the coolest of all known brown dwarfs in terms of M$_{\mathrm{Mons}}$ color indices. Nevertheless, comparing its H-M colors to those in the PARSEC model reveals it has a relatively short age of roughly 10 million years. Spectra obtained from MOSFIRE and WFC3 cameras show quiet H-K and H-WMPC spectra, but rather than being cool, this Y dwarf exhibits H-M colors that suggest a very low mass. In fact, estimating its mass based on these colors suggests a maximum mass of no more than 10 M_J. In an effort to better understand this brown dwarf's origin, researchers have calculated the probability of it being a wide companion to other stars using data from the LAMOST survey, but found no significant connections. Ultimately, identifying the exact nature of this brown dwarf's parent star or stars may necessitate the use of direct imaging, possibly with aid from Gaia DR3's brown dwarf candidate list.

The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that the radial flow remains 
constant regardless of colliding system at the same multiplicity level, 
with observed particle ratio patterns holding true in medium-sized nucleus 
collisions. Also, our research confirms LHC's energy's particle count trend seen in 
previous experiments, along with observed phenomena verifying quark-gluon 
plasma's state of matter's universal characteristics, thereby providing 
significant insights into the phase transition's nature in nucleus collisions.

We develop a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The DPD evolution process utilizes a cost-effective grid-point scheme, enabling the incorporation of two distinct renormalization scales for each parton. The proposed methods account for NNLO DGLAP kernels and flavor matching.

Specimens made of Martian and Lunar soil substitutes, in the form of cylinders, were created using a combination of saltwater and heat, and then fired at various temperatures to analyze their internal structure, strength and contraction. The internal structures of these materials were studied under a microscope and their mechanical properties were tested using a universal testing machine. The experiment was performed twice using different types of simulants for Martian and Lunar soil, resulting in manufactured samples resembling traditional building blocks and the initial stages of 3D printing with a binder. The results indicated that the optimal firing temperature for both types of simulants lies between 1100 C and 1200 C. The compressive strength of these materials met the requirements for building structures on other planets, suggesting their potential for use as building materials in extraterrestrial construction and also as binders in a range of geometries and shapes fired at a lower temperature, similar to those used in traditional building techniques.

The dynamics of a thin liquid film on a fiber heavily depend on the boundary conditions at the liquid-solid interface. This understanding has led to a theoretical model that uses the axisymmetric Stokes equations to examine the effect of liquid-solid slip on a film coated on a fiber. The model reveals that when slip is taken into account, a stable equilibrium state emerges, characterized by a stable two-point or four-point pattern. The stability of these states has been analyzed through linear stability theory, showing that liquid-solid slip can induce the growth of perturbations and lead to a more unstable configuration compared to the case with no slip. The model has been further validated by observing similar behavior in a experiment utilizing microfluidics and a custom designed device to replicate the conditions. The outcome of this study has the potential to provide essential insights into understanding and controlling particle aggregation driven by capillarity.

By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we examine how the observed flux varies with redshift and find that the Prospector predictions match the observed trend at a redshift of about 2. By comparing the Prospector-derived star formation rates to those obtained through another analysis, we confirm that the results are relatively consistent, especially when the stack includes galaxies with a certain range of stellar mass. Finally, we propose that the stack could be used to create a calibration that allows for the reliable use of the stack galaxies and the determination of the galaxy sample's average star formation rate.

This is the initial paper outlining a comprehensive approach to categorize a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the specified category of known type II subgroups under certain conditions on the central charge and level.

We have developed an approach to understand the 4-dimensional C*-algebraic completions of category theory-related concepts, including orbifolds, equivariant objects and morphisms, by applying the concept of base change.

Our approach enables the identification of four unique orbifands that do not fit into any of the existing type II subgroups, and we have made a conjecture regarding the equivariant base change method in relation to quantum completions.

Our findings also suggest that the base change method may have applications in other mathematical fields, such as representation theory and non-commutative geometry.

The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome. Despite its unconventional appearance, the proposed solution aligns with established theories and accurately captures the equation's largest eigenvalue along with associated eigenfunctions, which are quintessential to various applications within population dynamics, neurophysics and other fields.

This work addresses the UbiComp 2021 Challenge presented by Stabilo, classifying handwritten mathematical terms based on time series data from the DigiPen Challenge. We propose a binary classifier for identifying specific terms in mathematical expressions, especially those requiring more digits, given that the provided dataset distinguishes written terms from non-written terms. Our classifier leverages sequential data analysis by applying a Markov chain model to determine classification probabilities. Notably, we developed a comparative framework to evaluate different models and contributed two alternative methods for the DigiPen Challenge. Our solutions, however, focus solely on addressing the mathematical term classification problem.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to generate phone transition probabilities frame-by-frame. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on specific distribution types and mean durations for synthesis, this new approach can model any distribution on non-negative integers. We explore a median-based output generation strategy, which offers advantages such as being more representative, robust to training data irregularities, and enabling incremental synthesis. This method is in line with a broader goal of concurrently modelling durations and acoustic features at a frame-level. Evaluations show that this approach performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods in predicting the median duration of unseen natural speech.

Species distribution analysis can be effectively conducted through occupancy modeling, taking into consideration inaccuracies in species detection data. To address multiple species, states, interactions, false positives, autocorrelation, and data from various sources, various modifications to the fundamental single species occupancy model have been introduced. However, creating high-performance software that can analyze large spatial data sets is still a developing field. A newly developed package, spOccupancy for R, is designed to fit single, multiple species, and combined occupancy models that are sensitive to spatial relationships. Utilizing a Bayesian approach with Pólya-Gamma data augmentation and Gaussian Process neighbor techniques, this package enables efficient model computation even for extensive datasets. spOccupancy provides intuitive model fitting functions that can address various data challenges and offers a flexible predictive framework for multiple purposes. Demonstrations of the package's capabilities are presented through several case studies that highlight its effectiveness in handling diverse data types and scenarios.

Due to a lack of dermatologists, patients experience long waiting times for dermatologic care. Moreover, studies have shown that general practitioners make fewer accurate diagnoses compared to artificial intelligence. The Skincare project aimed to address this by creating an innovative diagnostic and decision support system in dermatology. It combined the capabilities of interactive machine learning with deep learning to enhance the skills of doctors and augment diagnostic capabilities, particularly in the identification of malignant skin lesions. A baseline model, trained using a large dermatology image dataset (ISIC), delivered outstanding results and demonstrated potential for widespread application, including support for both general practitioners and dermatologists. The project also focused on creating effective communication channels between humans and machines to accelerate machine learning progress. In a series of experiments, we examined the impact of varying amounts of annotated data on model performance and found that interactive learning models performed well even with limited data annotation. The project explored four distinct communication protocols with their pros and cons and showed that interactive learning can be an efficient technique for training deep learning models when working data.

To capture the intrinsic variability of type Ia supernovae from limited spectral data, we developed a probabilistic autoencoder that incorporates a Normalizing Flow component after initial training using an Auto-Encoder. The model's two-stage generative architecture can identify a reduced-dimensional representation of SNe Ia, accurately modeling their spectral evolution across wavelength and time directly from data. Introducing a penalty term to address variability correlations and a multi-stage training framework within our physically-parameterized network enabled the separation of intrinsic and extrinsic variability, eliminating the need for magnitude standardization models. The PAE was applied in several tasks to improve cosmological analyses, such as automatically detecting outliers, generating sample spectra consistent with data distribution, and resolving noisy spectral data to infer the correct light curves. Notably, we found three intrinsic parameters that sufficiently describe SNe Ia variability, in line with previous studies. The PAE's two-stage design offers a versatile framework for the probabilistic training of deep generative models on diverse astrophysical data sets.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a gravitationally lensed star-forming galaxy. The outflow is visible in a specific OH+ absorption line, which was measured by the ALMA telescope at high spatial resolution. The data also include CO emission, dust, and stellar light. Analysis of the outflow shows that it has different properties than other elements within the galaxy. The mass of the outflow is estimated to be approximately 6.7 billion solar masses. The outflow's properties are best explained by a conical shape. Depending on the inclination angle, the outflow's rate of gas loss and kinetic energy could be quite high. This suggests that the outflow may impact the galaxy's star formation. The outflow may eventually be re-accreted back into the galaxy, but this would depend on various feedback mechanisms. The estimated gas depletion time in the galaxy is one million years. The presence of the outflow means that other mechanisms, such as feedback, turbulence, and magnetic fields, could also be influencing the galaxy's development.

To study the movement of fluid into a swirling, turbulent plume containing heavy particles that sink more slowly than the plume moves, researchers used controlled experiments in a lab setting. The experiments focused on the effects of particle size, density, and the direction in which the plume gains mass, as well as the direction in which the particles move within the plume. The studies showed that when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, the movement of fluid into the plume increases significantly. The rate of fluid movement increased in direct proportion to the ratio of the particles' gain of mass to the fluid's gain of mass, and this increased rate was independent of particle size. In contrast, when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are the same, adding particles has no effect on fluid movement. The observed increase in fluid movement, which occurs when the direction in which the plume gains mass and the direction in which the particles move are opposites, can be attributed to inertial clustering, a phenomenon where particles move to regions with high turbulence. The increased concentration of particles can cause convective instability in these areas, which affects fluid movement. The observed behavior, which varies based on the direction in which the plume gains mass, can also be attributed to this mechanism. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. By adopting hyperedges to model these interactions, we create more comprehensive models, allowing the transmission rate to depend on the number of infectious contacts a person has. This approach leads us to develop new spectral conditions and study various types of contagion models, considering both the stochastic individual-level model and the mean-field approximation. Numerical examples and the analysis that follows enable the differentiation between inherent disease characteristics and the impact of individual actions. Ultimately, this framework holds potential for a more precise evaluation of the effectiveness of virus containment interventions.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors, exemplified by the study of CrI$_3$, have generated significant enthusiasm due to their intriguing spin-dependent properties and their potential to revolutionize spintronics and magneto-optoelectronics. Through advanced theoretical calculations, researchers investigated the behavior of spin polarization within the prototype ferromagnetic CrI$_3$ bilayer, which has an N$\mbox{m}^2$ magnetic order arrangement. Their investigation includes an in-depth look at the origin of spin crossovers in different layers, the distribution of spin within the layers, and the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of the two magnetic subplanes. Their study showed that spin crossover is primarily caused by the valley-spin coupling effect and also due to spin orbit interaction-induced valley mechanical strain effects. Their results show that spin crossover can be manipulated by applying external strain, which has significant implications for the design of spin valves and other magneto-optoelectronic devices.

Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models with localized $\alpha$-effect and flux-transport dynamos can still exhibit local polarity

Deep multimodal learning using K-fan deep Boltzmann machines offers a novel approach to combine multiple input sources. This method can learn a common representation using contrastive divergence and is applied to classification, information retrieval, and other related tasks. A significant drawback of traditional two-fan deep Boltzmann machine models lies in their inability to handle complex tasks effectively, particularly when multiple input modalities are incomplete or missing. We present a K-fan deep model, featuring a K-branch architecture for handling multi-input, multi-output tasks efficiently. Each branch of the model can comprise multiple layers of neural networks. A shared representation is learned in a discriminative manner to tackle multiple tasks. We propose two optimization methods tailored to joint visual restoration and object recognition tasks. Model parameters are initially estimated through maximum joint distribution and then fine-tuned using backpropagation based on the specific task. Experimental results confirm the effectiveness of the model in utilizing multiple information sources to perform well across various competitive baselines.

The use of model checking has become increasingly essential in validating the correctness of multi-threaded programs, whether they be executed in hardware or as software. Existing model checking techniques, however, fall short when it comes to verifying multi-threaded programs that can be reconfigured or modified on the fly, known as live, dynamic multi-threaded programs. Current testing methods, such as unit and functional tests, also fail to adequately cover these programs by missing complex race conditions and failing to ensure consistency in dynamic scenarios. To address this, we've developed a new testing framework that leverages model checking to systematically identify and counteract severe race conditions in dynamic, multi-threaded programs, even those with intricate patterns of interaction. Our approach, known as RaceRefine, employs explicit hardware models and incorporates a novel type of test generation known as Bounded Scheduling Tests, which are unimplemented and serve as a proxy for actual program executions. By refining these tests within an expanded program model, we're able to identify and prove satisfaction of critical system properties. Our case studies demonstrate that RaceRefine effectively detects and resolves difficult race conditions, outperforming Bounded Model Checking in terms of performance and surpassing existing testing methods in terms of coverage and reliability.

The globally predominant messaging app, WhatsApp, boasts a distinct characteristic 
in its closed nature and user-friendly capabilities of transferring multimedia and
large-scale information sharing to groups, which often facilitates the rapid spread 
of anonymous, encrypted messages. However, the direct delivery of messages to user 
phones enabled by WhatsApp, although personal and immediate, can be exploited to 
circulate baseless rumors and fuel misinformation campaigns. Recent elections in 
Brazil and India are notable examples of such abuse, which have led WhatsApp to 
initiate countermeasures like limiting forwarded messages to a single recipient. 
Despite this effort, the success of these measures remains uncertain. In our study, 
we utilize an epidemiological model coupled with real data from WhatsApp in Brazil, 
India, and Indonesia to investigate the impact of limiting features that contribute 
to rapid information dissemination. Our analysis reveals that current WhatsApp 
restrictions can delay the spread of information but are ultimately insufficient to 
halt the dissemination of highly viral misinformation campaigns within public groups.

We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new individuals at random times following a Poisson process independently of each other. It is assumed that individuals experience mutations at a specified rate under an infinitely many alleles model, leading to population partition by genetic type. This gives rise to a frequency spectrum, denoted by $A(k,t)$, which counts the number of family groups of size $k$ in the population at time $t$. The frequency spectrum process represents a type of non-Markovian branching process belonging to a class of random-characterized branching processes. This work aims to propose approximation methods that replace this frequency spectrum with simpler quantities and assess the asymptotic error associated with these approximations using central limit theorems. Finally, we apply this model through numerical analysis, focusing particularly on the relationship between one of the proposed approximations and Sabeti's Extended Haplotype Homozygosity measure.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. By selectively amplifying key input characteristics and suppressing irrelevant ones, AReLU enables our system to prioritize artifact-related features. Our proposed system was applied to the logical access task using the ASVSpoof2019 dataset and demonstrated improved performance compared to systems utilizing standard, non-adaptive activation functions.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model with local supersymmetry, may offer a way to describe new phenomena beyond our current understanding.  Exploring the cosmic applications of supergravity provides a platform to investigate the potential outcomes of this theoretical framework, which could serve as the low-energy effective theory of superstrings-a potential quantum gravity candidate.  Developing inflationary models in supergravity, however, poses significant challenges stemming primarily from the constraints on scalar potentials and complicated interactions within the framework, as well as the excess degrees of freedom.  Addressing these issues requires navigating the constraints on desirable inflationary paths, moduli stabilization to achieve a stable de-Sitter phase, and ensuring the models' compatibility with established observations of cosmological parameters.  Additionally, the possibility of leaving an indelible mark on the early Universe through topological features or the impact of an axion-like component requires consideration.  This research focuses on the intricate interplay between the Universe's early phases and the supergravity framework, investigating how the cosmological phase could reveal the unique benefits and complexities of supergravity theory.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices.

We are looking for infinite cardinals $\kappa$ that allow for a division of the real number line $\mathbb R$ into $\kappa$ unique Borel sets. The well-known Hausdorff solution indicates that $\aleph_1$ sets work in one instance. Our research shows, however, that the size range for these divisions can vary extensively, allowing a specific set of natural numbers $A$ with values 0 and 1 included to dictate when $\aleph_n$ sets work in a specific forcing extension. The study is expanded to closed sets and similar results found that show uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ sizes for these divisions are fairly arbitrary.

In the 2000s, commodity trading advisors experienced notable gains, largely resulting from their long-term trades in commodity futures. However, their success was suddenly thwarted by a group of traders who engaged in extremely short-term reversals and were able to outmaneuver the commodity advisors. These short-term traders were highly effective and generated substantial profits, which we will refer to as the "paradox of the CTAs." We propose a strategic trade strategy that capitalizes on the complementary nature of CTA investment opportunities by contrasting them with the rapid trading patterns of these short-term reversal traders. The core of our approach involves incorporating simple, straightforward signals that are generated from the analysis of technical indicators on a daily and weekly time frame. It has been tested on a dataset covering the period from 2005 to 2016 and revealed that a strategy of "splitting the road" between these two types of traders yields an annual return on investment of 14.1 percent, outperforming the commodity trading advisors by 13 percentage points and matching the average annual returns of a broad index that tracks the performance of commodity-based trading strategies.

Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, particularly for obscure or fragmented traffic, a reliable detection method is essential for thorough analysis. The main issue with conventional approaches is that they rely on specific criteria for each protocol or application, which can be difficult to modify or extend for less common traffic. In contrast, we present an innovative method for efficient and adaptive application protocol identification, focusing on distinct communication patterns rather than arbitrary headers or footprints. This approach utilizes a sophisticated finite state machine, trained on comprehensive, publicly available traffic datasets, which enables it to detect protocols efficiently and accurately. The proposed technique exhibits superior performance, particularly in cases of fragmented or encrypted traffic, outperforming existing methods.

Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is difficult to regulate. However, we found that superconducting strips atop thin magnetic films can completely reflect magnons through their magnetic resistance to stray magnetic fields. The significant frequency shifts resulting from this response effectively halt the forward flow of magnons perpendicular to the magnetic field. By positioning two superconducting gates in parallel with the magnetic field, we were able to create a confined magnon system. The added capability to control coherent magnons enables new functionalities in magnonic devices, including reconfigurable logical circuits and stronger connections to other systems of degrees of freedom.

A beneficial approach for gathering user insights while safeguarding user anonymity exists in federated learning. Nonetheless, novel classes emerging from unauthorised access to sensitive data pose a significant threat to the privacy of users, which was unforeseen during FL development. The ease with which such invasions can be utilized to build deceptive models that deceive other users or the central server illustrates the gravity of this issue. In response to this, we have created a system using federated learning that can counteract the impact of such invasions, particularly those resulting from unauthorised access to sensitive data, through a sophisticated information-theoretic approach called the Wasserstein GAN metric, allowing for the measurement of the impact of such invasions, the detection of their occurrence, and the prevention of their effects on the central server. Our novel solution has been successfully tested across various scenarios, which demonstrate its usability and effectiveness in the real world. Our code and data are publicly accessible and can be found at https://github.com/IIAI/IGWAN.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing high-dimensional entangled systems, specifically the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. Initially, we apply our approach to measure a complete three-photon GHZ state across three dimensions and then extend it to multi-photon systems within higher dimensional settings. In our model, both hyperentanglement of photons and the quantum Fourier transform are crucial components. The proposed solution will serve as a useful resource for developing high-dimensional quantum computation and communication.

This research paper delves into the problem of uplink cascaded channel estimation in multi-user multiple-input-single-output systems aided by intelligent-reflecting-surfaces operating within the sub-6 GHz frequency range where channel propagation isn't sparse. A high-performance, low-overhead estimation protocol has been developed to minimize reflection power loss without requiring on-off amplitude control. The proposed solution exploits a common structure within the system, significantly reducing pilot transmission overhead by decomposing the complex cascaded channel into separate user-specific and shared variables. The challenge of highly coupled estimation variables is overcome through the use of optimization-based estimation methods utilizing channel covariance. An alternating optimization algorithm has been developed to efficiently solve the resulting non-convex problem, with an efficient initialization technique ensuring a local optimal solution. The research further introduces a successive convex approximation algorithm for optimizing the protocol's training phase, leading to improved accuracy. The authors conduct comprehensive simulations, which demonstrate the proposed algorithm outperforms existing solutions by up to 12 dB in terms of estimation quality.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences. Using a distinct dataset of over 750,000 articles from over 300 outlets between April 2020 and February 2021, our results show that local news outlets initially covered COVID at a rate influenced by national death rates but ultimately became less correlated as other issues like the U.S. elections dominated headlines. Additionally, our research reveals that local news COVID coverage varied based on the area's politics, news outlet popularity, and audience size, and also indicates that disadvantaged populations received less pandemic-related information.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To simulate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. By testing this system with the 'give-N' task - where it's given a binary vector and has to pick 'N' items - we discovered that it showed a similar inflection point in learning. Furthermore, our AI, built using the modular network structure known as the ESBN, was able to learn patterns that allowed it to accurately select items outside of its initial training scope, similar to how humans can apply learned concepts beyond what they initially learned.

Bloom filters provide quick approximations of set membership while consuming minimal memory. These filters help engineers prevent time-consuming actions, such as accessing a disk or the network. A potential substitute for Bloom filters is the cuckoo filter, which often needs less storage and processes information faster. A different solution, the Bloomier filter, has been proposed as an expansion of the Bloom filter. A modification to this concept has also been explored, particularly by Dietzfelbinger and Pagh. Their variation of the Bloomier filter can serve approximate membership queries efficiently, though no comprehensive testing of it exists to date. A different filter was developed, the xor filter, as an implementation of their idea, offering more effective efficiency and speeds. Notably, the developed xor filter can surpass both Bloom and cuckoo filters in performance, all while consuming even less storage space than these solutions. A compact variant of the xor filter was also designed (xor+), resulting in storage needs similar to or smaller than already compressed sequences while providing similar speeds to those seen in Bloom filters.

Several key connections between convex geometry and holomorphic line bundles on smooth projective varieties or K\"ahler manifolds are explored. Our investigation focuses on the relationship between positive products and mixed volumes, leading to the definition and examination of a novel addition technique for divisor classes and mixed divisor classes. We establish new geometric inequalities for divisor classes and provide alternative interpretations of classical convex geometry concepts within the framework of algebraic geometry. Specifically, we recontextualize the Alexandrov body construction, Minkowski's existence theorem, demonstrating their analogues with divisorial Zariski decomposition and the duality between the pseudo-effective cone of divisors and the movable cone of curves, respectively.

A new approach aims to derive market trend insights from dynamic price equations, specifically those that describe how future prices converge to optimal values, thereby maximizing trading volume per unit of time. This methodology stands out for its inherent ability to select a suitable time frame, which is automatically identified by analyzing past market activity and determining the state of highest trading efficiency. To facilitate trend analysis, both historical and forecasted price data are considered, with past prices represented by lagging values and forecasted prices represented by advancing values.

This paper presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, FLVoogd is an implementation of the Voogd protocol, a federated learning distillation method considered robust and trustworthy. To protect user privacy, FLVoogd employs differential privacy and arm-based client data encoding techniques. This implementation was validated through rigorous testing on various attack scenarios, utilizing real-world data from the MNIST dataset and the CIFAR-10 dataset, with the support of open-source code availability.

We successfully submitted the winning entry to the NeurIPS 2021 - AWS Deepracer challenge, which required developing a self-driving vehicle model that interacts with its environment through action-reward interactions. The objective was to create an autonomous vehicle model that navigates a simulated track, adapts to real-world settings, and completes a lap at maximum speed while staying on course. The competition was part of The AI Driving Olympics (AI-DO), a series that fosters embodied intelligence advancements in autonomous driving, by bridging the gap between theoretical advancements and practical challenges in the field.

Significant progress in deep learning technology has enabled the creation of more convincingly authentic deepfakes, which have sparked interest across multiple sectors due to their vast potential applications, despite raising serious societal and security risks. This chapter examines the advancements and difficulties in the production and identification of deepfakes, and also explores the potential solutions to improve the resilience of deepfake detection for a broad range of media, such as real-world images and videos. Furthermore, it proposes future research directions for tackling deepfake-related issues.

The identification of sub-Neptune exoplanets receiving irradiance levels similar to Earth's revitalized the prospect of discovering potentially habitable worlds over the coming decade, with some temperate planets potentially harboring liquid water oceans, provided they do not possess massive H2/He envelopes that would cause them to be excessively hot. Characterizing the masses of these envelopes in planets larger than Earth, especially those with masses of 1.7 to 3.5 Earth masses, remains a challenge to assessing their habitability potential. We demonstrate that observable differences exist between the solubility equilibria and thermochemistry of carbon and nitrogen gases in small vs. massive H2 atmospheres, with the requirement for a liquid water ocean and thermal equilibrium being inherently conflicting. Thermochemical recycling of carbon and nitrogen in the massive atmosphere of a temperate exoplanet typically produces CH4 and NH3, while a small atmosphere atop a liquid water ocean would contain CO2 and N2, with the presence of photochemically produced CO and CH4, and reduced NH3 due to dissolution in the ocean. These distinctive atmospheric compositions produce distinctive features in the planet's transmission spectrum, primarily driven by the absorption features at wavelengths around 4.2, 7.8, and 9.8 microns. We utilize modeling of the planet Kepler-452b to demonstrate that carbon dioxide's ocean-saturated pressure, which significantly influences the planet's radius, depends heavily on the atmosphere's thermal structure, primarily

Inspired by the classic discrete-time model of nervous activity proposed by McCulloch and Pitts in 1943, a new continuous-time model, known as the McCulloch-Pitts network (MPN), has been developed for sequence learning in spiking neural networks. This model employs a localized learning rule, in which synaptic weights update solely based on the accessible information at each synapse. The model leverages the asymmetry of connections between binary neurons to effectively learn and memorize multiple temporal patterns of binary vectors, an ability similar to that of symmetric Hopfield networks for spatial patterns. Furthermore, our study reveals the model's capability to efficiently acquire sequences of binary images and generate neural spike-train data. Our model adheres to spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) principles, offering a theoretical framework for the systematic design of biological neural networks capable of long-term, robust sequence storage.

This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) challenge.
The competition highlighted an underinvestigated area in Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology: accurately reading previously unseen text in real-world images during model training.
The dataset compiled for the competition comprises a diverse collection of 326,385 images, encompassing 4,864,405 text instances.
To address the challenge, a distinct validation and test set was created, comprising scene text that was not present in the training data.
The competition featured two recognition tasks: a holistic approach to reading full text and a focused task involving cropped text segments.
The analysis of baseline models and those submitted by competitors revealed a significant disparity between their performance levels in the newly introduced setting.
The proposed dataset will play a crucial role in further research to enhance the development of more versatile scene text models capable of providing more reliable predictions when given less context.

A specific type of chaos expansions can effectively analyze differential equations with uncertain factors by approximating random equilibrium states associated with such equations. This study integrates principles from validated calculations to provide precise error assessments alongside findings about chaos expansions representing random equilibrium states. This approach also develops a new framework for validated tracking, which entails accurately calculating separate solution branches in parameter-dependent systems and generalizes seamlessly to multi-parameter tracking.

The increased use of sensors in industrial settings has led to the widespread collection of high-dimensional data, despite this comes with its own set of difficulties. Notably, gathering a comprehensive set of readings is challenging due to the inherent limitations of sensors and available resources. Moreover, industrial applications often involve complex systems where the degradation of components typically results in subtle, initially hidden changes in the data. To tackle these problems, this research focuses on developing an adaptive monitoring strategy for high-dimensional data, emphasizing both effectiveness and resource efficiency. Our approach begins by accurately identifying the relevant features within the data using a normalized fuzzy clustering method on a subset of features. Subsequently, a meta-guided classifier is utilized to detect anomalies in the selected features, where the classifier is informed by a fuzzy classifier operating on the full feature set. To minimize resource usage, our method involves dynamically resizing the feature subset as needed, initially expanding it as anomalies are detected and then refining it further when possible. Our approach is evaluated through simulations using both synthetic and real-world data, where its performance is shown to surpass that of alternative methods.

We have created a detailed analysis of the origins and development of two disrupted galaxies that merged with the Milky Way's outer layers: the Gaia-Sausage Enceladus (GSE) and Wukong/LMS-1 systems. Our sophisticated computational model, designed to simulate galaxy growth patterns, is based on exponential infall scenarios and allows for reliable fitting of these patterns. Our analysis led to the discovery of key time frames: 1.01 billion years for GSE to form new stars, while 10 billion years ago, the system experienced initial infall and then maintained its stellar formation for about 1.5-2 billion years. Conversely, the star-formation times for Wukong/LMS-1 were roughly estimated to be 3.36 billion years. Our model showed strong consistency with predicted patterns in metal spread, radial movement, and mass relationships when comparing the two galaxies. Our findings also indicated slight discrepancies between our results and other researchers' estimates of these galaxies' formation metals, spheroid ratios, and mass estimates. Our infall model showed strong consistency with observed data across multiple systems, including both galaxies mentioned above, as well as other systems that merged with the Milky Way. Our analysis developed the use of reliable time frames for studying these galaxies' development and the resulting dynamical movements within their structures. Our computational model, designed for analytical purposes, is now ready for integration with other researchers' data to explore the rich history of galaxy interactions within our cosmic

Given a profinite group G, an S[[G]]-module is a G-spectrum that fulfills certain criteria, leading to the definition of the homotopy orbit spectrum X_{hG} associated with an S[[G]]-module X. When X's constituents meet specific finiteness criteria, a homotopy orbit spectral sequence arises with an E2-term being the continuous homology of G, taking coefficients from the Tate cohomology of G's continuous groups, further mod 2 or 11. This sequence converges in a way that its graded pieces are isomorphically paired.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling cuts labeling costs by nearly twenty to one, while maintaining comparable performance to traditional fully-labeled datasets.

The EuS/InAs interface has gained attention due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using a computational model that incorporates machine-learned data and density functional theory, we have studied how varying the bonding configuration at the interface impacts the electronic properties. Across the examined configurations, we observed that the energy levels at the interface in InAs are positioned higher than those in EuS. Furthermore, we discovered novel states that arise from the interaction between the two materials, and are localized at the interface due to charge transfer. The arrangement of atoms at the interface significantly influences both the energy position and distribution of these states. While an induced magnetic effect is evident in InAs, the magnetic moment is relatively weak.

A comprehensive classification system for subsets of Baire space, categorized by Borel Wadge classes, has been introduced with enhanced effectiveness. Based on Montalbán's true stage machinery, we leverage this innovation to offer an alternative demonstration of Louveau and Saint-Raymond's separation theorem. This leads to a demonstration of Borel Wadge determinacy within the $\text{ATR}_0+\Pi^1_1$-I system of second-order arithmetic.

Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising demands for accurate predictions and thorough analyses. However, they necessitate a considerable amount of computational power and time for processing. Previous studies on pruning have focused on enhancing inference efficiency, but there's been limited research on effectively decreasing training costs. Our proposed framework, ClickTrain, efficiently and accurately enables both the pruning and training processes of CNNs by incorporating a series of innovative techniques, including a structured and adaptive pruning method, a weighted path removal approach, and a module-based re-training strategy, all of which are integrated into an end-to-end framework. Experimental evaluations have demonstrated that ClickTrain can significantly reduce the training velocity by a multiple of up to 14 times while achieving nearly complete and 90% of the original accuracy within a similar timeframe, respectively. Moreover, ClickTrain can be applied to diverse pruning techniques, such as different types of metrics, filters, and reduction ratios.

We establish a dual introduction to monoidal extensions introduced by J. A. Dunn for certain mathematical structures, specifically bounded distributive residuated lattices. This specific introduction focuses on the core properties of these structures, similar to a previous introduction by S. Metcalfe and D. Meyer for negation in various mathematical contexts. This new introduction is part of a comprehensive framework developed by the authors to introduce concepts such as implication, fuzzy connectives, and modalities in a duality consistent manner. This particular study also explores the relationship between introductions and extensions, specifically how certain mathematical extensions affect the introduction of concepts within that structure.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy.

A new discovery has been made regarding a gas giant exoplanet, which orbits around a star called TOI-5542 approximately every 75 days. Initially detected by the TESS satellite, the exoplanet, which has a radius similar to that of Jupiter, has been further confirmed using data from ground-based spectrographic equipment. Analysis of this data has shown that the exoplanet, which has an estimated mass roughly equivalent to that of Jupiter, likely formed through migration or by remaining in its original location rather than being formed by a specific high-energy migration mechanism. Further study found that the host star, which is approximately 10 billion years old, has a metal composition that deviates from a commonly recognized trend of metal-rich giant planets being formed around metal-rich host stars. Interestingly, this study found that both heavy and lightweight gas giants orbiting either warm or hot stars have higher-than-average metal compositions. TOI-5542b is a notable addition to studies of planetary composition due to its relatively cool temperature, which prevents it from expanding in size as a result of exposure to its star's heat.

Sequential decision-making in operations management problems, such as those governed by constraints, can be addressed using the constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). Two main obstacles arise when attempting to solve CMDPs for the development of optimal operational strategies: they are often characterized by large state and action spaces, and it is difficult to quantify the likelihood of certain situations. To overcome these challenges, we develop an algorithm that employs a sampling approach to generate data based on the policy being evaluated. By refining our initial findings, we derive conditions under which the CMDP solution can be considered asymptotically optimal. We also expand upon our method by presenting variants that address specific challenges, such as situations where actions do not have a direct correlation with the outcomes, and scenarios where the objective is to maximize a mixture of short-term and long-term rewards. Through numerical experiments involving a production control problem with a complex system characterized by stochastic and dynamic properties, we demonstrate the efficacy of our asymptotic algorithm, and we also analyze its performance relative to established solutions for the exact CMDP.

This research outlines a method for recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols when not using an actual input device, offline. The approach involves segmenting symbols accurately into over 300 categories. Since many complex mathematical symbols require both horizontal and vertical projection to be split, but certain symbols, like the square root symbol, can't be processed this way. What's more, handwritten mathematical symbols can look very similar, for example, handwritten zero and the Greek letter null. Given the numerous mathematical symbols, over 300 in total, a highly effective classifier capable of recognizing such a wide range of symbols must be developed. Initially, this study addressed the challenge of segmentation by applying the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering method. Results showed that the accuracy of the designed kNN classifier was 84% for the salient features, while 57% and 53% accuracies were achieved with the Histogram of Oriented Gradient (HOG) and Linear Binary Pattern (LBP) methods respectively for the salient features. Also, pixel intensity had an accuracy of 43% for the 66 classes considered. The use of the modified LeNet architecture achieved an accuracy of 90% for 87 classes and the SqueezeNet architecture reached an accuracy of  for 101 classes.

A geometric interpretation is provided for superconformal quantum mechanics based on a hyper-Kahler cone that has a symplectic resolution with equivariant symplectic properties. In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. The growth characteristics serve as a theoretical prototype for the duality concept we introduced between a 7D black hole and superconformal quantum mechanics.

We examine the relationship between network architecture and disease propagation in the contact process. Starting with a general probability distribution for network nodes' connections, we map the problem to a specific model of random walk. We observe that the probability of disease spread exceeds that of a homogeneous network with the same average connection rate, and we provide specific examples to illustrate this phenomenon. Additionally, we offer an intuitive explanation for these observations and outline potential future research directions.

Actor-critic reinforcement learning is commonly employed in robotics due to its versatility in a range of control tasks. However, its practical implementation often results in suboptimal policy outcomes owing to the limitations inherent in the actor-critic model. To address these shortcomings, our approach integrates the actor-critic model with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) for a hybrid framework termed the Hamiltonian Policy. In doing so, our novel method has numerous benefits, primarily in the reduced noise level produced by generating action recommendations, thus resulting in more efficient learning and improved transferability of the learned policy across a range of related tasks. To evaluate the effectiveness of the Hamiltonian Policy, we utilized the robotic swing-up of a double pendulum as a test case and observed that our method resulted in a notable 2.5x reduction in the regime change frequency, in addition to achieving 3x and 1.5x more robust pendulum control than the standard actor-critic model and its variant with Guided HMC, respectively.

It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, searching for these twin primes at the level of their respective generators makes practical sense. This paper introduces a novel strategy for verifying the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing a sieving approach to extract all twin primes at their corresponding generator levels. In the context of $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers, $x$, we are referring to numbers that satisfy the condition that $6x-1$ and $6x+1$ are relatively prime to the prime $p_n$. We can demonstrate the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing the average gap distance $\bar{\delta}(p_n)$ between the $\omega_{p_n}$-numbers in an indirect manner.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects.

Nereid, a satellite of Neptune that holds the distinction of being the largest outer satellite that can be spectroscopically analyzed, exhibits an irregular orbit. Our analysis focuses on Nereid's spectral characterization utilizing its reflectance spectrum between 0.8-2.4 $\mu m$, particularly in the unexplored 0.8-1.4 $\mu m$ range, as we attempt to identify the spectral absorption features that correspond to its icy composition. Our findings indicate the presence of crystalline water ice, coinciding with existing observations. Nonetheless, using simple models consisting of intimate water ice mixtures, we fail to attain a comprehensive match of absorption bands, especially considering the spectral continuum, at the wavelengths of 1.5 and 2.0 $\mu m$. This could be resolved by accounting for both crystalline and amorphous water ice, as well as taking into account the influence of sub-micron grain sizes. Furthermore, combining magnetite with components of the CM2 chondrite Murchison offers a feasible framework for understanding the spectral variations among objects like Nereid, particularly in those with neutral-sloped spectra. It's worth noting that magnetite provides a fitting explanation of Nereid's spectral continuum, eliminating the necessity of incorporating Tholin-like organic substances. Our analysis also reveals that non-ice components of outer solar system bodies may closely resemble those found in carbonaceous chondrites, as proposed by Fraser et al. (

Let $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$ be the ring of lower triangular matrices of order $n \geq 2$, consisting of elements from the finite field $F(q)$ of order $q \geq 2$. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2T_n(q)}$. Studies have proven that over the projective line based on $T_n(q)$, we find $(q+1)^{(n-1)}q^{\frac{3(n-1)(n-2)}{2}}$ affine planes of order $q$, where points and lines within such a plane satisfy specific submodule properties. These affine planes are ultimately shown to be extendable to a projective plane of order $q$, where free cyclic submodules corresponding to non-unimodular pairs form the 'line at infinity'. This approach offers the possibility of generalizing this concept to arbitrary $n$ in a direct manner.

In a 1986 paper in J. Symbolic Logic, Pawlikowski demonstrated that under specific conditions regarding Cohen and random reals, certain model properties can be inferred within extensions of those models. This is proven through a novel application of Tukey-order with models, expanding upon an existing concept introduced by Vojtáš in 1991. By leveraging this notion, it can be shown that certain model properties can imply each other, thereby establishing key theorems related to random and Cohen reals within these models.

A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. The proposed method uses Monte Carlo counterfactual policy evaluations and minimizes the potential loss in untreated states to create a pessimism-based Q-function. The pessimism-based value function is found by optimizing this function under the constraint that the current state's Q-values sum to zero. The method has been shown to consistently outperform alternative offline data methods, like Q-learning and Bayesian Q-learning, in both small and large problems, as well as online data-based approaches, when the coverage condition isn't met with offline data. The method has been implemented in R through the dtreatlearn package and applied to two practical problems in policy evaluation and optimization, which consistently yielded superior results.

Dualities between subcategories of finitely generated modules over Artin algebras can be defined by the relationship to Wakamatsu tilting bimodules, with specific cases yielding known dualities. When restricting these relationships to subcategories of finitely generated modules with particular dimensions, previously established correspondences and dualities on tilting modules are reaffirmed. The implications of this relationship include demonstrating equivalences of derived categories of finitely generated Gorenstein-projective modules, as well as the invariance of certain algebraic invariants under tilting transformations.

A proposed Witting configuration, with a different complexity of 40 rays, could reformulate the Penrose model for spin-3/2 systems based on a dodecahedron's geometry, to study quantum mechanics' nonlocality and contextuality. An alternative setup using 120 states is examined in this work. Despite their different sizes, both arrangements are linked to a common 8D lattice with 240 fundamental vectors, tied to the E8 Lie algebra. An exploration of this setup's properties employs many comparisons to the E8 Lie algebra itself.

In a certain class of superconductors with flat bands, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. For this type of superconductor, we've developed a theoretical framework that describes the behavior of bosonic and fermionic excitations using a effective field theory. By applying our framework to study bosonic dynamics in flat band superconductors, we've discovered that certain properties of these superconductors are similar to those seen in ultracold atomic gases. By examining the impact of weak interactions between bands that are far apart, we've found that certain excitations in these superconductors are able to carry energy and momentum. Furthermore, we've discovered that these superconductors may exhibit signs of instability, such as developing density waves or stripe patterns, under certain conditions. By studying these possible instabilities, we've found that certain excitations in these superconductors may be able to transfer their energy and momentum to the superconducting state, leading to a possible transition to a peculiar state known as a Frohlich superfluid.

The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid.

Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies, genetic information, and linguistic analyses examining word occurrences in texts. Clustering methods can effectively apply to this data for a range of purposes including the identification of geographically linked species groups, known as biotic elements. Various clustering approaches can be utilized to process such data including the use of latent class mixtures under the assumption of local independence, hierarchical clustering based on the Jaccard distance, or applying continuous data methods to the multi-dimensional scaling representation of the data. These methods can be varied significantly by altering their underlying assumptions, and there is no universal consensus on which technique produces the highest quality results. To evaluate and compare these methods, a simulation study was conducted, where artificial presences-absences data was generated and then analyzed using the mentioned techniques, assessing their performance through multiple metrics such as the adjusted Rand index, as well as a new metric, the adjusted Kulczynski index. Our results indicate that the performance of the used methods differs depending on the true cluster structure, and certain methods perform well in simulations that mimic real-world conditions, while exhibiting lower success rates in other scenarios.

In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing with RGB and RGB-D images separately often necessitates the design of specific network architectures. This paper proposes an efficient and unified structure that integrates cross-attention context extraction to effectively tackle both tasks. By effectively fusing two inputs (for RGB images) or three inputs (for RGB-D images) with a cross-attention mechanism, our framework leverages the rich information present in both RGB and depth features. This structure's simplicity and efficacy enable efficient extraction and fusion of contextual information. As shown by experimental results, our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on various datasets in terms of multiple evaluation metrics.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8136 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5243, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

A number, N, can be termed a palindrome if its binary format is symmetrical. In this paper, the relationship between the quotients of these symmetrical numbers is explored and several fundamental questions about the resulting sets of integers and fractions are answered. We demonstrate the feasibility of solving this problem using a precise formula, by ascertaining if an integer, N, can be expressed as a division between two identical symmetrical numbers, A and B. Upon determining representability, we pinpoint an upper limit on the value of the smallest numerical component. We then prove that a certain set of numbers has a higher frequency of occurrence within the set of all natural numbers, N.
