We achieve analogous results when examining quotients of numbers whose binary format is anti-palindromic, meaning the second half mirrors the reverse of the first. In addition, several numerical data points, as well as intriguing hypotheses and areas for further investigation, are provided.

Computed Tomography (CT) is extensively utilized in both engineering and medical fields for creating detailed images of internal structures within various subjects and objects. Since most X-ray sources emit X-rays of multiple energy levels, which vary in their absorption rates, the process of reconstructing images typically involves a reverse ray transformation process. Omitting these variations may result in image distortions such as beam hardening, which poses an additional challenge. In certain settings, the dual effects of radiation and electronic signal degradation caused by devices such as CCD cameras contribute to image degradation. A proposed variational reconstruction model effectively accounts for these two distinct types of noise as well as the polyenergetic X-ray source, and further distinguishes between materials with unique attenuation characteristics. In support of this model, the proposed iterative algorithm has been mathematically justified and verified with numerical reconstructions of data collected from a test setup.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, this study develops a novel data creation approach rooted in Bayesian Program Learning (BPL). Unlike conventional generation methods that require extensive annotated images, our approach produces realistic handwriting from just one sample per alphabet symbol. After creating these symbols, synthetic lines are produced for training leading Handwritten Text Recognition models without the need for line segmentation. Thorough evaluation and analysis affirm the efficacy of the proposed solution.

We have developed a novel storage approach that significantly decreases the required memory by approximately two orders of magnitude, allowing us to compute three-nucleon interaction matrix elements with more precise limits in ab initio calculations. Our scheme enables us to reach higher energies of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements than was previously achievable. We have demonstrated that our storage approach leads to converged calculations for the ground-state energy of a certain nucleus. Our study further examined how the computational methods converge when calculating three-nucleon interactions. Our findings indicate that certain computationally costly elements can be disregarded due to being artifacts that vanish with more precise calculations. Our study ultimately shows that the ground-state energy of a certain nucleus agrees with its measured value. Our work now makes it possible to compute accurately heavy atomic nuclei through ab initio calculations.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to explore one-dimensional topological phases through practical investigations of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This includes analyzing zero-energy states, evaluating insulating and conducting properties, and examining the effects of different wave functions on the system. Hands-on calculations with realistic parameters are encouraged to illustrate the concepts of edge states, backscattering, and topological transitions.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators within Bergman spaces associated with certain bounded, convex domains in complex n-dimensional space containing non-trivial analytic circles in the boundary. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc.

We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to harmonic sums, specifically alternating nested ones up to weight three. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that they converge to a finite value.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.

We introduce family universal U(1)X models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, by defining U(1)X as a composite of SO(10) U(1)Y and U(1)χ gauge symmetries. To incorporate quantum gravity effects, we propose the introduction of a Dirac fermion χ as a dark matter candidate that's odd under gauged Z2 symmetry post U(1)X breaking, leading to a natural realization of isospin-violating dark matter with a natural f_n/f_p ratio of -0.7, thereby evading LUX, PANDAX and XENON1T experimental constraints. Furthermore, our work encompasses the investigation of masses and mixings for Higgs and gauge bosons, LHC constraints on Z' mass, dark matter direct and indirect detection experiments, resulting in viable parameter spaces for further study. To determine LHC Z' mass bounds for generic U(1)X models, four different scenarios are examined, with scenario II featuring no U(1)X charge for right-handed up-type quarks allowing a relaxation in the LHC Z' mass bound.

A specific measurement technique must be used for assessing the mechanical characteristics of straw tubes designed for charged particle detection, operating in a vacuum environment. The underlying equations that govern straw behavior when subjected to internal pressure are documented, alongside the introduction of an experimental approach in this paper to investigate strained, pressurized straw tubes. The presented research also focuses on measuring the Poisson's ratio of the straw wall for the NA62 spectrometer, with the ultimate goal of determining the minimum pre-tension required for the straw's structural stability.

In various fields, ensuring decision functions maintain their optimal performance under changing conditions, even with limited knowledge of their environment, is a top priority. Our study introduces an approach for quantifying how well decision functions withstand uncertainty in the form of credal Bayesian networks, which are parametric models representing the unknown environment with confidence intervals on key variables. Focusing on the 'Maximum Marginal Probability' (MARmax) issue – the maximum possible error probability when misclassifying data, given varying parameter possibilities – our approach transforms MARmax into a more manageable problem on a probabilistic circuit with restrictions. Utilizing an efficient simplification, we provide a theoretically grounded upper limit to MARmax, calculated within linear time relative to the circuit's size, and our experiments demonstrate that this bound is usually precise, and our approach outperforms existing solutions in terms of efficiency.

In a supersolid Bose-Einstein condensate with a spin-orbit coupling, an accelerated impurity atom exhibits oscillations that mirror Bloch oscillations in solid matter, despite causing condensate excitements that give rise to internal phonon modes. However, these oscillations have no impact on the condensate's roton minimum position, thereby preserving its periodic matter wave pattern. Notably, the oscillations fade primarily due to wavepacket dispersal; yet, by assuming the impurity behaves as a bright soliton, the decay can be largely countered.

In a generalised quadrangle, a code is a subset of the vertices with its minimum distance determined by the shortest path between distinct elements. The elements of this subset are divided into distinct sets based on their distance from the code. Given the quadrangle's graph has a diameter of four, both the minimum distance and maximum distance from a vertex to its closest code element cannot exceed four. If the minimum distance is four, it signifies the code is a partial ovoid or partial spread; a code is fully classified as either an ovoid or spread if it also has a maximum distance of two. A neighbour-transitive code is defined as having an automorphism group that transitively acts on both the code and its closest neighbouring elements. The study focuses on classifying neighbour-transitive codes admitting insoluble automorphisms in thick classical quadrangles and finding neighbour-transitive codes of minimum distance four in the classical quadrangle W_3(q).

Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring-like formation, where analysis of the 870 $\mu$m continuum map from ATLASGAL, obtained via the APEX Telescope Large Area Survey of the Galaxy, revealed notable anisotropy in gas density within this area using a two-dimensional correlation function. By applying a two-dimensional Taylor expansion method to a high-density map filtered at 40 pc, we identified both radial and angular anisotropies in gas density; their respective contributions varying with distance. While the signature of radial anisotropy dominates at distances less than 80 pc, the signature of angular anisotropy becomes apparent beyond this distance. We further observed that the angular anisotropy exhibits a notable shift towards higher densities at larger radii, where it displays approximately double the correlation scale at 220 pc as at 50 pc. We hypothesize that this shift might be a sign of the CMZ transitioning from highly dense, small-scale structures to larger, more extensive, molecular complex formations.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering swift changes within the material's electronic system that unfold over the duration of the pulse. The way X-ray fluence influences nanoscale electronic dynamics is intricately tied to the material's initial conditions, yet precise predictive models are hampered by our limited comprehension of initial conditions' impact on developing electronic excitations. We've conducted an exhaustive study that explores how varying fluence affects XANES changes in nitrogen-doped water, attributing this phenomenon to two distinct influences: changes to the absorption edge energy resulting from local electric field effects and electronic structural modifications within pre-existing excitations.

This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling techniques. The design, which consists of a simplified digital unit and an analog temperature measurement system, offers exceptional accuracy and reliability, ultimately resulting in a robust temperature sensing system. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process and thoroughly tested through comprehensive thermal experiments. Specifically, the temperature sensor demonstrated a 0.1°C resolution, an absolute inaccuracy of 3.5°C, and a stability of 50ppm over a 0.1V voltage range. Moreover, the design's digital subunit enables dynamic temperature measurement even when the analog circuitry is in a power-down state, thereby minimizing energy consumption during idle periods.

Quantum entanglement serves as a cornerstone for quantum information science and technologies. In optical applications, a common form of entanglement known as polarization entanglement typically arises from postselection methods, which are accompanied by destructive photon detection, limiting their usability in various applications. In this research, a new strategy is proposed to create entangled states of polarized photons without requiring postselection, instead opting for a heralded approach that ensures ready availability of entangled resources. By applying the quantum scissors technique to manipulate a specific type of entanglement known as continuous-variable entanglement, it is possible to create the desired hybrid entangled states, which are a combination of both discrete and continuous variables. We present two methods of implementing this technique, each utilizing a different technique to create the desired polarization entangled states: the first based on single photons and linear optics and the second using a two-mode squeezer. By examining both implementations and discussing the benefits and limitations of each, this research provides a foundation for developing entangled resources for practical applications in quantum information processing.

This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. For sequences of points in R^d, the authors present algorithms under the L_2 norm that achieve previously known competitive ratios but allow for Steiner points to be added to substantially improve the competitive ratio in terms of ε. However, the authors also prove that eliminating the dependence on n in dimensions d ≥ 2 is not possible, while providing improved lower bounds under the L_1 norm: Ω(ε^(-2)/log ε^(-1)) in the plane and Ω(ε^(-d)) in R^d for d≥3.

Accurate categorization of IoT devices is a critical requirement, with implications extending to security and data protection aspects. Research has successfully applied machine learning methods for identifying IoT devices, with positive outcomes; yet current approaches disregard the costs involved in extracting device features from network data. This work presents a more practical viewpoint, contending that feature extraction comes with expenses varying across distinct features. Moving beyond existing binary misclassification assessments, this study proposes adopting multiple loss measures according to device misidentification rates, thus introducing the first limited regret algorithm for IoT device classification. This approach ensures the algorithm's performance loss remains within predefined bounds as long as its data input is drawn randomly from a specified uniform distribution. Additionally, the study simulates different network environments to demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

This research presents a novel and straightforward technique for word-alignment that leverages bilingual information from external sources like machine translation platforms. We demonstrate that a model with limited parameters can achieve performance comparable to GIZA++ when trained on a relatively small dataset. Furthermore, in contrast to GIZA++'s increased complexity with additional features, our approach's training time and parameters do not scale up. Notably, our method's reliability is ensured by the external translation data, eliminating the need to set threshold parameters. Additionally, since translation data is abundant and diverse, the method can be augmented with various sources without difficulty.

We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting primordial black holes using PopSyCLE, we modified the code to account for a dark matter halo composed of these hypothetical black holes. Our population model includes key factors, such as the ratio of dark matter to primordial black holes and the average mass of these black holes. By running simulations with different combinations of these variables, we generated a probability distribution of lensing event rates and masses less than 0.1 solar masses, providing a theoretical basis for future lensing surveys to guide their expectations and evaluate the validity of primordial black hole models.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of six aligned spheres of gradually decreasing sizes, and the shape of these molecules was defined solely by the ratio of the smallest to the largest sphere diameters, referred to as parameter $d$. The systems' phases were studied as a function of parameter $d$ and the packing density $\phi$ of the molecules. When the packing density was below a certain threshold, such systems displayed liquid crystalline properties with multiple possible smectic and nematic phases present. These findings were in agreement with previous peer-reviewed articles. The simulated systems displayed periodic structures in multiple directions, determined by parameter $d$, and these patterns flipped in response to changes in the system's temperature, and were dependent on the length of the molecules' wedges. These periodic structures emerged in two forms: one where the molecules were packed tightly together in layers, and another where the molecules formed chains. The layers themselves were found to consistently exhibit the same pattern of molecule arrangement across the system, while the molecule chain pattern showed more variation. The occurrence of layer pattern and molecule chain was found to be influenced by the average area of the system's cross-section per molecule, and these two patterns were found to coexist in certain regions defined by the parameter $d$.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

A conventional imaging scenario hinges on three essential elements: a light source that illuminates and scatters off the subject of interest; a means to detect this scattered light; and a detector that can resolve spatial information. However, the typical ingredients of imaging may be insufficient for delicate biological specimens or sensitive samples due to the inadequacy of available light-detecting capabilities and potential harm from light interaction. To overcome these limitations, we have developed a quantum imaging protocol that achieves all this by leveraging the unique properties of a Michelson interferometer and combining it with induced coherence-based nonlinear interferometry, coupled with the use of a single-pixel imaging method. By doing so, we have successfully performed interaction-free imaging of a structured object using undetected photons, thus pushing the boundaries of quantum imaging to the point where object interaction and photon detection are minimized. This innovation lays the groundwork for utilizing induced coherence-based nonlinear interferometry for various applications, including but not limited to, quantum and classical microscopy, and light measurement, without the need for direct interaction with the sample.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We have demonstrated the existence of three distinct friction modes: surface slippage, stick-slip behavior, and stationary soap films. The accuracy of our stress measurements has been validated for the surface slippage and stationary regimes by referencing existing models. Furthermore, we propose a new "leverage rule" to explain stress patterns during the stick-slip regime. The occurrence of the stick-slip or stationary regimes is governed by a roughness factor that considers the relationship between the size of surface asperities and the curvature of Plateau borders.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective.

We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement of its electronic mass is slightly less than expected from earlier research. These findings amplify the need for theoretical models more advanced than the random phase approximation. Contrary to the hypothesis suggesting significant acceleration of the carriers due to their interaction with spin fluctuations, our results do not support this theory. Additionally, a comparison with previous electron loss data indicates that sodium's mass enhancement due to dipole-type electron-hole interactions is substantially less than its mass enhancement due to monopole-type interactions measured using ARPES.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We present an innovative solution to overcome this limitation, using a system that undergoes free expansion without an external influence, and demonstrate that the proposed method aligns with thermodynamic principles. Our solution identifies the dissipated energy as a thermodynamic average of work performed by each individual microstate and confirms its nonnegative value during free expansion, which holds surprising implications.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections and curvatures within a symplectic manifold framework, specifically focusing on globalization. We'll demonstrate how curvature graph weights can be explicitly defined through a hypergeometric function and an even simpler expression that combines it with a formula for connection graph weights. Notably, we examine a cotangent bundle case, leading to a substantial simplification of the curvature expression.

We explore solitary waves known as "nanoptera," characterized by exponentially small oscillations, in two precompressed systems based on the Hertzian model, particularly woodpile chains and diatomic chains with woodpile structure. These solitary waves emerge from the interaction of two waves in the respective systems. Our analysis focuses on the existence and dynamics of nanoptera in the precompressed woodpile chain, where it has been assumed that certain small parameters are involved. We establish the existence of nanoptera in the precompressed woodpile chain and woodpile trimer, and also investigate their localization through numerical computation, revealing that nanoptera exhibit strong site-to-site oscillations. Additionally, we reveal the dynamic behavior of nanoptera in the precompressed woodpile chain and woodpile trimer, and also control their movement by imposing specific forces at selected sites. Furthermore, we gain insight into the general behavior of nanoptera in the precompressed woodpile chain, and also its associated spectrum, through the application of semi-classical methods, where it has been observed that the spectrum is composed of multiple bands, each associated with specific modes of motion, including internal and external motions, and also solitary waves, where the peak amplitude of these solitary waves increases with decreases in a certain small parameter. Lastly, we also establish the existence of nanoptera in the precompressed diatomic woodpile structure, where it has been observed that the peak amplitude of these solitary waves can be made larger by introducing smaller and smaller parameter values.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the scale of their production, leading to unconventional cosmological outcomes. This is similar to how non-degenerate classical oscillations behave, affecting the inflationary dynamics in a predictable way. Primordial features, whether due to oscillating primordial features or other mechanisms, could give rise to classical energies exceeding the quantum scale, providing a more comprehensive understanding of their effects. This is evident in models like the Monodromy scalar inflation, where the feature's strength is directly proportional to the oscillator's amplitude. This proportionality allows for the possibility of the feature exceeding the quantum scale, giving rise to a new classical era of inflation, characterized by the oscillator's dominance and the feature's scaling. However, this scenario would render the scalar inflation unstable, leading to the prediction of a higher tensor-to-scalar ratio for the feature than for the background. This could serve as an indicator for identifying the feature, providing further insight into the inflationary dynamics.

Consider a graph of even order G and its complete graph counterpart K_G. A pairing of G refers to a perfect matching of K_G. A graph has the PH-property if for each pairing of K_G, it shares a perfect matching that, when combined, creates a Hamiltonian cycle of K_G. Cubic graphs that possess the PH-property have been fully characterized by Alahmadi et al. in 2015, and it follows logically that quartic graphs should be the subject of characterization next. In our work, a class of quartic graphs called accordion graphs is defined, parameterized by n and k, which we designate as A[n,k]. We find that a specified family of infinite quartic (also circulant) graphs that possess the PH-property belong to the general class of accordion graphs. The paper delves into the properties of accordion graphs in terms of pairings, which sometimes exist within them, as well as circuits within them, and establishes the relationship between the ACC-property of an accordion graph and its pairings.

We carry out a finite-time scaling analysis near the detrapping point in a three-state quantum walk model. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. The initial state is a symmetric superposition of two coin operator eigenstates with mixing angle $\theta$. One eigenstate corresponds to full wavepacket spreading at $\theta_c(\rho)$ where none of the wavepacket remains near the initial position. At the detrapping angle, key metrics such as survival probability and participation ratio exhibit one-parameter scaling behavior. Moreover, we demonstrate that the participation ratio grows with time, specifically in a logarithmic-corrected linear fashion, thereby resolving reported sublinear tendencies.

This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, our research highlights the significance of incorporating a momentum encoder, employing multi-crop training, and using small patch sizes when utilizing ViTs. Building upon these insights, we developed the DINO self-supervised method, a form of self-distillation without the need for labelled data, and demonstrated its effectiveness by achieving an 80.1% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when evaluating ViT-Base linearly.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate various cosmological parameters, including the Hubble parameter, the deceleration parameter, the density of the dark energy component, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its based cosmological model. Our results show promising agreement with the observed data. This model also successfully removes the discrepancies arising from the Lambda-CDM model when compared to the observed values of the cosmological parameters. Our analysis further confirms that the model is capable of describing both an early dust-like phase and a late phase of the dark energy component, characterized by a value for the equation of state parameter that is less than -1, which supports the accelerating

We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through multiple tasks, demonstrating its ability to create high-quality, tailored images and compositions.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these processes, we use effective field theories to describe interactions between fermions and spin-1 bosons. We particularly focus on the J/ψ decay into a dark current, which has been constrained by experiments. We discover that the J/ψ invisible decay into a dark current doesn't have enough signal to detect either light sterile neutrinos or sub-GeV dark matter within currently established limits. However, the invisible decays of the ρ and ω particles could be more indicative, given their similar characteristics to the J/ψ particle.

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely strong magnetic fields, present throughout the solar cycle. These features, extensively detected in solar images, play a significant role in understanding the solar atmosphere's behavior, particularly in addressing the long-standing issue of coronal heating. This research aimed to examine the size, speed, and distribution patterns of magnetic bright points in the solar photosphere, using datasets from the SOT/Hinode and HiFI/GREGOR telescopes, to gain insights into their characteristics. Employing an automated algorithm to detect magnetic bright points, their movements were tracked, and their statistical properties were analyzed, revealing distinct distributions of area, diameter, and speed. The results indicate that these characteristics exhibit two-component structures, pointing to the presence of two distinct populations of magnetic bright points, associated with different types of magnetic flux elements, and influenced by the varying spatial resolutions of the telescopes used.

Human vision can distinguish objects and actions using spatial or temporal data, but integrating these aspects remains unclear. This study demonstrates how the human visual system can effectively combine spatial and motion information, enabling recognition in scenarios where individual sources are insufficient. Researchers achieved this insight by analyzing'minimal videos' - brief clips that facilitate reliable object, part, and action recognition, but are unrecognizable when spatial or temporal constraints are compromised. Unlike existing deep networks, humans exhibit more adept performance in these complex configurations, highlighting missing dynamic vision mechanisms in current models.

Dark particles interacting through Abelian gauge symmetries and ordinary matter through kinetic mixing result in the manifestation of broken $U(1)$ magnetic monopoles in our observable universe as milli-magnetically charged entities confined under electromagnetism. However, the strength of their dark magnetic interactions with ordinary matter is significantly constrained by observations of galaxy halo ellipticities. Furthermore, the ground state of dark monopoles initially stable and chargeless becomes quantum mechanically unstable under an external magnetic field, potentially releasing energy on an astronomical scale. If even a single dark monopole were to be created, it is proposed that it would either be charged under a dark $U(1)_D$ or neutral under an unconfined $SU(N)_D$ gauge theory, leading to the conclusion that the dark monopole's mass would be minima when the confining scale of the dark theory is low, as this would result in a large mass from the static potential. Consequently, it becomes possible that the dark monopole's mass could be within reach of future experimental or theoretical adjustments to lepton or quark condensation, as the relevant numerical estimates demonstrate.

The rapidly evolving Earth Observatory research area has immense potential to utilize AI in real-time weather forecasting. This work addresses the challenge of accurate weather prediction by leveraging the video transformer network. Building on existing research into vision transformer architectures, we address the limitations associated with their high computational complexity and data-hungry nature. To achieve this, we propose combining Video Swin-Transformer with a dedicated data augmentation method, and employing a gradual spatial reduction on the encoder and cross-attention on the decoder. The efficacy of our proposed approach was tested on the Weather4Cast2021 challenge dataset, where we successfully predicted 8 hours of future weather frames from hourly weather sequences. After normalizing the dataset for evaluation consistency, our model achieved an MSE score of $0.4637$ using training data, and $0.4422$ with transfer learning. This effort documents the development of a new weather forecasting model, which outperformed existing approaches with a notable reduction in parameters and computational complexity of $2.96$ times and $1.52$ times respectively.

In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, determining which models can host dark matter. The variety of models arises from different arrangements of vacuum expectation values, leading to vacua with either one or two vanishing expectation values. In our research, we concentrate on vacua where the $S_3$ symmetry is fully, partially, or partially then fully broken. Our findings reveal multiple potential dark matter candidates and valid scenarios, emphasizing the need for further study into the significant and vast $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet model space.

A comprehensive study on the PPT square conjecture is presented with a notable achievement: the PPT square conjecture's validity has been rigorously demonstrated for the case involving finite-dimensional space.

Intracellular transportation is crucial for delivering vital substances to complex branched neural structures, enabling their survival and operation. Disruption of this process is associated with various neurodegenerative diseases, making it vital to understand how neurons control transportation to target essential areas. We introduce a new optimization model that simulates the material transportation mechanism in complex neural geometries by minimizing congestion. The model adheres to partial differential equations that describe transportation based on molecular-motor-assisted models and is solved in complex tree structures through isogeometric analysis. We test our model by introducing different parameters that mimic traffic congestion, specifically investigating the effects of reduced microtubules and swirling structures on material transportation. Our simulations effectively demonstrate both the optimal material transportation in healthy neurons and the occurrence of congestion in neurons with abnormalities, illustrating the significance of both geometry and microtubule structure in facilitating optimal neural transport processes.

Billion-dollar losses inflicted by banking fraud across the globe make graph-based fraud detection in transactions increasingly significant. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to identify real-world transaction network patterns, specifically network motifs within a heterogenous transaction dataset. We also present a method for generating genuine banking transaction graphs via randomization. The goal is to evaluate the practical application of this method in the real-world, aiming to improve graph-based transaction analysis accuracy.

In a black hole-white dwarf binary system, we examine electromagnetic and gravitational waves emitted during a process where a white dwarf loses mass to a black hole through tidal forces. We simulate this scenario using a quantum hydrodynamic model and represent the white dwarf as a zero-temperature Bose-Fermi droplet. When the white dwarf approaches its point of closest approach to the black hole, it loses a portion of its mass, causing the black hole to experience an influx of matter. This mass accretion leads to the generation of intense bursts of electromagnetic and gravitational radiation, echoing patterns observed in recently discovered X-ray sources. The energy emitted from the accretion process initially manifests as brief, high-frequency bursts at each close approach, but eventually, the surrounding disc becomes a sustained source of radiation, emitting electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a continuous pattern.

Three-body decays of heavy hadrons in the form of $X \to YZ$ are commonplace,
notably when $X$ and $Y$ are part of the same heavy doublet and share a common
$u$-quark, as in the case of $\Sigma_b^+$ and $\Lambda_b^+$ decays.
To describe these types of decays accurately, a new approach is proposed,
utilizing form factors in an expanded manner to account for the contributions
of all four possible two-body decay modes linking $X$ and $Y$.
The form factors' dependencies on $q^2$ are examined, with the observation that
they exhibit distinct patterns for different heavy hadron doublets.
Further research is needed to analyze the $X \to Y \to Z$ transition form factors,
as well as the resonant states $X(3872)$ and $X(3960)$ for their respective
decays $\Sigma_b^+ \to \pi^+\ J/\psi$ and $\Lambda_b^+ \to D^0\bar{D}^
{-} \pi^0$.

Jim\'enez, Becerra, and Gelbukh (2013) introduced the "symmetric Tversky ratio models" with parameters $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ where $\alpha$ ranges between $0$ and $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than $0$. The inverse of each $S_{\alpha,\beta}$ function, denoted as $D_{\alpha,\beta}$, represents a semimetric for all possible subsets of a given set. Our research found that the function $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ is indeed a metric if $\alpha$ lies within the interval from $0.5$ to $1$ and $\beta$ is greater than or equal to $0.5$. The verification of this outcome was confirmed by showing that $\alpha$ can be treated as a nonnegative weight of the first term in $D_{\alpha,\beta}$. Furthermore, each $D_{\alpha,\beta}$ can be expressed as a linear transformation of the standard metric $D_1$ and the evidence-based metric $D_{0.5}$.

Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only during training, a constraint that's hard to meet in practice. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an innovative framework consisting of two stages. Firstly, it adapts the synthetic blur data to match real-world blurry images by learning a module that simulates real-blurry data. Secondly, it uses this adapted data to supervise a motion deblurring network previously trained on synthetic data on a path that's continuously active during inference. This framework allows for reliable and accurate motion deblurring results even with low-quality real-world blurry inputs, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in various scenarios.

Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of exhibiting autonomous Hebbian learning through multiple input channels. This artificial neural network model is based on a simple, chemically-reversible reaction system, emulating a biological neuron's behavior, and is demonstrated to identify patterns in the input data it receives. In addition to the fundamental reaction system, the researchers propose more complex variations that incorporate enzymes and compartmentalised reactions to simulate biological systems, as well as a DNA-based system built upon the principle of DNA strand displacement. These innovative models offer promising avenues for exploring autonomous learning and potentially developing biological intelligent systems.

The ultrapower of any ordered set is created as a refined version of the set itself by taking into account infinite sequences of elements from it. This process involves dividing the sequences into classes according to a set of rules defined by an ultrafilter, leading to a set that always satisfies a fundamental property of ordered sets. It turns out that a set's openness determines its ability to fulfill the open completeness property in the refined version, whereas its original cardinality dictates whether the refined version is complete.

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those datasets, thus overlooking each dataset's distinct features. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework that integrates dataset profiling into the benchmarking process, matching models with the most compatible profiles and ranking them accordingly. To accomplish this, we develop a dataset profiling module that extracts, annotates, and analyzes the fine-grained, computational implications of each dataset. Then, a new benchmarking strategy is designed to identify models that excel on the dataset-specific computational axes it identifies. Our approach was tested in experiments involving real-world scientific datasets and deep learning models for image, sound, and text analysis, where dataset profiling successfully predicted up to 80% of the performance differences observed when these models were applied. Furthermore, the profiles themselves were found to be predictive of model performance, suggesting that certain computational characteristics of datasets may be inherent to their domain and utility. Ultimately, this research underscores the importance of considering the unique computational needs and capabilities of scientific datasets in benchmarking applications, enabling the accurate and efficient evaluation of models based on their relative fitness to these datasets' characteristics.

Hadwiger's Coloring Conjecture asserts that every graph with t colors includes a complete graph with t vertices. This has been reinforced by another theory suggesting if a given graph is assigned t colors, where a certain set of its vertices uses every possible color, then that graph must have a complete graph with t vertices within it. This more robust idea has been tested with success for the case of t = 4. This result holds further implications for 5-colored graphs; specifically, we can confirm a revised and more robust version of the original Hadwiger's conjecture, where 5-colored graphs contain complete graphs with 5 vertices within them. This has further implications for 5-critical graphs in the same scenario.

This research introduces an advanced algorithm for efficiently recovering smooth graph signals through generalized correntropy, and a specific loss function is formulated accordingly. Derived from the aforementioned principle, the algorithm is developed, and its optimal parameters are mathematically justified. Utilizing the beneficial properties of kernel width in adaptive algorithms, the paper proposes a systematic approach to choose the kernel width and the correlation coefficient. The theoretical stability of the algorithm is guaranteed, and its performance is compared with state-of-the-art methods through numerical simulations, demonstrating its superior recovery precision and reduced computational complexity.

Theoretical investigations are conducted to design and control entangled atomic states formed through spin-changing collisions within a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate for use in a more robust atom interferometry capable of withstanding common technical problems like detector limitations. It is discovered through both analytical and numerical examinations of the spin-changing collision process that utilizing a small initial disturbance as a trigger, as opposed to vacuum fluctuations, yields superior results despite reduced entanglement. Our findings have implications for optimizing entangled atomic state production for future large-scale entangled atom interferometers.

The purpose of this research paper is to derive optimal estimates for the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem involving the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. This problem seeks to minimize a specific functional over all nonzero functions in the Sobolev space, and involves several variables and constants, including $p$, a bounded mean convex domain $\Omega$ in $N$-dimensional space, and a smooth norm $F$ on this space. We discovered new lower and upper bounds for this eigenvalue problem based on the first eigenvalue of a one-dimensional nonlinear problem. Specifically, for positive $\beta$ we proved a lower bound for the eigenvalue and for negative $\beta$ we proved an upper bound. Furthermore, for positive $\beta$ we were able to derive a lower bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the anisotropic inradius of $\Omega$, and for negative $\beta$ we were able to derive an upper bound for the eigenvalue in terms of the parameter $\beta$.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a framework that can deal with irregular data. Our analysis explores how the complexity of GCNNs can be broken down into manageable components of simpler NNs and discusses the implications of these findings for the development and interpretation of GCNNs.

A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Comprehensive experiments have been conducted across multiple languages in diverse settings, and the results clearly indicate that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin.

We've investigated the transition form factors $f_+(q^2)$ and $f_-(q^2)$ [alternatively $f_0(q^2)$] for exclusive semileptonic $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ $(\ell=e,\mu,	au)$ decays using the standard light-front quark model based on light-front quantization. Conventionally, $f_+(q^2)$ can be determined without considering troublesome elements, but $f_-(q^2)$ typically includes such difficulties. However, our study reveals in the Drell-Yan frame ($q^+=0$) that the results obtained using $(J^+, J^-)$ for $f_-(q^2)$ are equivalent to those derived from $(J^+, { f J}_\perp)$ without including treacherous components. Furthermore, our calculations provided the form factors and branching ratios for $B	o D\ell
u_\ell$ $(\ell=e,\mu,	au)$ decays, enabling comparison with experimental data and theoretical model predictions. While our findings for ${m Br}(B	o D\ell
u_\ell)$ generally agree with experimental data except for $B^0	o D^-	au
u_	au$, we also evaluated the ratio ${\cal R}(D)$ for various $B	o D$ transitions and contrasted these with other predictions.

Theories of supersymmetric Yang-Mills with algebra so(4N) can have non-trivial, invertible-defying symmetries. By utilizing holographic duality, we can determine the branes equivalent to these symmetries, and deduce the fusion principles for the symmetries through brane dynamics.

Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the isomorphism problem for unordered Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs, known as the CFI-query, which has remained undefined within CPT despite being classified as a PTIME decision problem. A significant development has been achieved in understanding CPT's expressive power in addressing this issue by formulating a partial characterisation of solvable instances based on symmetric Turing closures of CPT: for every graph class, the CFI-query is defined within CPT if and only if it can be automated through a Turing machine with symmetric oracle queries. This breakthrough reveals that the CPT model's inability to resolve the CFI-query issue stems from its inherent limitations in handling queries dependent on the graph's structure rather than its vertices, leaving numerous questions about the intersection of CPT and PTIME, along with potential applications in database theory, intensely debated.

In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition with increasing amounts of Bi substitution at the Eu site. To explore the electronic and magnetic properties of the material, researchers performed a comprehensive study using various computational methods incorporating experimental data. Utilizing structural information, researchers evaluated various electronic band structure models to find the one with the closest match to experimental results. Ab initio calculations were then conducted on several concentrations of Bi-doped Eu2Ir2O7 to gain a deeper understanding of its electronic properties. Surprisingly, these calculations revealed that the metal-to-insulator transition can be attributed to a shift in valence electrons from Ir 5d to Eu 6s states, rather than a change in Ir 5d states' bandwidth. Additionally, the lack of significant spin-orbit coupling influence on the electronic structure led researchers to speculate that Eu2Ir2O7 may exhibit weak Ferromagnetism due to electron correlation. Notably, these calculations also discovered that the material exhibits a strong tendency toward electron pairing in various Bi-doped concentrations, suggesting that the compound could potentially exhibit novel superconducting characteristics.

Consider a metric space ${\mathfrak M}=({\mathcal M},\rho)$ and a Banach space $X$, with a set-valued mapping $F$ that maps ${\mathcal M}$ to the family ${\mathcal K}_m(X)$ of compact convex subsets of $X$ of dimension $m$ or less. Our recent joint research with Charles Fefferman established a principle that enables the existence of a Lipschitz selection for $F$, which is a mapping $f:{\mathcal M}\to X$ that satisfies $f(x)\in F(x)$ for every $x\in{\mathcal M}$. This paper presents alternative proofs for the existence of a Lipschitz selection under two specific conditions. Firstly, when $m=2$ and $X={\bf R}^{2}$, and secondly when $m=1$ and $X$ can be any choice. These proofs leverage a simple reiteration formula for the core of a set-valued mapping $G$ that satisfies $G(x)\subset F(x)$ and is Lipschitz in the Hausdorff distance. In addition, the paper presents several criteria that can be used to constructively prove the existence of a Lipschitz selection under the conditions $m=1$ and $X$ can be any choice, as well as $m=2$ and $X={\bf R}^{2}$.

Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exist unique, independent random variables $(U_1, \ldots, U_n)$ where the likelihood of $U_{i+1}$ being greater than $U_i$ is $x_i$ for $i$ ranging from 1 to n-1, and the likelihood of $U_1$ being greater than $U_n$ is $x_n$. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find the exact values of $p_3$ and $p_3^*$, and establish upper and lower limits for $p_n$ in cases where n is 4 or greater, indicating a probability approaching 1 as n increases without bound. Our research also identifies the specific probability distribution associated with the smallest, central, and largest components of a 'cyclic' triple.

Many software systems have adjustable settings through run-time options, such as input parameters, allowing users to modify them to fulfill different purposes, such as reducing the system's footprint or improving security, yet these configurations often have limited or no relevance in other scenarios. A notable example includes Android apps, which often have varied system settings that can impact performance, but these settings are usually unnecessary in other situations, leading to a waste of computational resources and energy if not optimized properly. By addressing this issue, we propose a method to optimize Android apps by adjusting system settings to their most efficient values, which is feasible without requiring source code access or modification, which is often impractical in real-world scenarios. Our goal is to identify the optimal setting for each parameter, which could significantly improve the app's binary size, overall system speed, and other critical characteristics. Our extensive tests involve evaluating the impact of system settings on various apps, which involve different categories such as productivity, entertainment, and social media, which are popular examples found on the Google Play store. These tests involve adjusting system settings for memory, thread pool, and compression levels, which have a notable effect on the app's characteristics. Our results show that we were able to reduce the binary size, improve the system's speed, and reduce memory usage, which were drastic improvements in most cases, especially when comparing maximum and default settings. Our data indicates that we achieved a notable average reduction in binary size, as well as improved system speed and lower memory usage. These improvements

Light dark matter particles, particularly those weighing less than a GeV, offer an attractive option over heavier, weakly-interacting massive particles. Directly detecting such lightweight particles, however, poses a significant challenge. But if the recoil of a struck nucleus leads to electron ionization, even if the recoil itself is too subtle to be measured, it could still be possible to detect the released electron. This process has been found to significantly boost the sensitivity of direct detection experiments to sub-GeV dark matter. In the present, experiments set global records, and future experiments are likely to reach the cross-sections critical to understanding thermal equilibrium.

This paper proposes a method to produce the most connected pairs of qubit states
via an anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction system, resulting in maximally entangled
anti-polariton qubits. The study finds that in the initial absence of any photons,
the quantum fluctuations of the anti-Jaynes-Cummings interaction behave in the opposite
direction of the standard Jaynes-Cummings interaction process and the rate at which
these states become entangled has a similar pattern in both processes. Furthermore,
utilizing this maximally connected state and entanglement swapping, a near perfect
transfer of an atomic quantum state via quantum teleportation is demonstrated.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases by analyzing heart rate variability (HRV). However, low-resolution ECG signals, such as those obtained from mobile devices, lack the necessary detail for accurate HRV analysis. This limitation is addressed by developing an adaptive algorithm that enhances the resolution of raw ECG signals and extracts reliable BB-interval data for HRV analysis in real-time. The algorithm's performance is evaluated against expert-verified clinical HRV standards and is shown to surpass existing signal enhancement and HRV estimation methods when tested on the 2017 MIT-BIH Challenge Database.

We analyze the large deviation principle of a power variable that measures against a background noise process, acting within a multidimensional system. This power variable, which represents energy, is calculated based on the particle's transition probability from an equilibrium state, and its analysis involves both free and confined scenarios across different dimensions. Our research indicates that the rate function has a particular form, and this form can be expressed through specific functions, particularly in the free case, where it relies on the particle's starting point. Additionally, in the confined case, the rate function's asymptotic behavior is found, and its exponent is calculated across various dimensions. Notably, in the confined scenario, this rate function exhibits distinct features, displaying both a minimum and a maximum, along with a specific symmetry property.

This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, facial expressions, hand gestures, posture, and clothing variations across a range of subjects. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing 107 synchronized high-definition cameras to capture and capture high-definition footage of 772 individuals, representing various demographics and styles. Using these multi-view images, we apply advanced 3D mesh modeling to accurately reconstruct and represent diverse human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. The proposed dataset demonstrates exceptional efficiency in learning and reconstructing a complete human model, effectively supplementing existing human body expression datasets such as MPII-Gaze, Multi-PIE, Human3.6M, and Panoptic Studio datasets, which were previously limited to single viewpoints or fewer subjects. Based on HUMBI's capabilities, we outline a new benchmark challenge focused on leveraging pose data to generate highly realistic, photorealistic human body expressions in three-dimensional formats, with a total of $8$ hours of video data and corresponding annotations freely available online at https://humbi-dataset.github.io/.

Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt existing neural models to new languages with minimal modifications, as long as there's unlabeled parallel data and a loss function based on task representations. We put our framework to the test by transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages and discovered that it surpasses the performance of numerous strong baselines while matching or even exceeding state-of-the-art results obtained through more resource-intensive and complicated methods. Moreover, our framework successfully facilitates cross-lingual sentiment transfer with only a small performance loss compared to the same task in the source language.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning top rankings among human annotators.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, we've
observed that model-based methods may actually suffer when trained on multiple
tasks simultaneously. This drop in performance is attributed to the generation
of state distributions by model-free agents, which can vary significantly
across tasks. To tackle this issue, we've developed a new method that leverages
the benefits of both model-free and multi-task learning. This approach employs
a multi-task transformer model to encode raw observations and extract relevant
features on the fly. We've tested its effectiveness against a range of
single-task and multi-task continuous control benchmarks, outperforming existing
methods significantly.

We have improved the performance of heat engines working within specific timeframes, employing a time-varying energy function in conjunction with experimentally grounded limitations on the bath temperature and the scale factor. A broadly applicable geometric proof has demonstrated that the maximum efficiency in these systems can be achieved by alternating between the maximum and minimum permissible temperatures and scale factor values. For situations where the scale factor range is restricted and the system's thermal state closely matches its equilibrium values at temperature plateaus, this protocol also ensures maximum output energy production. These findings are valid for a wide range of physical systems, including an overdamped heat engine driven by a particle in an optical tweezers setup characterized by a scale factor related to the stiffness.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

We define new families of parametrized piecewise affine transformations on 2D and 3D spaces as generalized versions of the heterochaos baker map, initially developed as simplified models for unstable dimension variability in complex systems. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches.

Following the groundbreaking detection of the Higgs boson in 2012, the field of particle physics has entered an exciting period. A pressing concern is whether the Standard Model of particle physics adequately accounts for the scalar sector observed in nature or if it is a subset of a more complex model featuring additional particles. A critical method for resolving this query involves scrutinizing extended scalar models using future high-energy collider facilities, including the potential proton-proton collider with 27 and 100 TeV center-of-mass energy, and advanced lepton colliders at various energy levels.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis.

Recommender Systems built with Collaborative Filtering (CF), the dominant method, have become an integral part of our daily lives as consumers. However, their limitations become apparent when dealing with recommendation data due to the complexities and idiosyncrasies of user preferences. Researchers attempted to overcome these challenges by integrating CF with Biclustering techniques. This research aims to evaluate the efficacy of Biclustering approaches for CF, analyzing various algorithmic decisions, and identifies CF with Biclustering as a promising field of study. As a contribution, the authors propose CBiClus, the first comprehensive framework to address CF with Biclustering, providing a systematic basis for future development and guidance for practitioners.

Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that distinguish planetary signals from stellar noises is essential. We used data from the Kepler telescope, combining stellar activity features and binary orbital characteristics, to develop a new classifier for identifying planetary candidates. Unlike previous studies, our activity indicators were selected using unsupervised learning, providing a fresh perspective on the problem. The results show that our multi-dimensional classifier outperforms existing ones and identifies novel features associated with planetary candidates. The method's effectiveness was verified by cross-validation and further validated using data from the K2 telescope, showcasing its broad applicability.

To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising as temperatures decrease in proportion to T^(2r-1), with r defined as the exponential product of the resistance and a universal constant divided by the Planck's constant (all values below 1/2), non-Majorana-induced zero-energy peaks fragment into two separate peaks at non-zero temperatures, displaying varying conductance in relation to temperature by way of a power law. Furthermore, tunneling associated with a Majorana mode falls within the same broad class of universal behaviors as does the case for unstable critical points with a non-Majorana mode when it comes to conductance's variation with resistance.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles are applicable to these operations. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of identifying a unique solution. Conversely, our research aims to harness style-specific information, extracting it from paired images to condense into a two or three-dimensional vector, resulting in a more efficient and understandable framework for style-based image editing. By representing the relationship between global color tones across paired images as a flow conditioned on the polynomial characteristics of the image pixels, our technique proves superior to other low-dimensional encoding methods, ultimately achieving accuracy ratings of 90.66% and 81.81% on the widely used PyTSS and SIBR datasets, respectively.

This technical report showcases the winning model of the AQTC task, recently introduced in the LOVEU challenge at CVPR 2022, where experts faced significant challenges in processing multi-step responses, multiple modalities, and dynamic button representations within video content. To overcome this, we developed a novel context-grounding module that enhances feature mapping using attention mechanisms. We further explored the effects of varying button counts, conducted ablation studies on different network architectures and video feature types, and attained a 2nd place ranking overall in the LOVEU track 3 competition.
