Notably, we achieved a 1st place ranking in two of the four evaluation metrics. Our open-source code is accessible via the repository link at https://github.com/jaykim9870/CVPR-22_LOVEU_unipyler.

This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at low altitudes, their settling rates are influenced by a combination of lift and drag, resulting in unique settling paths that are linked to the turbulence patterns above the ground, which in turn are affected by the snowflakes' response to updrafts and drafts. Our findings show that at high winds, the largest snowflakes tend to concentrate in specific areas, creating a snow-covered surface that is uneven and fragmented, contrasting with the uniform snow layers that form under calmer conditions, where smaller snowflakes create a more even base for accumulation.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, incorporating it into robotic decision-making systems has been a challenge due to the high computational costs associated with maintaining a highly detailed model of the environment. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages the power of cloud computing to efficiently handle active inference-driven robotic control. This cloud-based robotic control system relies on a distributed computing framework, allowing it to tackle complex optimization problems and generate precise control commands in near real-time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our cloud-based implementation by successfully navigating a mobile robot through a simulated environment, and showcase its capabilities on the AirSim virtual reality simulator.

In experimental facilities specializing in high energy physics, nuclear physics, and cosmology, the task of processing large amounts of data in real-time is proving to be a substantial hurdle. As an alternative to standard compression methods, the use of machine learning algorithms has gained attention for real-time data reduction. Yet, data sets generated from scientific endeavors often comprise vast 3D data volumes characterized by significant portions of zeroes, non-uniform distribution of values, and high generation rates. Consequently, direct applications of popular compression methods along with standard compression methods yield unsatisfactory results. Therefore, to overcome these complications, the concept of Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE) is developed to tackle the challenges posed by the unique properties of these data volumes by addressing both regression and sparsity simultaneously through the utilization of a dual-head architecture. The proposed AE variant produces superior results in terms of compression ratio, compression throughput, and decomposition quality when evaluated against competing approaches, showcasing its efficacy through experiments involving diverse data sets and scenarios.

Utilizing Finzi's gravity theory that enhances interactions at large scales, we analyze galaxy clusters from a thermodynamic perspective, establishing a statistical model to derive thermodynamic equations and comparing clustering behavior with Newtonian gravity. We also explore the general distribution function's behavior as the clustering parameter varies in strength, with the finding that phase transitions are feasible, albeit hierarchically organized.

A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from strictly convex point sets in the plane. In this study, researchers explore a specific type of problem associated with cghs: saturation problems that correspond to earlier studied extremal issues. Using a mathematical approach, the study determines the maximum capacity of certain geometrically separated groups of points and establishes an exact value for a specific instance, as well as approximate values for seven out of eight possible geometric hypergraph configurations up to a specific level of accuracy, and a related but less accurate figure for the eighth configuration.

To gain a better understanding of the relative contributions of different processes, the angular distributions and energy spectra of $\alpha$ and deuterons resulting from breakup, transfer, and incomplete fusion have been measured and calculated. Cross-sections for the $^6$Li + $^{51}$V system were measured at energies near the Coulomb barrier, with experiments indicating that the angular distributions of $\alpha$ and deuterons exhibit a characteristic pattern. Calculations employing a coupled reaction cross-section method further revealed the dominant processes contributing to the observed $\alpha$ and deuteron yields. It was found that the first excited state of the target nucleus $^{51}$V plays a crucial role in determining the reaction cross-sections. Data indicating the influence of an energetic gateway state in the target are also presented, with analysis showing that the yield of this gateway state through the present reaction is much lower than that observed in the Bergholt-Semkow effect involving a different target nucleus, $^{27}$Al.

A previously overlooked ability in bio-inspired snake robots is dynamic vertical climbing. A novel locomotion technique mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's movement has been discovered, which enables a robot to navigate on flat surfaces while climbing at near-vertical inclines. A simplified model has been created to analyze the correlation between robot motion and actuation, resulting in the development of a new, adaptable robot inspired by the Pacific Lamprey. The new robot, called Trident, successfully demonstrates dynamic vertical climbing at speeds of up to 4.8 cm/s and can also move horizontally at 9 cm/s. Furthermore, its climbing strides can be 14% longer than the Pacific Lamprey's, making this innovative design a promising approach for robots navigating steep surfaces with limited support points.

This paper outlines a novel probabilistic framework designed to identify the most effective combinations of treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune response. An Itō stochastic process models the colon cancer dynamics, whose probabilistic evolution is governed by the Fokker-Planck equation. To identify optimal treatment combinations, an open-loop control optimization issue is proposed. Simulation results demonstrating the use of Doxorubicin chemotherapy and IL-2 immunotherapy validate the introduced framework.

Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Analytically derived expressions demonstrate how the network's overall AoI and throughput are affected under complex spatio-temporal interference. Furthermore, a neural network is designed to learn an optimal mapping between geographical locations and scheduling parameters under a random policy, eliminating the need for Channel State Information (CSI) after training. Additionally, a novel method is proposed to back-propagate the loss through the network, which enables efficient learning. Experimental results show that the proposed neural network achieves near-optimal performance comparable to the local optimal algorithm with significantly higher computational requirements. This research provides insights into the performance trade-off between data freshness and throughput in wireless D2D communications.

Moffatt first discussed the concept of helicity in a fluid without viscosity in reference [25] and explored its preservation in the case of barotropic, compressible flow with smooth solutions. This paper demonstrates that weak solutions to this system in a specific mathematical space ensure the conservation of helicity. Additionally, similar results were found for both homogeneous incompressible Euler equations and the surface quasi-geostrophic equation.

The researchers in a particular study extended the solutions found in complex geometric optics to a related system of equations, which was initially investigated in contexts of electrical impedance tomography and the integrable Davey-Stewartson II equations, focusing particularly on the large spectral parameter $k$ in a specified reference \cite{KlSjSt20}. They now examined how this work can be applied to the reflection coefficient and derived new asymptotic formulas for specific domains with potential functions and smooth, strictly convex boundaries.

Calculations involving the orbital dynamics of merging compact binary systems,
including higher-order effects of gravitational wave radiation, reveal that late-time
eccentricities of inspiraling binaries are typically underestimated by standard
models by up to 30 percent for heavy systems like 300-solar-mass binaries at
10 Hz, and less so for lighter binaries. By incorporating more refined equations,
a novel, accurate analytic formula for eccentricities at late times is formulated.
Furthermore, this model's results remain largely insensitive to the masses of the
binary components, with deviations below two percent, and generalizes previous
work by Peters and Mathews.

Achieving high efficiency in free-electron lasers (FEL) is crucial for their optimal performance.  The "hosing" effect, a common problem that impairs the laser's quality by creating tunable spectral modes, has long been a challenge for FEL developers.  However, these modes can also serve as effective taps to enhance the laser's filling factor and overall efficiency.  We've adapted the "hosing" effect into a practical optimization strategy, known as SOHO, which manipulates the electron and radiation axes misalignments to maximize the laser's efficiency.  By applying SOHO to two separate simulations, one using the standard undulator and another using the unique properties of the Coherent X-ray source for Bio-Medical applications (LEXBMA), we've successfully improved the laser's efficiency by as much as 30% and 50% respectively, while also reducing the required filling factor by a factor of 10 to 20.  The SOHO strategy demonstrates great promise for optimizing FEL efficiency in various configurations.

Event identification is crucial for informed decision-making in graph data analysis systems.  Graph-based machine learning has made notable advancements lately, but detecting events in evolving networks still poses difficulties for current frameworks. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes.  To address these limitations, we propose a new approach, called DyGED, for recognizing events in evolving networks using a combination of temporal self-attention and structural awareness.  Through extensive testing with diverse datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternative methods in accuracy, achieving up to an 8.5% improvement.  Notably, it also offers improved scalability compared to the best-performing models, along with insightful case studies that highlight its key features.

The solutions of the Guderley problem involving an imploding shock wave in an ideal gas are examined, focusing on how a power law initial density distribution affects the accelerating shock. This is achieved through in-depth analysis of self-similar solutions and their similarity exponents under different symmetry conditions and varying parameters of adiabatic index and spatial density exponent. Moreover, we show how these theoretical solutions can be accurately reproduced in Lagrangian hydrodynamic simulations, thereby validating and verifying these codes for a range of scenarios.

The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties.

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization.

In the context of zero-error source coding, our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage and has been extensively studied. In contrast, we examine a more general scenario where the adversary follows a different model, making a single guess but unable to perfectly synchronize with the true sequence. This analysis reveals that determining this quantity is no easier than determining the maximal leakage and it can be computed efficiently in specific instances, such as when the confusion graph is a tree or in the case of Markov sources. Additionally, we show that the leakage in these two scenarios is related and can be bounded by a constant factor multiple of the maximal leakage.

Deep learning-trained generative models can function as a prior in under-determined inverse problems such as generating images from limited measurements, like a sparse dataset. A new hierarchical generative model called MrSARP is introduced in this research, specifically designed for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) image generation, to produce SAR images at various resolutions simultaneously. The MrSARP model is trained alongside a discriminator that assesses multiple-resolution images together to verify their realism, representing a target at various resolutions. The study demonstrates the applicability of the MrSARP deep generative model in retrieving high-resolution images from lower resolution images of the same target. The cost function of the model is modified to improve its ability to recover input parameters based on multiple-resolution images. The performance of the model is assessed using conventional super-resolution error metrics on simulated data and is compared with conventional up-sampling and image sharpening methods that utilize sparsity.

A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm variant employs a combined quantum-classical strategy to achieve approximate solutions for complex optimization issues.  To optimize a quantum circuit's parameters, we utilize a Bayesian approach as an auxiliary routine, evaluating its efficiency in contrast with alternative global optimizers.  The proposed technique leads to considerable reductions in circuit access frequency, typically the costliest QAOA component.  The framework performs well even at slow circuit repetition rates and with minimal quantum circuit measurements, yielding a reliable energy estimate.  Moreover, we investigate how our approach handles noise during circuit operation, discovering that for short circuits it remains resistant to disturbances.  The outcome of these findings supports the use of the suggested method as an adaptable tool to exploit the mixed capabilities of QAOA within imperfect quantum devices.

A versatile method has been devised for determining the overlap area between two ellipses. The proposed approach relies on computing segment areas between the two ellipses, using a secant line that intersects each ellipse at given points. The Gauss-Green formula enables calculation of an ellipse sector area, with a triangle either added to or subtracted from this sector area to obtain the segment area. For calculating the overlap area of two ellipses, the areas of relevant sectors and polygons are combined. The algorithm identifies the intersection points of two general ellipses by utilizing Ferrari's quartic formula to solve a resulting polynomial formed by combining the two ellipse equations, allowing for handling all cases of intersection points, including none, one, two, three, or four points. The proposed method has been implemented in C and validated through numerous tests with diverse input ellipses, demonstrating its efficiency for applications involving multiple overlap area calculations in simulations.

Building upon the work by Wang et al. (2020) for reinforcement learning, we examine the continuous-time counterpart of Q-learning under the entropy-regularized exploratory process framework. To handle the collapse of the traditional Q-function in continuous time, we derive a first-order approximation and introduce the term "small q-function". The q-function has connections to both the instantaneous advantage rate function and the Hamiltonian. We develop a continuous-time "learning equation" for q-learning, analogous to the Bellman equation, and establish its uniqueness, as well as the stability of the corresponding value function. We also demonstrate that initial exploratory biases can be eliminated, leading to stable convergence, and use our results to address policy optimization. The theoretical findings are accompanied by numerical simulations, illustrating the effectiveness of our models.

Quantum magnets' dynamical structure factor is a critical measurement, but making predictions for multi-dimensional models like Hubbard is complicated due to computational and theoretical constraints. We investigated magnetic excitations of the Hubbard model on a triangular lattice with longer-range hopping. Beginning with the 120-degree and striped patterns of magnetism, we used the self-consistent random phase approximation to determine magnon frequencies. We discovered a correlation in the striped phase related to a long-standing theoretical issue from the analogous Heisenberg model, where quantum fluctuations stabilize this pattern. We were able to outline the entire phase diagram using this new understanding and our results surprisingly matched recent numerical research. We compared our results with data on real triangular lattice materials and explored the link to a theoretically proposed state known as the chiral spin liquid phase.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility and metallic streak artifacts in CT scans) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents an advanced and precise method that leverages in-depth anatomical knowledge of the spine to aid in accurate vertebrae localization and identification. By employing a novel key point localization model, vertebrae center activation maps are generated, which are then adjusted along the spine's central axis to produce optimized activation maps that can be aggregated into 1-dimensional activation signals. Building upon this, an anatomically-constrained optimization module is integrated to jointly determine the optimal positions of the vertebrae. The optimization is performed under a flexible constraint that ensures the distance between vertebrae and a rigid constraint that maintains consecutive vertebrae indices. Upon being evaluated using a well-established public dataset consisting of 302 CT images characterized by significant spinal pathologies, the proposed method achieved the highest identification rate of 97.4% and surpassed the best comparable approach, which reported an identification rate of 94.7%, by significantly reducing the relative error rate.

Stochastic thermodynamics leverages Markovian jump processes to simulate spontaneous changes between quantifiable microscopic states. The flow rates of physical processes are calculated from the anti-symmetric transition measures defined on the network of states. The statistical behavior of these flow rates can be represented by normalized cumulants. This study applies the mathematical and topological structure of Markovian models to demonstrate the gauge invariance of the normalized cumulant-generating function. By taking advantage of this invariance, we have developed a streamlined method for the practical calculation of asymptotic averages and correlation functions. This method also generalizes the existing approach to the average entropy production rate, while providing a unified framework for the analysis of deterministic and stochastic models.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Two piezoelectric materials placed near each other can transfer energy across an intervening vacuum gap by transmitting acoustic waves. Our research provides a mathematical explanation for how this energy transfer occurs, and reveals that specific conditions allow for complete transmission of these waves. This finding holds true for a limited range of frequencies and distances between the materials, and can be observed within a narrow range of angles. Furthermore, we analyzed how to optimize the design of these gap structures to enhance energy transmission.

We explore a cutting-edge method for optically manipulating polariton condensates at a microscale, relying on highly coherent fluids of semiconductor-based light-emitting systems. Theoretical research indicates that modern spatial light manipulation technologies can be employed to redirect and concentrate these polariton condensates away from their initial sources of excitation. By strategically modulating non-resonant energy beams, an underlying exciton reservoir is generated which red-shifts and intensifies the polariton emission, allowing the formation of micro-scale lens-shaped structures that can steer polariton wave propagation. Multiple approaches are suggested for controlling polariton flow and demonstrate the feasibility of producing robust and localized light-emitting systems isolated from negative reservoir-induced effects.

The disintegrating exoplanet K2-22b displays erratic patterns in transit best attributed to a dissipating debris cloud, with the formation process of this debris still unknown. Analyzing grain size and sublimation rate is essential in comprehending the environment that contributes to planetary disintegration. In this study, dual photometric data obtained through the Large Binocular Telescope, with wavelengths of 0.48 and 2.1 microns, are presented during a period of reduced dust activity, revealing a refined upper limit of the planet's radius of approximately 4500 km. Medium-depth transit observations also suggest particle sizes ranging from 0.5 to 1 micron, suggesting extremely high mass loss rates of about 3e8 kg/s, coherent with hydrodynamic escape theories. In contrast, explosive volcanic eruptions or other mechanisms generating this activity would demand exceptional geological activity levels. Combining these results with the maximum possible planetary size, our findings estimate the remaining lifespan of the exoplanet at approximately 370 million years; conversely, incorporating predictions from hydrodynamical simulations yields a remarkably reduced lifespan of only 21 million years.

We develop a novel algebro-geometric approach to studying the Milnor fibration and establish a significant condition for holomorphic function deformations to maintain the Milnor fibration intact. In consequence, we derive a strategy to divide the space of polynomials with a specified degree into discrete, localized segments where the diffeomorphism of the Milnor fibration remains unchanged within each category.

Daany is an open-source, cross-platform C# library focused on data analytics and linear algebra. Designed for.NET environments, this tool facilitates data preparation, feature engineering, and other data transformation operations. Developed atop.NET Standard 2.1 and compatible with.NET Core 3.0+, Daany consists of multiple VS projects that can be easily installed as a NuGet package. At its core, Daany utilizes the DataFrame data structure, complemented by data science and linear algebra capabilities, including time series decomposition (SSA, STL, ARIMA) and optimization methods (SGD). The library also integrates matrix and vector operations, as well as data plotting functionality. Daany's implementation bears similarities to Python's Pandas library. This guide serves as a comprehensive developer manual, outlining Daany's features, functionality, and usage, as well as a listing of related papers.

I challenge the conventional view of Galileo's influence on science by suggesting that he struggled with mathematical proficiency. This perceived weakness drove him to focus on experimentation and empiricism, as well as embracing the telescope's capabilities. His emphasis on hands-on research, which is often credited as an innovative aspect of his scientific approach, might actually be a consequence of his inability to make meaningful mathematical contributions. Similarly, his extensive discussion of basic scientific principles was, arguably, an outcome of his limitations in mathematics, as they often say "those who can't do, teach." It is proposed that Galileo's scientific vision, which is typically viewed as groundbreaking, was actually based on long-established ideas from mathematicians. The main difference lies in that Galileo chose to articulate these ideas in philosophical writing, as his mathematical colleagues were too preoccupied with advancing scientific work to bother doing the same.

The increasing popularity of Tsallis' thermodynamic framework is largely attributed to its capability to describe phenomena exhibiting anomalous thermal properties, which requires adherence to generalized thermal equilibrium. Our study focuses on examining non-Gaussian influences on Saha's ionization through the application of Tsallis statistics. We addressed this challenge by generalizing the number density with a non-Gaussian distribution based on Fermi-Dirac theory and then formulated the Saha equation for cosmological recombination. Our analysis reveals two novel non-Gaussian impacts:  the establishment of two distinct equilibrium conditions and the identification of a hydrogen binding energy related to q-value. Our results demonstrate that a minute 'a-parameter' is required to generate continuous shifts in binding energy. We further discovered symmetrical behavior around standard binding energy. Using the q-value, we investigated other hydrogen energy levels, determining the relationship between the 'a-parameter' and temperature for these levels. Our study has significant implications for understanding non-Gaussian effects on deuterium bottlenecks, recombination, and particle-antiparticle excess.

The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model, MHD simulations paired with fixed embedded PIC regions, and full PIC simulations. The examination of reconnection rates, magnetic island spacings, and ion dynamics within these scenarios indicates good agreement among the models, with notably large adaptable PIC regions required within the MHD domain to achieve such convergence.

This document provides a summary of the content from a course held at Stanford University in the spring of 2018.  The course brings together insights from cognitive neuroscience and systems neuroscience to create intelligent systems by combining human and machine intelligence.  The course uses a tangible example - a digital assistant that learns and evolves through ongoing conversations with an experienced software engineer while beginning as an effective analytical and problem-solving tool.  Over time, these intelligent assistants develop essential thinking strategies and learn to rely on intuition through lessons learned from their expert counterparts.  As a result, these intelligent assistants become capable of working side-by-side as equal partners - serving as cognitive enhancements and digital prostheses that help their human partners make informed decisions and access powerful computing tools more efficiently.
